div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

There is no doubt that, for a little while at least, the ' tri-car is to enjoy a certain amount of public favour, although, personally, we du not believe that such popu- larity will be long-lived. The recent show at Islington, I however, indicated that a good many makers are quite prepared to meet the present demand for this type of I vehicle, and we noticed ttiat several patterns contained 1 some rather striking designs, both in details connected with the motor itself and also with-the carriage portion of the machine.

In connecticui with the latter point, two firms showed tri-cars having covered-in bodiea resembling somewhat in general appearance a small governess car, or the body work of a little Yfabley or. Whilst not being particu- larly handsome, so far as mere looks were concerned, this would certainly ensure the passenger being properly protected against draughts, which, however well pro- vided he or she may be with rugs, cannot be altogether overcome upon the ordinary type of fore-carriage.

Another advance in tri-car rsonstruction generally is the frequent adoption of a multi-speed gear. The control, too, is much improved, many of these vehicles being fitted with wheel steering, and having the throttle, air, and ignition levers placed on the steering columns. Further, more often than not, the driver is now provided with a comfortable little seat in place of the saddle with which he was formerly expected to be content.

The motor bicycles, turned our by the best firms, are' greatly'improved in many respects, although it is true that a few new makers of this class of machine, who made their first bow to the public during the last year,apparently have had no greater object in viewthan the reduction of the total weight at almost any cost.in one instance, WA observed a motor attached to the frame of a bicycle that was of quite ordinary construc- tion, save that it was somewhat weaker than would have been passed by a reputable firm for a good pedal- bicycle. The importance of weight in the right place does not always appear to be appreciated by those who rush blind-folded into the manufacture of a class of goods of which they know nothing.

There were one or two devices connected with wheels %end intended to disperse with the use of pneumatic res displayed at the Stanley show. The most inter- esting, and certainly the most practical, was the Halle Spring Wheel, which is constructed upon original lines that quite avoid the usual objections to which this class of wheel has hitherto been exposed. No d6ubt there is a very strong feeling at the present time amongst motorists that something must be done to secure im- munity from the troubles generally resultant from the use of pneumatics, and we noticed that the " Thor " car, which is specially sprung, and fitted with solid tyles, received considerable attention from the public. Indeed, Mr. Moffat Ford tells us that the enquiries he has received concerning his own anti-pneumatic suspen- sion point to the fact that,unless some decisive step be taken by the tyre companies, there will be a very marked tendency to adopt some such device and be done with the never-ending worry and expense of pneumatics

A very nice little vulcaniser, by the way, was shewn for pneumatic tyres at the Agricultural Hall, being of a. size that would be quite easily packed away with sun- dries in the tool-box of a car. Both inner tubes and also outer covers can be mended by its aid, and, as the. price asked for it is extremely low,it would practically pay for itself very speedily.

1 The Royal Family at Sandringham.—The King and Queen had nearly all their children and grandchildren with them at Sandringham for the celebration of Her Majesty's birthday this week, the gathering including Princess Charles of Denmark and her little son. Princess Charles will spend the winter at Appleton House near Sandringham returning to Copenhagen in . the early spring, when Prince Charles will be back from ' his cruise in the Mediterranean. The Princess has always been a great favourite in her home circle, and the King and Queen like to have her with them for the Christmas holidays. She has only recently celebrated her birthday having been born at Marlborough House in November 26th. 1869. and is therefore thirty-five years of age. Her Royal Highness was married to Prince Charles, the second son of the Crown Prince of Denmark in 1896, and their first child, Prince Alexander was born at Sandringham last year. Ormskirk Gingerbread.—Royal gitests always receive a gift of the far-famed Ormskirk gingerbread on their departure from Lathom House in Lancashire. The King received such a present when he paid a visit there some sixteen or seventeen years ago, as did also the Prince and Princess of Wales who were quite recently enter- tained by Lord and Lady Lathom at their Lancashire seat. The Lathom family can trace their descent back to Saxon times, but the present house is a compara- tively modern building, constructed in two sections, the main part being connected with the offices and servant quarters by a corridor. The house is thus less ex sz osed to the danger of fire than is the case with most of the old and historic mansions. The present Lady Isathom is one of the most talentedlmusicians in Society, and is voted quite the most delightful of hostesses. The First Spell of Winter.—The sharp touch of real old-fashioned winter has been quite a change for the King and Queen of Portugal, who in their own country are unaccustomed to such weather. The King however is of the robust type and has quite enjoyed it, whilst to Queen Amdlie, who spent her childhood in this country, our fogs and snows are nothing new. At Chatsworth the cold was intense, as it was also at Wood Norton where their Majesties spent a few days on a visit to the Duke of Orleans, Queen Am‘lie's brother. The house is situated in the Vale of Evesham and was built by the Duke's great uncle, the Duc d' Aumale, who lived there for many years. Country. House Fires.—Usually the setting in of cold weather Is accompanied by the firing of some of our historic country houses, and this year several, including the fine old Enville Hall, which was originally built in the time of Henry VIII,. have been destroyed. The loss on such occasions is more than a private one, as the contents of many of the great country houses are precious and sometimes priceless. The buildings alone are in many cases unique, for there is nothiug in the -world quite like our old manor houses,and their destruc- tion by fire often means the loss of a Raphael or a Titian, or perhaps some priceless manuscript. It is surprising that owners are not more careful in having their mansions inspected by experts, and fitted with an efficient fire apparatus. Most of the buildings are remote from towns, and they were builtat a time when there were no dangers from elect ric wires, gas escapes, and flues from tire grates creating a fierce draught. Old oak beams which were safe enough a hundred years ago become a source of danger under new conditions,as was the case at Sandringham, which from this very cause, came very near being destroyed by fire, less than a year ago. She thus runs some risk of becoming what Miss Frances Low would call, a " breadsnatcher," but though she has no occasion to work for her living, she has joinei the staff of the Children's Hospital in London. Children's Party Frocks—For dance and party frocks for young girls,nothing is better adapted than accordion- pleated Japanese silk, or soft nuns veiling, the bodice as well as the skirt being built of the same material. It is better that the bodice should befitted into a shaped waistband, as this helps to detract from anything like an ungainly appearance, which is invariably presented by growing girls. Long rucked monsquetaire gloves are worts with such frocks, in which fell elbow sleeves are usually inserted.. This is also an advantage, as amongst the young, the average girl's arms are not as a rule, her strong points.
MADGE.

ALLEGED STEALING. At Widnes, on Monday, Thomas WCormick, thirteen, 9, Elizabeth-street, was charged with stealing 441 b. weight of coal value 3d., the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company, on the 25th inst. —lnspector Cartcr, of the Railway Company, said the cy)al was similar to that lying at the Widnes Dock, The defence was that the coal had dropped from the waggon on to the line, and he had been told by a man to take it away.—The bench adjourned the case for a week, so that the parents could be'suMmoned.

Church Army Captain's Departure. Coptaia LangtAin, of St. Peter's Church Army Mission,bas this week left Warrington for Blackburn, where he will assist temporarily at Christ Church. He came to Warrington about 15 months ago, from West Essex, having been the captain in charge of a mission there for two years. During his stay in Warrington, he 'has made many friends and has done a ''(treat deal .of useful work in the parish. A men's club has been 'organized by him and is now going on satisfactorily. A teachers' preparation class has also been organized and worked by him as a new feature of the tuission work. He has had charge of St. Peter's Band of llope, and has associated himself with the Sunda y school.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 3, 1904.,
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 3, 1904.,

FASHIONS OF TO-DAY. r The first lady in the land has set us the example of wearing what best suits us in- dividually, for especially in regard to head- gear she has unwaveringly affected a neati small, close fitting toque which becomes her to perfection, and has never been known to affect any of the large or very elaborately trimmed hats which at intervals of a few years find a certain vogue. In regard to the matinee hat which has been the subject of so much ill-feeling and so many wordy contests, I see that an attempt at a compromise has been recently introduced in the form of a cap (for so one must term it for want of a more descrip- tive name) of velvet ribbon bows draped by a lace veil which also is arranged so as to form a fall down to the shoulders of the wearer. It is wide and flat in shape but sits lightly and
(Copyright.)

My uncle smokes them,- she replied to his second apology. After these preliminaries Patrick had no more trouble with this young lady. He had a varied stock of questions at command, and she answered rusdily. cable-train ran smoothly, silently, end swiflly along the lines. Londoners, who have unly had experience of such cumbersome machines of the kind as lumber through Brixton, can have no idea of the fairy cars of Australia. There von spin along with the speed and steadiness of a sledge along a frozen river. The way they go cp and down hills and round corners is positively sensa- tional to a straffer. Friendships likewise in Australia are of iniishrorin growth, while eh con- ventionalities are less oLserved than they are in England. With a young man like Patrick Traynor, nothing short of an appeal to the conductor could ha-e stopped him after this self-introduction. He had mastered the art of flirtation from the stories he had read by writers who gained their scciety experience from Sunday evening Park Duchesses. His present companion had likewise acquired her knowledge of high-bred manners from the same lofty and refined source. Therefore they got along beautifully together. , By the time they had reached Woolloomooloo he depreratory and apologetic hesitancy of Patric.k had vanii-hed, with the nunlike shyness of the maiden. By the time they reached Ocean-street she was talking to him with the simplicity of a schoolgirl confiding in an o!d friend, while his air was protective, yet. ardently respectful. All this was according to the precedent of high- toned Park etiquette on a Sunday ,evening. He bowed, drew back, advanced, becanlie bold and deferential, each instant growing mok priggishly familiar. She blushed, glanced shyly, smiled archly, waxed cold, only to pardon, and played all the tricks in her pack by turn, greatly to the delight of the other passengers. It was all so lovely, so genteel, so distinguished, so ingenuous, so innocent. By a hapey chance (one of those chances Cupid is ever managing for lovers), Patrick discovered that Irene Montford was also going to Double Bay. When she dismounted with his aid, it seemed only Latural that they should walk down the hill side by side, and continue their mutual confidences. She had given him her name. He addressed her as Miss Montford, sometimes inadvertently as "my dear Miss Montford," oK "my dear," without the Mont ford, and once or twice as "Irene," without her noticing the liberty. They were getting along splendidly, and Patrick was delighted with his progress. She did not call him by his Christian name, however,. at this date, although he had informed her that it was "Reginald." She always remem- bered to call him Mr. De Courcy, which surname he had also given her. "Shy little thing," thought the aristocratic detective, with triumphant complacency, "I' ll be her Reggie' before the moon rises, I vow." And he was. By the time the round moon appeared above the rum trees she had consented to sail with him back to Pott's Point, where her mother lived. He had gallantly given her tea at the Double Bay refreshment, rooms, and walked with her after- wards through the short gloaming and under the lustrous stars. They were no longer strangers by the hour they sat at tea. She told him about her people, in the most artless fashion, while he responded by spinning a tale of family greatness that must have satisfied the aspirations of any lady. Her mother was pocr, but Irene had -a wealthy uncle, who loaded her with presents of jewellery. He was a bachelor, and she was his nearest relative after her mother. All these items she told her admirer, with the most unaffected innocence, as they walked together under the stars. The noble and gentlemanly Patrick began to have a little regret that he had not divulged his true name - and position when he learnt her future prospects. He had only meant a little aristocratic pastime when he began this flirtation; to puss a pleasant afternoon and evening with a most charming girl, and then part with her as he had parted with so many before, lightly and affably. It would be something for the little thing to remember grate- fully aft erwavds, like a glimpse of paradise. Something to wake Double Bay for ever sacred to her, where she had listened to the rare music of his modulated voice; blushed under his masterful gaze; trembled within his strong arms, and glowed with his well-trained and delicate kisses. Ah, yes, if ever girl had cause to be grateful for the condescension and kindness of superior man, -Irene Montford was that girl, for he had piled on the agony without stint, generous young gentleman that. he was. But when the hour of parting came and he left her, with his most graceful bow, standing at the garden gate of a palatial mansion, he wished he had gone to,work on realistic instead of such romantic and fictional lines. True, they had exchanged tender vows, and she promised to meet him the next evening, which was a point gained. But, if he meant real business, as he now felt inclined, he wpurd have to make his confessiir before he could visit her people. As a true dude and bounder, he shuddered at the thought of, dropping from Reginald De Courcy, heir to a baronetcy, to plain Patrick Traynor, detective. The fact of his father being an M. F. was small consolation. Sydney members of Parliament, even although they are called by courtesy Honourable while in office, are not greatly respected, even by day labourers. However, he consoled himself, as he sauntered lazily away from that witching form. Ske had experienced the charm of hits faseinations, and once undcr the witchery of that spell, no female could ever bresk free. He would meet her again secretly, and forge the fetters so firmly round. her tender heart that she would forgive everything rather than bear to part with him. "I'll evade her attempts to introduce me to her people until she can introduce me in my own name. Then it will be all plain sailing. Dear little girl, she is a stunner, and interests me greatly. Now for home, and a quiet spoke while I study up my case."

Irene bfontford leant against the closed gate, and sent kisses after her departing lover each time he turned to wave his hand. While his long back was towards her, however,-she only watched it. The full moon shone vividly upon her shapely figure awl bright dress,' but her hat being a broad one, it buried the biggest half of her face in deep shadow. Only a small portion of her chin shone out of the darkness; her expression therefore was lost. But her attitude was most romantic and sentimental. After the detective had disappeared in the distanee, she still listened and looked long after his steps had ceased to ring on the hard, echoing road. Then, satisfied that he was gone beyond any likelihood of returning, she swiftly left the gate and went off in the opposite direction. A cab passing, she hailed it, and was driven to one of the side streets of Paddington. Here she entered a cottage by the kitchen door, and was hailed by several female voices. Half a dozen young ladies were having .supper when she entered, and the attendant waiting upon them was a Chinaman. "Well, Daisy, how have you got ..on with the Dude Tee?" they inquired with one voice. ( "All right," replied the innocent Irene Montford. "He gave me a sham name, of course, but managed .to put the blunders on him. I have got his papers also, so that he won't be able, to move until I have trapped and muzzled him. Hand me a grog. Wang, for I am dead tired of this even- ing's fun."

div.head: USEFUL
div.p: A USEFUL

firmly on the couffeur, and is the original creation of a well-known society lady who has sought in this way to obviate the difficulties of the woman who not possessing a carriage and unable, perchance, to afford the luxury of a cab to and from a theatre dislikes to trust her hat to the scant mercies of a cloak-room attendant and is therefore in a dilemma as to what to do with the necessary but incon- venient headgear, upon whose removal the manager and public alike insist. It is often this very bat question which comes between the girl of small means and many little enjoy- ments, and it is therefore to be hoped that some compromise will be arrived at and the theatre toque will be generally recognised. My first sketch does not illustrate any of these millinery creations which , are designed for festive occasions, but sets forth the fascina- tions of a smart and yet useful every day hat of simple style and of an inexpensive descrip- tion. It is made of a silky surfaced felt and is trimmed by a couple of quills, the ends of which are thrust through the brim. There are many pretty felt flop hats which can be modelled into fashionable shapes by the home milliner who is clever enough to take careful stock of the best models displayed in the windows of the smartest shops and make up her raw materials into as close an imitation of

div.head: PRErn: GOWN.
div.p: A PRErn: GOWN.

the model hat as possible. It is always advis- able in such cases aite, a little preliminary practise has been gone through with the aid of half-worn and almost discarded pieces of millinery to select good materials and to care- fully avoid undertaking anything at all very elaborate or ambitious. Fix upon a really pretty hat which catches the eye at once by reason of its smart simplicity, for it ,requires the skilful touch of a trained and much ex- perienced milliner to give the correct caehet to an elaborate piece of headgear and .to select and blend the colours so as to form the har- mony which reaps its reward of general admiration. Whereas the more inexperienced and humble imitator may find herself landed in pitfalls of various characters of whose existence she had never dreamt. This is no doubt the reason, par excellence, of the long life of the black picture hat, for with black the difficulties are greatly reduced and the possessor of some good ostrich feathers will not find the task of evolving a charming and becoming piece cf headgear at all a difficult one.

My second illustration introduces a charm- ing tea gown of such, a simple style as to almost threaten its classification as a dressing gown of artistic possibiliiies. The gown itself is of .a thick woolly surfaced material in a soft blurred pattern in which • numerous artistic tones are blended and harinonised. The chief
feature of the gown is, of course, the deep cane-W collar of sof t thick white silk finished by sundry small tuckings from which a full trill of soft lace falls king in design
AN AFTERNOON I3LUUSE.

that which forms a soft fall over the hands, but is wider than that which finishes the collar. The sleeves are full, but are caught in a little below the elbolys forming 'a pouch. A good street dress will wear much longer if changed immediately .--one gets home for a comfortable • loose-fitting gown. As strong contrast to the afore described, gown, the subject of my last sketch will appeal to those who never prefer to adopt the lazy lounging mode, while even to those who do the charms of the afternoon blouse will meet with due appreciation. The mode is an original one and is yet expressed on the linee which fashion has approved of recently as the most modish. The line of the shoulder is carefully defined and followed„ for there is nothing in the long close-fitting yoke of lace to conceal the grace- ful curves Of neck and throat. The lace is lined by silk, and the blouse itself is of soft silk fulled into a band of lace insertion which extends across the upper arm and after pass- ing over the bust is brought down to the waisti . _ Cogurrts,

div.head: YARD OF RIBBON
div.p: YARD OF RIBBON
By HUME NISBET, inthor of "Bail Up," "The Revenge of Valerie," "A Sweet Sinner," "The Rebel
Chief," "The Swampers," Sm.
Patrick Traynor, detective, took his seat in the tram-car at Pitt-street for a run out to Double

Bay. - He was a good-looking and strapping young Irish-Colonial, not yet twenty-eight, who had been raised from the Sydney Constabulary into the detective force. That he had a fair opinion of his own mental gifts and external attractions must be taken for granted, considering the race he sprang from, and the ardent land of his birth.. Self- depreciatien is not the common drawback of an Irish-Colonial, and humility is a vice discouraged in the service. The father of Patrick was a member of the Sydney Assembly, that House where good and refined manners are cultivated; therefore it was to be expected that the son should shine in those out- ward observances whereby gentlemen are generally recognised. As the elder Traynor was on the side of Government, influence had not been wanting to advance the young man in his chosen career. He had a sufficiency of money at his command, there- fore he always dressed in the most up-to-date New South Wales :fashion of men about toe n. By watching closely the latest arrivals from England and reading carefully the so-called society magazines, he did his best to live up to the characteristics of the gentlemen he knew and read about. He assiduously cultivated the lazy saunter, with the general languid weariness and gentle inso- lence, that are supposed to mark the high-toned club swell of the present day. He did his utmost to curb his natural Hibernian impetuosity, and never to appear interested nor curious about any- thing, no matter how startling it was. He had learnt to lift his hat with the latest flourish, and shake harlds at the proper elevation; in fact, as far as he could, he moulded his behaviour on the most approved pattern of cadism at his disposal. That he was not quite all affectation, insolence, and conceit, was proved by the fact that he had been entrusted with a few rather ticklish cases, and carried them to a successful issue. These were not great cases certainly, and chance had favoured the young detective, yet they were sufficient to wint commendation from his superiors, and increase his own innate conviction that he was a genius in the right place, if limited in his field of action. Some men become puffed up and swollen-headed when they arrive at the point of conviction that they are invincible masters and geniuses, who have reached the apex of human experience and acute- ness, and thus become intolerable boasters. Patrick Traynor was saved from this gabbling parade of his innate opinions through his affecta- tion. He seldom bounced in words, as this would entail the relinquishment of that studied air of weary calm which lie valued so highly. He only looked his superiority and self-approval. On this afternoon, eye-glass over eye and cigarette held daintily between his saffron-stained finger-tips, he watched the approaching cable-tram slow down, with his most wearied air. Yet, although outwardly indifferent, inwardly he felt as elated and proud as conscious merit can be, when it has been recognised. He had just interviewed his chief, and been entrusted with an undertaking which, if successful, would spread his fame over the borders of New South Wal, s. If his chief had any doubts, 1-i.trick Traynor had none as to his capabilities of running his quarry to earth. What had puzzled older hands appeared an easy game for hint to play. He was young, cool, daring and artful. He would soon prove that he had not studied the works of Edgar Allan Poe, Wilkie Collins, Gaboriau, and their more modern imitators for nothing. He would unravel the conundrunr in no time. At the present moment he was going for a rapid, spin on the cable-tram, and a good think on the sunlit sands of Double Bay. He would thus focus his plan of action, and then proceed to work in his customary methodical manner. The reports of the case were in his bietst-pocket, as yet unread. He had received his verbal instructions ; therefore there was nothing else to do at present except enjoy himself. . In order to see a man properly, a young man particularly, it is strictly necessary to look at him from two points of view. First, as he appears to himself, and second, as he appears to the ordinary spectator. The presentiment of Patrick Traynor, as it appeared to himself, was that of a blond, tall, nobly-formed and most distinguished-looking gentleman of the world, with irresistible manners, mairsrl smile, airiest regal dignity when he chose to be ignifled, ni d iii at bewitching Of ey s. He fe t genuii j gratefut for these and the outer items which made him such a superior person to others, and , this knowledge of hi:2 own gifts rendered him generally, if somewhat intolerably, urbane. To disinterested outsiders he appeared an over- dressed bdunder of the inkist aggressive type; his superciliousness, impenetrable affability and wearied condescension were always trying to sort tempers. His collars, cuffs, spats. eye-glass and t -twisted moustache were quite esiough in them- selves to raise Cain in most bosoms, without that carefully worn, lofty and contented smirk with which he regarded strangers. He greatly enjoyed contemplating his person in mirrors, and practising poses and expressions; and when satisfied with the yose and expression he used them for ths benefit of his fellow-creatures, especially the youthful feminine members of his race. This, of course. was only natural in a bird of his species. While such birds can get credit frtiin their tailor they never become old. As he stood .in one of his favourite poses, waitisg for the train to stop, and feeling that he was a decided ornament to Pitt-street, his quick eye rot iced a remarkably pretty and tastefully- costoaned young lady, sitting by herself on the side nearest td hi:U. That 'decided him' .to forego the joy of shelving, his elegant paces by sauntering ,roind the car. He therefore languidly moved in front of her, picking his way daintily over imaginary roughnesses in the sun-laved roadway, and sat dawn gently beside her. He wits easy, yet elaborate, in his movements, as a true dude ought to be. The masculine fashion of the moment was leng=waisted, lengthy-tailed coats, with short vests, and somewhat loose, wrinkly lower gaaments. To fulfil all the obligatitrns which this ridiculous fashion demanded a young man was expected to look and behave as much like a doddering idiot as he could./ Patrick did all he could to look up to date. He raised his coat-tails carefully before he sat down. HA drew up his trousers from above the knees until the tops of his ,white spats could be seen, with an inch of striped socks. He had already abstractedly thrown portions of his voluminous skirts over the young lady's lap, and after he had re-adjusted his eye-glass and taken a meditative stare at her, while he ben6. forward and sucked the top of his cane, he remembered his cigarette and had a turn at that. His next proceeding was to snread his knees in a womanly way and fold his hands together, the gloved one under the ringed and naked hand, while he turned his head more fully towards her, and examined her more critically, like a laughing jackass looking at a butterfly. The young lady sat sedately under his examina- tion and gazed unconsciously straight in front of her at the houses they were so swiftly gliding past. She was remarkably pretty, with soft, clear com- plexion and viulet-tinted eyes. Satisfied with her profile and hat, this lordly fascinator bent his head a little more ov--r his stiff collar and glanced at her .figure and cost tune. Then apt earing to notice, for the first time, that his coat tail covered her hands, lie seized the opportunity to aplogiot in his blandest and most dulcet tones. The exquisite always begins his campaigns with a profuse apology ; sometimes he is compelled to end it with an abject one when lie encounters a lady. In the present instance, however, he was not greatly afraid of Icing rudely treated ; not that your exquisite is ever much more afraid c" this kind of treatment than is a philanthropist ...sten he proffers a tract to it beglar, both philanthropist and exquisite being too well supported by the sense of their own worthiness to be abashed at trifles. There was in the unco scionsness and demureness of this young lady an odie sympathy whim It made hint perfectly at. ease. As he tendered his apology, and gently transferred the garment extremity from her knee to 1 is leg nearest her, touching one of her , gloved hands softly, she turned her violet eyes on 1 hint and flushed prettily. A faint smile also appeared on her lips as she,sassnred him that she had not observed it. "I trust my cigarette is not objectionable?" "Not at all; I enjoy the perfume of cigarettes.

When the detective reached his rooms he was considerably nut out to find that he had lost his carefully pi epe red instructicmc. He could get another copy by applying for it, but that would involve somewhat unpleasant explanations and reflections, with possibly the present duty shifted from him. He felt. that he must lie low, and hope for a chance of either recovering the lost manuscript or procuring a copy unknown to his chief. Now, although he affected languor to the outside world, Nature had really gifted him with an energetic disposition, and he was not such a ninny as he tried to appear. His inordinate vanity was his weakest point. The first thing he did was to lay in a good supper; then he went quietly to his father's stables and saddled the best horse, without troubling the groom. Mounting, he rode back again to Double Bay, reviewing as he went along all the events of the evening. For a'moment the unworthy suspicion crossed his mind that he had been robbed of his papers by Irene. He dismissed this, however, when he re- membered how she had invited him to call upon tar ther and uncle. No. She would not have

shewn him the house, nor asked him in, if she had been guilty of such a deed. The packet must have slipped out on one of the occasions when he was playing recklessly the role of Claude Melnotte. Reaching Double Bay, he spent the midnight hour harching diligently all the spots which he had rendered sacred in the memory of his fair friend. Then he returned home to meditate on his nest step. It was the robbery of a large haberdasher's shop which he was commissioned to investigate. ahe owner of the shop was at present absent from Sydney, so that he could not be again questioned. lloweves, Patrick resolved to visit the premises that day, and get what information he could from the assistants.

"Reggie, I have only known you two days, but already I feel I can trust you absolutely, and wish for your advice. I hope you will not consider me too previous." "Command me, dearest Irene. You ought to know I can deny you nothing," answered her loverl gallantly, with his finest bow. "Well, dear, it is this. My uncle has given Ina so much jewellery that I cannot wear a quarter of it. I wish to raise some money for a certain pur- pose, and I thought I might get what I required on some of this superfluous stuff, without losing it altogether." It was early in the evening, and she was leaning on his arm as they walked under the trees of the domain. Irene looked at her knight in such a significant manner, while she pressed his arm, that he felt she wished for money of her own in order to shew her gratitude, by buying him a present. He responded promptly: "That is easily done, my dear—pledge them." She shuddered prettily as she replied hastily: "Oh, I could not do this myself, and T would die if anyone else, except you, knew that my trinkets were in any of those horrid three-ball places." He paused a moment, and then he said "Well, I don't mind doing it for you. When do you want it done ? " _ .

"At once, if possible. 0 Reggie, you are a darling! See! I can give you my bracelet and a couple of rings. They are good diamonds. Could you manage this for me at once—to-night ? " "Yes. There is a shop opposite here. If you will wait for me for a few moments, and tell me what sum you want, I'll get it for you, I daresay." "How good von are, Reggie," murmured Irene, as she placed the trinkets in his hand, and sat down on the seat he led her to. "Twenty pounds will do." He left her, and in a short time was back again with the money and a pawn-ticket, which he gave her. "Take care of the ticket, dearest, and when you wish to take them out again, I shall do that for you." That evening Irene shewed him that he need have no doubts of the future as far as her love was con- cerned. She was his adoring slave. Before they parted she consented, shyly, to go with him the next evening to the theatre. The only condition she made was, as she could not dress without explaining matters at home, that they should go to a quiet part of the house. This arrangement suited Patrick, as it would cost less, and he was not over-fond of spending money out- side himself. He left her even more delighted with his amour than ever.

Irene Montford was costumed divinely when her hero met her the following evening, and he felt proud of her. . She was in ordinar3 walking dress, but that was stylish enough to satisfy any dude. Withja gush of generosity he invited her to dine with and she accepted gracefully. Into the most fashionable restaurant he led her, outwardly wearing his most exquisite air of aristo- cratic weariness, inwardly swelling with pride at the admiring flutter which passed over his acquaint- ances who were dining there. He was supremely gratified at the sensation which this composed young lady caused amongst his fellow-bounders. He fixed upon a table where they could be well seen by everyone in the room, and then gave his orders with haughty urbanity to the waiter. They were just finishing their soup when another waiter came up with a card, which he handed to Patrick. He glanced at the card carelessly, and read the name of his client, the haberdasher. "The gent wishes to see you at once on most pressing business, sir," whispered the waiter. Patrick wanted to see the gent also, very urgently, for his chief had been growing pointed in his inquiries during the past two days. Therefore, with a bland apology to his companion, he rose slowly, and dragged his wearied limbs after the waiter. At the end of the room he found the haberdasher at a table by himself in a wild state of excitement. He was glaring at Irene with It mast unfriendly eye. Without giving the young man time to pull up his trousers he burst out impetuously: "I say, you are the detective who is looking after my affairs, ain't you?" Patrick finished his sitting down operations,. and then put up his glass and ogled the irate, red- visaged man coldly. He resented being hustled in ' this fashion. "Yes, I am managing them," at last he replied, icily. "Let me congratulate you on your success, sir. You are a smart fellow to bring her here with the evidence on her for me to identify. Now, what is your next move? You heard I was back, I suppose? That ribbon at her neck I can swear to as a piece of the stolen property, for not a yard of it has yet beeebn show in Aultralia." While the haterdasher was pouring out these words Patrick had followed both them and the angry glances with professional quickness, and now understood the whole position. Bet, than, to his acquired habits ef dudism he betrayed n. surprise, nor embarrassment. He merely played with his tooth-pick, and listened, while he looked supercilious, until the other paused for breath. Then he said, loftily: "My dear good fellow, you have guessed exactly why lam here. Thanks, awfully, for year good opinion of my poor merits and the help you have given me. Now compose yourself and finish your dinner, and leave all the rest to me. I promise you some satisfactory news to-morrow. Ta-ta. Don't stir, or you will spoil everything." He rose up and sauntered bade to the fair Irene in the same languid style in which he had come, while the haberdasher looked after him with intense admiration. After dinner he rose and led Irene Montford from the dining-room with the same easy non- chalance as ever. As they passed the haberdasher he gave him a quiet glance and a slight nod. He had matured his plans by this time. . In the hall he asked for a private room, and when Irene asked him what for, with startled eyes, he smiled gently as he looked at her and touched the ribbon at her throat.- "For your sake, my dear child." Irene followed him meek*.

- - Next day a dudish young gentleman stood on the wharf watching a steamer leaving for the north. On the deck of the steamer Irene Mont ford stood, with several other young ladies. As she waved her handkerchief to this gentleman on shore she murmured: "Ile isn't such a fool as he looks." The young gentleman was also smiling and soliloquising as he waved his hat. "But for that feminine vanity of yours, In ne, you'd have had me, 'cute as I am, and but for that pawn-ticket I'd have had you as well as the swag, my dear. So .long. It has cost me twenty pounds eight and fourpence, but I think I've made my name." Patrick Traynor stands high in the profession since that affair, even although the burglars escaped. The haberdasher got his property all back with the exception of about a yard of ribbon. [Tug END. 1,

div.p: ROR OF AUSTRIA.‘ (4) ADMIRAL' FOURNIER.

There nas been a good deal of backing ano 'fling and diplomatic delay on •the part of Russia with reference to the North Sea In- Amiry, but it was finally signed at St. Petersburg at the end of last week. The general text was already known, but it will •be seen that there are some modifications which are the result of the diplomacy of the Russian Foreign Office. The signatories to the Convention were Sir Charles Hardinge, our Ambassador to St. Petersburg, and Count I..nrnEdorff, the Russian Minister for Foreign Affairs, and it Was arranged to publish the details in both capitals simultaneously. The constitution of the Court has not been officially announced at the moment of writ- ing, but rumour has assigned the four places to be filled by English, Russian, French, and American admirals respectively to Admirals Beaumont, Kaziakoff, Fournier, and Dewey, while the Emperor of Austria will nominate the fifth and presiding member of the Ccsurt. Admiral Beaumont, our representative, is a man of fifty-seven and has seen forty-four years' service. He was on the Arctic ex- pedition of 1885-6, Naval Attache for Europe in 1882, Director of Naval Intelligence from 1894 to 1897, an A.D.C. to the late Queen from 1895-97, and subsequently in command of the Pacific Station. Admiral Dewey is, of course, a well known name after his exploits in the Spanish-American war, and the other ty,ro are prominent in their own countries. 'The Commission will meet as soon as it can be collected in Paris in the suite of rooms at the Foreign Office where the Spanish - American Treaty was adjusted. Meanwhile the Baltic Fleet is going on gaily on its way to the Far East. Since its wild explosion off the Dogger Bank it appears to have gathered sense, or at least a respect for British intentions, and with the exception of a small but disgraceful riot at Crete things haye gone on quietly. The fleet has been escorted all the way by our cruisers, and the Suez Canal Was policed all along by soldiers. The fleet is now in the Indian Ocean. and it is rumoured that the Japanese are not very far 0-9 but such a report is probably solely due to the Rusvian state of funk on the subect. It is unlikely that there will be any active opposition until they get near Japanese waters.

Mr. Leopold de Rothschild, owner of St. Amant, who went off so much after the Derby, is third, the Duke of Portland. fourth, Lord Carnarvon fifth, and Lord Rosebery sixth; and all good sportsmen will be glad to see the return of the fourth and sixth names to such prom- inence on the list. THE SAN CARLOS OPERA COMPANY.

The wonderfully successful season of the San Carlos Opera Compauy front/ Naples at i Covent Garden has ended in a blaze of triumph and has been a conspicuous success from start to finish. It was naturally an experiment and all parties concerned took a considerable *4l- hia+ _i* -is pleasant to an- nounce that it surpassed all ex- pectations. The public goes on upon every fresh opportunity proving that it is not the un- musical body which it is sup- posed to be, and most heartily has it lent its support to the Italian season. From the first it caught on. At the 'beginning Caruso was the great star, hut, by the tim et he had to leave tor Amenca, others had become well known to the operatic public, such as Madam( Giachetti, Madame Alice Nielsen, ri,i.td Madams Buoninsegna, with MM. Matirel, Anselmi; and others. The chorus also proved to be as good as anything ever seen ,at Covent Garden in the height of the season. So, too, was the splendid orchestra, which was con- ducted by Signor Campanini, who has shown himself one of the finest conductors in the world and has made as striking a success as anyone else in the company. The sea,on was full of interesting incidents with its new people and its new operas, and the final seal of success was placed upon its efforts when on Friday night King Carlos and Queen Amelia paid it a visit. It was impossible to make a proper gala-night of it, so only the royal box was decorated. The house was packed, and a composite programme (or a coupe, to give its technical term) was provided.

div.head: THE.HND OF THE RACING SEASON.
div.p: THE.HND OF THE RACING SEASON.

The end of the flat-racing season has been a. complete fiasco owing to frost and snow, and none of the meetings arranged for last week could be held owing to the dangerous state of the courses. For the first time in its h Aanchester November Han-
THE JOCKEYS LANE AND MADDEN.

dicap, which always rings down the curtain, had to be abandoned, and the executive lost all the fees and gate-money, while having to meet many heavy expenses. It is very unfortunate, but there is, of course, always a risk in fixing a meeting so late. A lot of -other money was sacrificed by owners and others in travelling expenses and boxing horses, while the railway .companies, although they received a certain additional sum for freightage, would have profited far more had the meetings been held. Usually a year is known in the, world of racing after the Derby winner, but 1904 in turf history will not stand out as St. Amant's year, but rather as Pretty Polly's. The filly has shown herself one of the most remarkable animals ever seen on the turf, despite her unfortunate beating in France, but she was, ,unfortunately, not in the entries for the Derby, or any of the ten thousand-

div.head: RETURN OF LORD CURZON TO INDIA.
div.p: THE RETURN OF LORD CURZON TO INDIA.

On the cold snowy morning of last Thurs- day Lord Curzon said good-bye to a large gathering of old friends, relatives, and officials at Victoria Station, and left by the P. and 0. train for his second term of office in India.. He goes out by the ss. "Persia," which, as is usual at this time of the year, a very distinguished group of pas-
LORD CURZON

sengers, for the most part bound for Egypt and holiday-making, hut Lord Curzon is in contrast setting out for another period of really hard work. He was looking older, and was obviously worn by the anxiety of his wife's illness, which has spoilt his well-earned leave. It will be remembered that he was actually on the point or starting for India with her at the end of September, and some of the luggage had been dispatched when she was taken ill with peritonitis at Walmer Castle, and for nearly a .month lay between life and death. It was a fear- fully wearing and anxious time, and for days Lord Curzon did not go to bed. Lady Curzon had relapse after relapse, and it is truly wonderful that she pulled through at all. She is now convalescent, though suffer jag still from the effects of her terrible illness, and has been moved/ from Walmer Castle, of which the sanitation is strongly suspected, to Highcliffe Castle, in Hampshire, where she will pass the winter, and it will be many months before she is fit to join her husband in India and do the honours of the Viceregal Court. Her place will be temporarily taken by the wife of Colonel Baring, Lord Curzon's A.-D.-C., who recently married Lady "(Arica Duncombe. Meanwhile, politically, Lord Curzon's renewed term of office is being looked forward to with no small interest, and he will undoubtedly con- tinue his work of the reorganisation of the civil side of Indian administration, as Lord Kitchener is doing with the military side

MR. ADOLF BECK

general and no- body in particular. Then it exonerates the police absolutely, and, lastly, it negatives the idea of a Court of Criminal Appeal. The principal conclusions which they arrive at are as follows :—There is not the shadow of any foundation for the charges made against Beck. Sir Forrest Fulton, the Common Sergeant, is condemned for his ruling at the first trial, which precluded Mr. Gill's defence, which would have made conviction impossible. The action of the police throughout is re- garded as having been perfectly Correct. But the •Home Office is censured for general muddling and the particular mistake which led ,to Mr. Beck s continued detention in prison and the retention of evidence which led to his re-arrest and second conviction. It is also pointed out that th, 1-...• gal system of the Home Office requires complete over- hauling. The prison authorii alone are blamed for the treatment of Beck as a previously convicted prisoner. The Com- mission concludes that in its opinion a Court of Criminal Appeal is unnecessary as they consider that the innocent can be safeguarded against conviction by a simple alteration in • the law. They recommend the adoption ot a procedure whereby a judge might be compelled to state a case for re-trial by the Court of Crown cases reserved_

div.head: Methodist Tune Book.
div.p: The Methodist Tune Book.

Mr. James T. Lightwood, Mus. Bac., Lytham, delivered a lecture under the auspices of the Padgate Wesley Guild on Mosday on "The Methodist tune book and its story." Dr. Bennett presided over a small attendance.—Mr. Lightwood said his tastes tended towards sacred music and hymns in his earliest days, and one of his chief delights was to pick out tunes. He was particularly anxious te know where they came from, under what circumstances they were composed and who composed them. He had little to work upon, but the task was enjoyable. He had spent a great deal of time in the British Museum in furtherance of the object he had in view lin inspecting old manuscripts of tunes, ad the result had been very satisfactory. He spent a great portion of his holidays in cycling, but be cycled with an object in view and that was to track out John Wesley and his wonderful journeys through England, Wales, t Scotland, and Ireland. (Applause.) He had unearthed interesting stories of men which, had hitherto been buried in obscurity. Some of the German tunes in the hymm books were neither more nor less than adapta- tions of old popular songs :of 400 or 500 years ago The" Old Hundredth" was in the remarkable con-. 1 dition of never having been written. (Laughter.) It had been made up out of other tunes patched together and a very successful patching it was too. (Applause.) Then there were tunes which were the very backbone of the lives of the martyrs who went to the stake singing them. A sketch Nvas given of the lives of the Brothers Wesley and their hymns, and Mr. Lightwood alluded to the visit of John Wesley to Warrington. Some of the Methodist hymns sung were of a rollicking character, and when Wesley visited Warrington he preached at an old chapel which was not now standing. He found the people singing one of the old rollicking tunes, and he exclaimed "Be quiet. None of this. I will have none of your Lancashire hornpipes here." (Laughter.) He (the lecturer) would leave the audience to find out for themselves on what occasion Wesley used the words he had quoted and what particular tune the people were singing.—A cordial vote of thanks was passed to the Lecturer and Chairman on the motion of Mr. Newton, seconded by Mr. Plinston.

div.head: Bazaar at Padgate.
div.p: Bazaar at Padgate.

The members of the Padgate branch of the Young Leaguers' Union held a bazaar in Padgate Wesleyan schools on Saturday, in aid of the funds of the Childreli's Home and Orphanage, London. The opening cerentony was performed by Mrs. Joseph Manning, of Warrington, the chair being occupied by Mrs. James Gandy, of Enfield Hall.—Mrs. Gandy said the object of the Young Leaguers' Union was to enlist the practical sympathy of the children of happy Chris- tian homes on behalf, of their less fortunate brothers and sisters, the orphan, crippled, and destitute. The homes were not purely Methodist institutions, and were not mainly supported by Methodist money, but were for children of all creeds. The cause was a very deserving one, and strongly appealed to a very. much .larger circle of friends than was represented that day (Applause.) Mrs. Joseph Manning said children from all parts of the country were admitted to the homes instead of entering a workhouse, thus bringing them out of their wretched surroundings and placing them in a pleasant atmosphere. (Hear, bear. and applause. 1 On the motion of Dr. Bennett seconded )by Mr. Fred Wright, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs Manning for her services.—Mrs. Manning and Mrs Gandy were the recipients of a bouquet each, pre" seated to them by Miss H. Lunt and Miss G. Bennett (Dr. Bennett's daughter who is the youngest leaguer), on behalf.of the Young Leaguers. —The sale of goods was then proceeded with, the following being the stall holders :—Fancy stall: Mesdames Wright and Plinston ; and Misses 11. and J. Bennett, D. Croughton, Rigby and E. Potter. Toy stall: \The Misses White, L. and E. Mason, M. and F. Turner, C. Rigby, and M. Dawson. Refreshment stall: The Misses Eaglesfield, Edith, Emily and T. Bennett, Maggie and May Gandy, M. and E. London, L, Ward, L. Mellor, B. • Povey, E. Rosling, and E. Antrobus. Flower stall: The Misses M: and L. Wright, L. Brough, E. Bennett, E. Lunt, G. Page nnd E. Antrobus. Dip bag: The Misses E. and H. Lister.— An excellent programme, consisting of songs, recita- tions, and violin solos was afterwards given, the following taking part in it. —Messrs. E. L. Pearce and L. Woods, Mrs. James Bennett; and the Misses L. Mason, M. and F. Bennett, Gandy, Henshall, Hudson, and Duckworth. Miss J. Bpnnett was the accom- panist.—The amount realised was about £2B.

div.head: GOOD SQUARE MEAL.
div.p: A GOOD SQUARE MEAL.

This,like many another expressive if not very elegant phrase, we suspect came first from America. Everybody knows what a .good meal id, but what is a good square meal? Why not a roma meal or a triangular meal? A good square meal is usually understood to mean a full and hearty meal, including numerous articles of food, To eat such a meal, being keen set and free from care. is one of the few perfect pleasures, while to digest it is to have one's strength renewed for the battle of life.

The man who can eat a good square meal and get nothing but good from it is a min to be envied. That, however, is just what Mr. R. W. New, of 248 Old Christchurch-road, Bournemouth, could not accom- plish. He ate the meal, and then—well, please read a few words from a letter written by Mr. New so long ago as January 6th, 1900. For a long time," says Mr. New, "I suffered greatly from chronic indigestion. Nothing that I ate agreed with me, and on the rare occasions when I did venture to take a good square meal it seemed to lie like a lump on my chest and caused me much difficulty in breath- ing. Indeed, my entire system was thrown out of gear, and I feared that it would become necessary for me to give up work entirely. But that calamity was averted by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. "It happened this way. One day I was describing my case to a gentleman, who said, bluntly: 'Try Mo ther Seigel's Syrup, and lose no time about it.' "I accepted this advice, and after the first few doses of the medicine was so much relieved that I needed no persuasion to continue its use. But it was not neces- sary to do so for long, for I was soon completely cured. Considering how long I had suffered, and how bad I was I think that comes pretty close to being a miracle. 'I can now eat a square meal against any man, and get the good of it." Surely this is a remarkable and convincing statement, but if any further proof is needed it is here. "I have no longer any troubletwith my stomach," writes Mr. New, under date April 22nd, 1904. "I eat just what I like and as much as I like, and nothing hurts me. Dyspepsia is for me a thing of the past. 1 am well and strong as ever I was in my life; and my cure, solthorough and permanent is, I know, entirely due to Mother Seigel's Syrup." The man who can always obtain a " good square ; meal" is to be congratulated, but the man who can I always digest it is to be envied.

div.head: "WHAT'S IN A NAME?"
div.p: "WHAT'S IN A NAME?"
Slight Error Leads to County Court Proceedings.

By a will dated the 12th April 1904, the late Mr. John Highfield, a retired farmer who lived at Moore, bequeathed to "The Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society" the sum of £lOO. As no society so named exists the executors of the will paid the money into the Warrington County Court, and on Thursday the Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society made an application to his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands for that sum to be handed over to them. They were represented by Mr. Edward White. The executors of the will were represented by Mr. H. Woods. For the claimants it .was pointed out that the Wesleyan Methodist Missionary' Society was the only missionary society connected with the Wesleyan body. That society had extensive work both at home and abroad, and in order to distinguish the work abroad the society was after designated the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society. The testator during his life had been connected with the Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society and had subscribed to the funds showing gen- erally an active interest in the financial wellbeing of that department of the Wesleyan work. Seeing theirs was the only Wesleyan Missionary Society and that the testator had been connected with it during his life the petitioners claimed that they were the persons men- tioned in the will. His Honour expressed the opinion that Mr. White was right in his contention. On behalf of the executors Mr, Woods said he was prepared to accept whatevpr order his Honour made. Mr. - White then '.applied that the money in court should be paid to the treaP- urer of the Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society. Mr. Woods also applied for costs. He contended there was reasonable ground to doubt that the claimants were entitled to the money and that he was justified in appearing. Mr. White opposed the application urging that there , was no necessity for the executors of the will to appear as the petitioners bad imdemnified them no matter what his .Honour's decision might have been. His Honour panted Mr. White's application, and also granted .C 2 2s. advocate's fee to Mr. Woods.

div.head: IDEAL CONDITIONS OF LABOUR.
div.p: IDEAL CONDITIONS OF LABOUR.
Mr. Budgett Meakin Lectures at Warrington.

A crowded audience assembled in the Parr Hall on Monday evening to hear a highly interesting lecture on "Ideal conditions of labour by Mr. Budgett Meakin. The lecture had been arranged by the recently formed Social Service League in conjunction with the British Institute of Social Service and its object was to bring before the townspeople illustrations of the comforts and advantages afforded to their employes by progressive and successful employers at home and abroad. This and kindred lec- tures, which form what is known as the Shaftesbury series, are being repeated nightly throughout the United Kingdom. They are an evidence of the valuable educational work which is being undertaken by the In- stitute and should serve a very useful purpose. At the lecture on Monday the chair was occupied by the Mayor (Alderman Bolton). The MAYOR remarked that many regarded as ideal conditions of labour, having little to do and being well paid for it. That, however, was not the case, as the lecturer would show them, and there were other con- ditions which went to make up the ideal. (Hear.hear.) Mr. MEAKIN has a clear and fluent delivery and speaks without notes. He succeeded in hold- ing the close attention of the audience through- out, and every point was brought home. The conditions described by the lecturer were only ideal, he said, in that they were so far better than those usually met with, as they had been realised already. The object of making these cenditions known was not to show what generous philanthropists could do, but what hard-headed men of business had found it paid to provide for their workpeople' what their rivals had but to understand to be provoked to like good works. This form of competition would injure none but would benefit all concerned. The better the conditions ukuler which work was done, the better the article produced and the less the possibilities of friction and waste. Time was when handicrafts were carried on in little workshops adjoining the home of the employer' which was often that of ,the apprentices as tvell, so that the interests of masters and men were closely linked, and family ties were a frequent result of common family life. Good workmanship was at a premium, and the skilful craftsman could look forward to a pleasant com- petency. But those were days of whole-hearted toil early and late, with few of the advantages common to all to-day. The introduction of steam had changed all that, placing countless drudges at the investor' s dis- posal to perform a dull routine of perfunctory motions, to tend and feed whirring monsters. The slight skill that often sufficed now left the workers untrained, unadaptable, to swell the ranks of the unemployed whenever changes took place. Concentrated manufac- tures produced the terrible overcrowding which forms a national menace, ana the status of the workman was degraded. Master and man had lost touch, and both suffered, for their real interests could never be conflict- ing; they were identical. In order to restore the old relations under the new circumstances it was essen- tial for employers to study the needs of their employees from the beginning, not waiting for a fortune to be made lest the insidious grasp of wealth should stifle their souls. It was still more important to remember that every shareholder in a productive concern was an employer of labour, sharing the re- sponsibility for the conditions of labour along with its profits. He would go a step further and say that the consumer of the goods was to some extent responsible for the conditions under which they were produced. Proceeding to refer to "ideal conditions' the lecturer pointed out that in some large works a social secretary was employed to fill the gap and watch over the inter- ests of the workpeople, affording a link in whom all could trust. Under such auspices there was no end to the improved conditions which it would be found worth while to introduce, quite apart from what the workers could demand by combination or the law enforce. Taking a rapid survey of the circumstances of factory life apart from the work performed, the lecturer illus- trated the conditions recommended and although most instances were from abroad,it was gratifying to notice that at least one of our great factories combined them all, that of Messrs. Cadbury at Bournville. Many other home-firms were, however, making rapid pro grees in this direction, and one could not but feel how the fact recommended their output, especially when this consisted of food or clothing. The position of the factory was a matter of no small importance. So long as the congestion of already over-crowdei districts was contributed to by its presence in the city, few ideal conditions could be realised in it; though there was no factory so badly placed that some- thing might not be done to improve the conditions of labour therein. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
DRCHMBHR 3rd, 1904.

Mr. BALFOUR is pained MR BALFOUR AND to observe that his sup- NATURE. porters have adopted an apologetic tone. They ought, he says, to be full of confidence and aggression. He gives them a piece of information which is evidently expected to raise their drooping spirits to fever pitch. Does this concern his own policy? Is it a decisive proof at last that the blessed formula of Retaliation is a perfect blehd of the principles and advantages of Free Trade with Mr. CEIAMBERLAIN'S OCOVOMiOS ? Not at all. It is the inter9sting historical fact that Mr. BALFOUR has led the House of Commons longer than any statesman since the first Reform Bill. What a talisman for winning elections! Mr. RICHARD RIGG must have got wind of it when he decided to resign his Westmorland seat as a Liberal and fight again as a supporter of Mr. BALFOUR. No intelligible explanation of Mr. RIGIG'S curious behaviour has been forthcoming; but this revela- tion of Mr. BALFOUR'S may be the key to the mystery. It may have struck Mr. RIGG that the man who has led the House of Common's more years than anybody else it. bound to win the next campaign. Mr. BALFOUR is evidently ef the same opinion. " With regard to the future]" he told the Knights Imperial of the Primrose League, "I entertain no more doubts of our success than I do of the great and immutable laws

of Nature." That ought to be very cheering for Mr. RIGG. The statesman who identifies himself with the laws of Nature must be infallible. Mr. BALFOUR once wrote a book called the" Founda- tions of Belief," in which he proved that there were no foundations. But at last he has discovered something which does not admit of scepticism. The great and immutable laws of Nature include the Unionist party, but not merely its existence but its success. Mr. BALFOUR is to go on leading the House of Commons for so many years that no Leader on the other side will ever have a chance of breaking his" record." All this is doubtless very comforting to Mr. Rion and the Knights Imperial; but it does not seem to infuse much spirit into the Unionist cause ' Mr. Balfour's scientific interpretation of the laws of Nature is not adopted with wild enthusiasm by the journals of his party. They show a disposi- tion to ignore it. DISRAELI once dismissed the doctrine of evolution with the statement that he was "on the side of the angels." Mr. BALFOUR tells the opposition that it is no use fighting against the great and immutable laws of Nature, which are on his side. But some- how the party managers in the Unionist camp are not reassured by that philosophy. They are not as proud as they ought to be of the legislation of this Government, particularly of the Education Act; and they do not indulge the fond hope of making the electors understand that Mr.BaLFouß's Fiscal policy and the laws of Nature mean one and the same thing. They might employ Mr. RIGG, who has no constituency to engage his attention just now, to go about the country delivering a lecturo (with dissolving views) entitled, "The Great and Immutable Laws of Nature, as illustrated by Mr. BALFOUR'S Leadership, and the history of the Unionist Party, Past, Present and To Come." Mr. RIGG would probably make this a most eloquent and convincing expesition;but for some reason the party managers do not rise to it. They have tried so many demonstrations, and have lost so many seats. There seems to be no consolation for them except the assumption that by Selections, running steadily against a Govern- ment, never mean anything except the habit the constituencies have of dissembling their love for the party in power. Perhaps this is also one of the lams of Nature ; but it does not greatly e hilarate the politicians who believe in it.

We notice from the agenda for next next Tues- days Council meeting that the Water Committee is instructing the Town Clerk to apply for sanction to borrow £20,510 for the completion of the Water Works undertaking. This is the sequel to a state- ment submitted by the Water Engineer, showing the amount overspent on the Water Works under- taking under the powers of the Act of 1889, and the further sum required to complete the works. Unfortunately, the statement is not printed in the agenda, but we presume it will be laid before the Council on Tuesday. The fullest information is required before sanction can be given to the spending of an additional £20,000 on this departmAnt. We have got an excellent water supply at present, and one likely to suffice for a long time to come, but apart from this fact there is not much that is satisfactory in the contempla- tion of the Water Works as a business undertak)np,°. We are informed that there has been a consider- able loss on the working of the department during the year, and we hope the Chairman will see the necessity for taking the Council and the public into his confidence before pressing for a further loan of over £20,000.

Twe widening of Warrington Bridge is, appar- ently, once more to be deferred. In addition to their threatened legal opposition, Messrs. James Fairclough and Sons, Limited, have refused to sell to the Corporation, a strip of land required on the south side of the bridge for the support of one of the new parapets. Opposition is also fore casted from "other qnarters," and con- sidering also the probable extensions of tram way services between Warrington, Northwich and Knutsfmrd, and the South Lancashire Tramways,the General Purposes Committee recom- mends that the widening be deferred. Thus it appears that the opponents—some of them rather I selfishly inclined—have again succeeded in block- ing this much-needed improvement. All the difficulties mentioned above have received full deliberation previously, except, perhaps, those included in the conveniently general term" other sources," and we fail to see that the position of the Corporation has changed very materially. It has already been decided in the Council that the widening of the Bridge by cantilevers shall be carried out, and a tender for the work accepted. All this shuffling and delay is not to the credit of the Corporation. Either it does not know its own mind or it is afraid to perform the duties it owes to the public.

When we say that we were pleased with the speech delivered by the Chairman of the inde- pendent Labour Party on Wednesday evening last, we hope our friends, who ar3 members of that party, will believe us to be sincere. There have been both speeches and letters from members of the Independent Labour and Socialist parties,the tone of which we have had occasion to deprecate in the petit and it is particularly refreshing to come ac- ross a gentleman who can afford to be above dealing in personalities and still make his address in ter- esting. We had expected Mr. Philip Snowde nto be reasonable in his demands because, so far as we know him, we believe him to be a fair-minded man and an honest ex- ponent of the ideals he strives to approach. We were not disappointed. And, although we may differ from him as to the means to be employed for the attainment of the objects he,and all political and social reformers, have so much at heart, yet we are glad to find that even our differences only amount in the aggregate to small proportion of the whole. "They believed, he said "in the possibility of creating a political party which would use political power in order to redress the glaring anomalies of enormous wealth„ on the one hand and abject poverty on the other. So do we, and if we mistake not so does every' person who is sufficiently conscientious to see that there is such a thing as equity. There should be no necessity for a political party to be formed with that object. The "glaring anomalies " referred to can be removed when every individual desirous of promoting and supplementing the good work of , domestic legislation will make it a plank in /115 political platform. The difficulty rests not so, much with the party as with the individual. And so long as he is content to leave his 'affairs in the hands of a discredited Government, so fickle end faulty, and with so little knowledge of the wants of the people, so long will he be grasping at the substance and receiving only the shadow.

"If the next Liberal Government," Mr. Snowden continued," made an honest attempt te carry nine-tenths of the Labour party's programme into effect he would pledge the Labour p artY that the Liberal Government would receive n? more earnest and whole-hearted support in their endeavour than from the Labour group in Parlia- ment." What, it seems to us, the Indep3ndent Labour party is prepared to do as a Labour grotll3 the members individually, whether members of the L.R.C. or not, ought to be allowed to do. Surely, if they can get nine-tenths of their demands from the Liberal party that ought to be sufficient for the present and for the immediate future, and if they wfll give their support to Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who, we believe, is in entire accord with most of their demands, it will be a step towards the realization of their ideals and will bethe means of keeping out. of Parliament a man who has proved himselt pledged to support a Goverment which panders tc! vesteu interests and would even tax the bread et the people.

a rod of iron. He pulled down ever so many of it houses to make room for a new castle and fortress, and when the citizens objected he let loose his foreign troops among them to plunder them. The employment of French, or Italian, or German mercenary troops to coerce an dragoon the English people was a grievance to which the people of York- would not willingly submit. So in 1069 there was a rebellion. The Saxons and Danes united their forces and drove the Normans out of the city. This so enraged William that he began a fearful war of extermination. He laid waste the district lying between the Humber and the Tees. One hundred thousand people were killed, and the whole district was rendered so desolate that there was hardly an inhabitant left. He shed rivers of blood, and destroyed the city of York once more. Its population fell from twenty thousand to three thousand, and many of these were French settlers and camp followers. After the second destruction of York it rose once more from its ashes, and in the reign of Stephen it regained some of its ancient power and glory. But in 1147, a ' third disaster overtook it. Nearly all its houses, and public buildings, and churches were built of wood, and one of these caught fire. The flames spread in all directions, Itnd the citizens were unable to put them out, so in a very short time the whole place was a veritable inferno. The Cathedral, the religious houses and thirty-nine churches were destroyed, and hardly anything was left but heaps of ashes and smouldering ruins.

• Among all the suggestions which have been wide for improving the lot of Mr. Thomas Atkins, not the least interesting is that put forward by a regimental officer in a service journal. In the present condition of service the soldier is treated very much as a child. He is fed, housed, and clothed by a paternal—or should it be maternal?— War Office with a solicitude whicb,excellent though it is in some respects, may be nevertheless a I cause of some of the distress which attends him when, having taken his discharge, and spent his deferred pay, he finds that meals do not come with the bugle's call, and clothes are not issued auto- matically when the anniversary of his enlistment ' comes round. • The officer in question believes that habits of thrift might be engendered in the soldier by the simple expedient of making him responsible himself for the purchase of his clothing —obviously no change would be possible in the general matter of feeding'and housing. The idea is that clothes should be sold over the counter," and that a man would thus acquire the habit of thinking for himself what he would want, of taking care of the things ha had got, and of seeing that he had the wherewithal out of the 4‘ consolidated pay" which would be his to pur- chase those things which he would require. There would, of course, be no relaxation of discipline and smartness, but amply the transfer to the man himself of the responsibility, who would then have the satisfaction, denied him now, of spending his wages on the necessary clothes for his calling. The scheme certainly appears to be feasible, and not the least attractive part of it is that it would reduce very considerably the clerical work at present thrown on quartermasters and colour- sergeants—and even tend, perheps, to the diminh- tion of the bonds of red-tapeisrn.

The Rev. John Yonge proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Parker for laying the foundation stone. He hoped their friends in Winwick would understand that the Free Churchmen were not coming there in any spirit of rivalry or of antagonism to any existing organization in the village. He supposed that was the first time that Free Church principles and the Free Church movement had 'found a lodgment in Winwick, but he hoped their friends who had been for so many years faithful supporters of the Church of England in the village would not look upon them as interlopers, rivals, or opponents, but as Christian friends who desired to provide opportunity for those who might have to come to live in Winwick of means, of grace such as they had been familiar with in the places they had come from. They had no wish except t good wish for the Established Church in that neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. Ormiston seconded, and the motion having been carried, Mrs. Parker briefly responded.

It was rebuilt once more, and in the course of a century or two it took its place among the foremost cities in the land. Then it got into trouble of another kind, for in 1390, during the reign of Richard 11., the plague broke out, and wrought fearful havoc among its citizens. Eleven thousand people died, and their bodies were flung into the plague pits, and all who could get away from the awful charnel house fled for their lives from the narrow streets and unsanitary dwellings and camped out in the fields till the danger waslover. You will agree with me that the history of York for mom than a thousand years was one long unbroken record of brute force, and wars, and insurrections, and disasters by fire, and floods, and plague, and pestilence. The old city has had as many lives as a cat. and after each new disaster, its citizens have rebuilt its walls,and given it a new lease of life.
