An instance of what a genuinely useful purpose a Free Church Council can serve is afforded by the successful inauguration of the Wiawick Free Church Hall scheme. By taking combined action the leaders of local Nonconformity, backed up by members of the various congregations, will shortly be in a position to congratulate themselves upon providing the first centre of Free Church activity in this growing village. The opening of the Asylum has caused 'quite a new colony to spring up but at present Winwick cannot boast of any place of worship for Nonconformists. The deficiency will very soon be remedied, for the foundation stone of a commodious Hall, which will be placed at the disposal of those pro- fessing all shades of Free Church opinion, was laid on Thursday under most encouraging auspices As was pointed out by the Rev,. John Yenge, the new departure does not imply any spirit of rivalry or antagonism to existing religious agencies, but it is simply destined to supply a much felt want. The scheme is a convincing illus- tration of what can be accomplished by unity in one common object and we wish it the fullest measure of success.

We have been asked to intimate that under Tecent Acts of Parliament passed for the protect- tion of children, the Warrington police intend making an effort to suppress the custom of carol singing from door to door by "hordes of dirty and ill-clad children." There is no denying the fact that the good old custom which used to be one of the delights of Christmas time has been so much abused as to almost develop into a nuisance. Indeed, we are told by the Chief Constable that it is made "the flimsiest possible pretext for wholesale begging" The fact that children and parents are now liable to prosecution and that the police are determined in some measure to enforce the law should act as a deterrent upon those who have no legitimate claim to be looked upon as carol .singers and whose mis- directed efforts only succeed in making night hideous and imposing upon the Christmas spirit of generosity. Of course, it wilThe incumbent upon the police to exercise a wise discretion, though it must be admitted that their task presents difficul- ties in the way of discrimination. We are, how- ever, assured that properly organized companies of vocalists ' and instrumentalists who make genuine efforts in accordance with time-honoured tradition will have nothing to fear in the way of police interference.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield had, to use his own words, a " night-off" from politics on Saturday, but he spoke at two social functions of a particu- larly pleasing character. At the first he acted as host and entertained a large gathering of Messrs. Crosfield's employes in celebration of the works band's highly creditable victory in the national competition at the Crystal Palace. In a short but particularly appropriate address Mr. Crosfield reiterated his desire for the maintenatme of cordial relations between employers and workmen and gave his hearty approval to the efforts which the firm is putting forth to encoprage benefical recreative projects. Later in the evening Mr. Crosfield had an extremely flattering reception on attencling the Foresters' dinner at the Lion Hotel,—a striking tribute . indeed, to his growing popularity amongst the members of this important organization. Although limited in the acope of his remarks he did full Justice to the toast entrusted to him, and the members and Mr. Crosfield himself will retain the happiest recollections of the function.

The E.C.O and the Athanasian Creed. The annual meeting of the Warrington Branch of the Englisn Church Union was held at the Masonic Hall yesterday afternoon, Mr. John White presiding over a good attendance, which included several non- members of the Union.—Mr. White said it was gratifying to know that they had friends outside the Union who were prepared to assist them especially during the present crisis when an attack was being made upon the Athanasian Creed. He trusted that every member of the Union would do everything they could to oppose that attack upon their fundamental doctrine. (Hear, hear).—The Dean of Chester in a lengthy address also supported the retention in the Book of Common Prayer of the Athanasian Creed in its present form.—On the motion of - tile Rev. W. Stanton, seconded by the Rector, the following reso- lution was unanimously carried :—" That this meet- ing earnestly deprecates as frought with danger to the preservation of the 'Christian truth, any mutila- tion of the Athanasian Creed or any alteration of its status in the Book of Common Prayer."

At Aldershot on Thursday night, murderous attacks on tradesmen were made by a soldier armed with a bayonet. One of the victims is in a critical condition. .11r. Richard Foskett, of Knowles Hill Crescent, Lewisham, on Thursday celebrated his 101st birthday. The old man, who is still enjoying good health, was born in Whitechapel, and he has lived in London all his life.

Mr. John Griffiths proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman and said he was sure that Mr. Parker's associa- tion with an event of such a unique character would stand out as one of the pleasantest acts of his life. The Rev. J. L. Milne seconded and remarked that he had not the slightest doubtthat it had been the greatest jov to Mr. Parker toosee the project advance so far. the vote was heartily accorded, and Mr. Parker acknowledged the compliment. A collection was taken on behalf of the Building Fund,and the ceremony conclude& with the singing of the Doxology. Afterwards refreshments were provided for the visitors.

SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN.
BY JOHN TAYLOR
Author of "Search Lights On Land, Labour and Social Problems."

SOCIAL PROBLEMS IN YORK. "I dare assure any wise and sober man that histori- cal. antiquities deserve, and will reward-the pains of any student. They will make him understand the state of former ages, the constitution of governments, the fundamental reasons of equity and law, and the rise and succession of doctrines and opinions."— KENNETT. I spent a 'fortnight in the city of York some time ago, very profitably indeed, exploring its antiquities and inspecting its Roman remains, and spelling out for myself the monuments of its former power and glory. York is one of the oldest cities in England, and it owes its early prosperity to the patronage and influence of the Roman aristocrats, who went there with the foreign legions, and who ruled over it wisely for nearly four hundred years. I.— ANCIENT YORK WAS PRACTICALLY A ROMAN CITY., When its legions first went there, in the year 79, it was little more than a clearing in the forest. The river Ouse was the great highway in those days and men sailed from the city in shallow flat-bottomed 'boats to the Humber, and then by larger vessels to the con- tinent. For ten or fifteen miles round York, the coun- try is level, and undulating,and well suited for cultiva- tion, but in those far off times the poor cultivators were harried, and chivied, and hunted, by raiding Scotch thieves from the north country. _

It was to check and overawe these- sentry that the Itomans built a strong walled fortress u. the camp at York, and set up towers, and gates, and garrisoned the place with trained troops, and invited the Britons to settle in the town, and accept their protection. But the natives and the invaders could not agree, so Hadrian brought over six legions or troops from Germany and dumped them down at York. By the aid of these troops he drove back the Picts and Scots into their own country, and subdued the rebellious Britons around him. Then he built the famous Roman wall, across the country: from the Tyne to the Solway Firth, to keep the Scots into their own country, but he might as well have made a barrier of tissue pAper, for these enterprising raiders came and went at their own sweet will. ' When the Romans were firmly established in York the city began to grow rapidly. Roman ladies settled there with their families, and they introduced all the luxuries and comforts of civilisation. Theybuilt good houses, and large baths, and fine temples, and public buildings. The remains of their tasselated pavements and statutory can be seen to-day in the Museum. There are more than seven hundred funeral urns, and forty stone cists, and numerous funeral and votive offer- ings, to be seen in the museum, and these all testify to the wealth and greatness of the city under the Romans. Side by side with the skeletons of Britons, ana Saxons and the ashes of emperors, you will find samples of Roman pottery, and metal work, and art treasures, that throw a good deal of light on the manners and customs of those times. The plumbers made their drain pipes either of tiles or sheet lead. When they used tiles they took four pieces and cemented them together in the form of a square, and then joined them to four more, till they had builtithe length they required. If they ' must use lead, they, took one square fiat piece and joined its edges together, as you fix your cuffs before you put the sleeve links through. Then they soldered the edges and made pear-shaped pipes instead of round ones. But let no man despise their cement. They could polish it like marble and make it as durable. It would defy frost or fire, and it would last longer than stone. Some of their tesselated pavements are marvellous works of art, and they were found buried under many feet of ooze, and mud, and slime from the river. While the new station at York was being built the excavators found ever so many precious treasures that had been lying there for fifteen hundred years. No man can study those works of art and human remains without coming to the conclusion that mechanical knowledge and skill existed in those days and this country had reached a high standard of civilization when Rams was mistress la the world. The city_ of York reached the height of its splendour under the Emperor Severus. lI.—THE WITHDRAWAL OF THE ROMANS RUINED YORK.

The ordinary residents of the city had become industrious law abiding citizens. Many of them were artisans and skilled labourers who had become prosperous and 'contented under Roman rule. The withdrawal of Ronre's legions was a very serious matter for these people. They were not strong enough to control the unruly spirits within their own gates, and they could not drive off the raiders and

iandals outside. The Romans went away in the year 450. rhey had been recalled because the decline of the Roman Empire in Italy had put an end to its Imperialism abroad. It had conquered the whole world, and yet it could not defend its own gates, so the foreign legions were ordered home and their conquered subjects abroad were left to look after themselves and trust to their own resources. To the citizens of York this was the beginning of sorrows. They had lived long enough under the civiliz- ing influence of the Romans to appreciate their pro- tection and good government, and they had a whole- some dread of falling into the hands of ignorant, fanatical, aid destructive foes. The Scots swooped down on the doomed city like vul- tures,Tas soon as they heard that the Romans had gone. They spent the first few days in eating and drinking all that was left, and then they commenced a fearful game of destruction. These disgusting vanklals could not appreciate fine buildings, and beautitll houses, and sumptuous baths, and gorgeous temples, and works of art, so they battered them to pieces, and destroyed them: Then they plundered all the private dwellings, and murdered all who opposed them. and, to complete their work of destruction, they set fire to everything that would burn and reduced the proud city to dust and ashes. During the next three or four centuries, storms and floods brought tons of mud, and slime, and choked up all the drains and streets, and buried all that was left of ancient York for ever. But a new city was built over the grave of the old one, and when it had become prosperous and contented, the Danes had a look in, and stole everything worth carrying off, and then set on fire all that was left. A century later it fell into the hands of the Saxons, and under their rule it rose once more to wealth and prosperity. I gather from the old Domesday Book that in the reign of Edward the Confessor there were ten thousand people living inside the city walls, and another tea thousandoutside. There were one thousand four hundred and eighteen houses, and two hundred of these belonged to the archbishop. Under Saxon rule York became one of the largest and wealthiest cities in the kingdom, and its citizens were ambitious to manage their own affairs, and elect their own magistrates and rulers. The city of London had a municipal court and guilds of its own, and the citizens of York demanded similar rights and privileges. An agitation began in the daystpf Edward the Confessor that lasted nearly four hundred years, and the chief bone of contention was the right to collect their own taxes, and elect their own rulers, and manage their own affairs. —III7-YORK FARED BADLY UNDER THE NORMAN KINGS.

In seeking municipal rights and privilegres.everything depended on the good will of the King. Unfortunately the citizens of York incurred the wrath and of William the Conqueror, by refusing to submit to him, and holding out against him to the bitter end. In revenge for their obstinacy he not only took away all their former liberties and privileges, but he ruled them with

div.head: CONCERTS IN PARR HALL. ' The Merry Japs and Mr. Wiliam Henley.
div.p: CONCERTS IN PARR HALL. ' The Merry Japs and Mr. Wiliam Henley.
- There are later and brighter pages in its history that tell of its straggles for freedom and its triumphs over its oppressors, but I must deal with these things some other day.

The numerically wretched audiences at the two con- certs, given by Mr. Horace Lingard's party of Japanese Serenader; must have been very disappointing to our townsman, Mr. R. H. Pearson who interested himself in bringing them to Warrington. The fog of last Saturday night might of, course, account for a poor house, but why Thursday evening showed no improvement it is difficult to say, especially bearing in mini. the extra attraction of Mr. William Henley as a violin soloist on that occasion.

The Merry Japs "party, in the two concerts under notice,proved themselves most versatile entertainers on the lines they have evidently marked out for themselves. Although they may not excel either as solo or concerted vocalists they are yet able to present in a uniformly pleasing style a number of songs, duets and quartets which go to make up an interesting musical evening. It is a little curious that while posing as Japanese Singers these people should give us only English vocal music tempered with coon and plantation minstrelsy. But without enquiring too deeply into the reason of such an anomaly, it may be said that such part-songs as Pinsuti's "In this hour" and" Good-night! beloved" were rendered with good taste, and with a point and precision secured only by intimate familiarity with such compositions. One of the most original things was the humorous song "Who did ?' with vocal interruptions by the other members of the party. This Mr. Richard Edge sang, and the others joined in, with evident zest, and the spirit of the piece was fully entered into by the audience. There were some other furny pieces such as "Lady Tom" in • which Miss Emma Barker was befittingly vivacious, "The Naggletons "in which Miss Noblet and Mr. Edge grew quite dramatic in affected connubial cross purposes, and the sobbing quartet in which the whole company were appropriately and amusingly hysterical. Of serious songs the best that were essayed were undoubtedly the recit. and aria "Scenes that are brighrest "(Miss Noblet) and " The Last Watch "rendered by Mr. John Hindle within the limitations of a light tenor voice which is produced too uniformly in the head register to be quite satisfactory. On Mr. William Henley was bestowed such enthusiasm as it was possible for so small an audience to shew. In course of his three appearances, and in the inevitable encores attending them' he showed himself in fine form. The " Ungarische " (Ernst) was especially rich in including so many styles in which Mr. Henley is known to excel. It is doubtful indeed whether so much that is interesting in harmonic playing, double-stopping, and interpolated pizzicato can be found in any other single item. Much that Mr. Henley played may be regarded as specimens of sheer executive difficulty and if we might be permitted a preferenoe it would be to listen td a much larger measure of the cantabile and purely melodious. In the specimens of unaccompanied violin playing to which Mr. Henley treated us, the G Minor Fugue (Bach) must be reckoned a fine achievement. But as " holding the listener in raptadmiration the harmonised version of the "Hymn to the Emperor" of Mr. Henley's own scoring; must undoubtedly be given the premier place.

div.head: MAYORAL" AT HOME."
div.p: THE MAYORAL" AT HOME."

The Mayor and Mayoress held an" At Home "at .the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon, and from half-past three to six o'clock there was a constant stream of visitors. Altogether about 1,000 ladies and gedtlemen attended to pay their respects to Alderman and Mrs Bolton on the opening of their second year of office. The entrance hall had been tastefully decorated with plants arranged by Mr. Parker, the head gardener, and presented a bright and animated appearance. During the afternoon Mr, R. H. Pearson's orchestra played a choice selection of incidental music. Light refresh- ments %ere served, the catering as usual being admir- ably carried out by Mr. Powys. s At a small gathering inithe smoke room the health of the Queen, whose birthday was being celebrated that day, was drunk on the proposition of Alderman SMETHURST.

In proposing the toast of the Mayor and Mayoress, Alderman Smethurst made the interesting announce- ment that the Queen had been pleased to accept a box of choice orchids, grown at Wilderspool, as a birthday present from Alderman and Mrs. Bolton. (Applause.) Other toasts honoured were those of Alderman Sutton, the father of the Council, and Alderman Fran- comb who attained his fifty-ninth birthday on Thursday. The "At Home" was quite as suocessful and enjoy- able as any previous functions of the kind, and was a fitting inauguration of the municipal year.

The Assessment of a Club. The Assessment Committee of the Warrington Union met yesterday at the Workhouse, Mr. A. J. Jollk presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. G. Mather, W. Houghton, S. Davies, T. H. Ashcroft, I, W. Hickman, J. Billinge, R. Forshaw, A. Brooks, J. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (valuer), W. H. Woodcock assistant overseer for Warrington), Er"-C. ... Cooper assistant overseer for Winwick), and H. Houghton assistant overseer for Newton-le-Willows).---The Valuer reported that since the last meeting he had made the following valuations and inspections in the township of Warrington :—Nressrs. J. M. Greenhalgh and Co., Cabinet works, Church-street, gross £164, rateable £l3O 10s. ; Messrs. The 'Whyman's Foundry Co., Foundry, Dallam-lane, gross £258 10s., rateable £209 ; Mr. W. A. Leslie, lock-up shop and show room Mersey-street, gross £37 10s., rateable £32 ; Mr. H. Smith, 77, Bridge-street, gross £BO, rateable £6B, no alteration. In the township of Newton: Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Ltd., gross £350, rateable £321. I have inspected this railway and am of , opinion the amount fixed by the Overseers should not be reduced. In the township of Wir wick : London and North-Western Railway, new sidings and land near Hulme Lock, gross £lB5, rateable £160. The only appeal of public interest was one by the Rev. , Dr. Mercer, on behalf of the League of the Cross, • against the assessment of the club premises in Bewsey-street which stood at £2O gross, £l7 rateable. He pointed out that the premises werB practically entirely used as a workingmen's club, although there was a cottage in the occupation of the caretaker. £2OO had recently been spent .upo.n renovating the building and he considered that in view of the nature of the work which was the encouragement of temper- ance and the fact that there was practically no "beneficial occupation," and the members. had con- siderable funds to raise, the assessment might be i reduced.—After discussion the committtee reduced , the assessment to £l5 gross and £l2 10s. net for the . ensuing two years.

Specimens of the new set of halfpenny stamps just issued from the General Post Office are already in some of the post offices. The design is the same as before but it is printed in a much paler green. The State Department at Washington has decided to ask permission of the British Government to present a handsome gold watch to Commander Nugent, of his Majesty's gunboat Algerine, as a testimony of the United States' appreciation of the services rendered by him in rescuing 33 seamen of the steamer Mineola, which was recently wrecked on the coast of Kamschatka.

Coming Events. The preacher at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Uhurch to-morrow will be the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees. At Bold-street Wesleyan Church the preacher both morning and evening will be the Rev. G. H. Carnson. The annual concert in connection with People's College will be given in Parr Hall on Thursday, December 22nd. The programme as usual will be of a miscellaneous character, and will include operatic selections and a character sketch. The plan for the reserved seats will be opened on Wednesday. A meeting of property owners and ratepayers will 'be held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Monday evening, to protest against the proposed expenditure by the Board of Guardians of £7,000 upon extensions at the Workhouse. The members of the Warrington Musical Society will give their second subscription concert for the season in Parr Hall on Thursday, December 20th. The programme will consist of Handel's Oratorio from The Messiah." The usual chorus will be assisted by Miss Lillie Wormald (soprano), Miss Edna Thornton (contralto), Mr. Gervase Elwes (tenor) and Mr. H. Lane Wilson (Bass). The plan of reserved seats will open to subscribers on Saturday next. In connection with the Warrington Needlework Guild, the annual display of garments sent by member of the guild will be held in the Town Hall on Wednesday next, from 3 to 5 o'clock. Lord Newton sailed on Thursday for Bombay on a visit to India. On Thursday Mrs. Annie Cawley, wife of Thomas Cawley, farmer, Newton-by-Daresbury, Warrington, was found dead in a cistern at the farm. Only a few minutes before her husband was talking to her in the house. Mrs. Cawley has been in indifferent health since her father died. How she got into the cistern

The Ragged School. The management desire to thankfully acknowledge the receipt of 15 articles of children's clothing, from the South Lancashire Division of the Needlework Guild 'per M-.-C. I. Watkins,hon. secretary.' Facing the Music. • The Hon. Treasurer of the Infirmary begs to acknowledge with thanks, from the Warrington Dramatic Society per their hon. treasurer Mr. Arthur Browne, the sum of £3O, being proceeds of their recent performances in aid of this hospital. Christmas Celebrations at the Workhouse. As Christmas Day this year falls on a Sunday it is proposed to hold the usual festivities at the Work- house and Padgate Cottage Homes on Saturday, December 24th. The sanction of the Local Govern- ment Board to the change is being applied for. GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES now On UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Jumble Sale. In aid of the funds of the mission connected with Holy Trinity Church, a jumble sale was held In St Luke's schoolroom, Liverpool-road, on Saturday after- noon and evening, when there was a good attendance, a satisfactory sum being realized. Death of Mr. John Porritt. Mr. John Porritt, of 39 Arpley-street—an old and widely respected resident in Warrington—died on Monday at the age of 70. He was the oldest male member and an honorary deacon of Wycliffe Church where (before his long and painful illness) he tough the senior men's class. SEE OUR NEW DESIGNS in the Gents' Healtherie, Waukeezie, Globe and "G" brands of Boots for Winter wear.—BOOTH & SON, 29, Buttermarket St. —Advt. Councillor Clegg Congratulated. A meeting of the Howley Ward Liberal Committee was held at the Liberal Club on Wednesday night. Councillor Clegg presided and heartily thanked the workers for having helped him to achieve victory at the municipal election. Mr. A. Downs congratu.ated Councillor Clegg upon his success and expressed the hope that now they had got a footing they would contest the other seats in the ward. Mr. Down's con- gratulatory remarks were endorsed by a number of other gentlemen present. GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES now on UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. A Shop Improvement. During the last few weeks the premises 48, Sankey- street (opposite Bold-street), formerly occupied by Messrs. J. M. Greenhalgh and Co. have under- gone great improvements. The shop front has been remodelled in a thoroughly up-to- date style and the windows are brilliantly lighted with a new type of arc lamps. The shop is now opened by Mr. W. T. Williams, draper &c., who has transferred his business from the corner of Legh- street, having found the'latter premises inadequate to meet increasing custom. The improvement has been generally and favourably commented upon. Caledonian Dinner. The members of the Warrington Caledonian Association held their sixteenth annual dinner at the Lion Hotel on Wednesday evening, when about fifty persons sat down to an excellent repast which was served by Mr. Lee.—After dinner the loyal and other , customary toasts at such gatherings were honoured, the speakers being Messrs. J. Monro, W. Skinner, R. Pierpoint M.P., E. Bindloss. E. Draper, J. A. Macgr, egor, J. L. Davenport, G. Bowman, and the Mayon—An enjoyable musical programme was sub- mitted by Messrs, F. Fieldhouse, Rabbitt, H. Holland, nd W. H. Payton. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SA..NKEY sTHEET, Warrington.—Advt. Musical Successes. At the Prescot Eisteddfod, on Saturday the follow ing local competitors gained first prizes :—Miss Carrie Hastings (pupil of Mrs. Arthur Booth) in the girls' solo competition under 16 years. Miss Hastings was also successful in the open soprano solo competition. Miss Lily Fairhurst carried off the prize in the con- tralto solo competition. The Lyric Prize Quartet placed another first prize to their credit, the adjudi- cator remarking that this was the ,best blend of voices and the best balanced quartet he had ever heard and they were well worthy of the prize. Mr. Arthur Greenough was equally successful in gaining a prize in the tenor solo competition. Warrington Photographic Society. There was a crowded 'attendance of members and friends at a meeting of the above society on Tuesday night to hear Mr. Hesketh, of Manchester. describe the Thornton Pickard prize slides of 1903 competi- tion. The Lecturer pointed out the qualities—good and bad—of each picture from a photographic point of view, dwelling at length on the work of Mrs. Barton and Miss Tomlinson, which specimens received very favourable criticism from the audience. Incidentally it was pointed out that much of the best work in artistic photography was accomplished by ladies. Mr. Mathias proposed a vote of thanks, Mr. Bishop seconding, and it was heartily accorded. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Primitive Methodist "At Home." 111 The Rev. and Mrs. C. L. Stowe were the host and hostess at an "At Home" held in connection with the ILegb-street Primitive Methodist Church on Thursday • evening, and the guests numbered about 250. A most enjoyable programme had been arranged by the Choi- rmaster, Mr. Spruce, and several songs were rendered by Miss Jowett, a singer of note, who has just recently taken up het abode in this town and has attached herself to the Legh-street Choir. This lady was accompanied by her father, and all her songs were heartily applauded. Mr. Grounds also favoured the company with two good solos in his usual acceptable manner. Altogether this new departure in connection with the church was a distinct success, and the officials are to be congratulated on their enterprising and highly successful effort. St. Mary's Dramatic Society. Lovers of the drama will no doubt be found in large numbers at the forthcoming performances of the , famous drama " Belphegor " the lliounte bank. In a sense the St. Mary's Society is playing to as well as for its audiences. The result of the recent competi- tion indicated that " Belphegor " was the most suit- able and the most desirable piece and the society is doing wisely in thus paying attention to the wishes of its many patrons. Another point that will help to make play a success is the new lease of life as it were into which the District Nursing Association has entered. The last annual meeting gave visible signs that the support of thec association would be in future regarded as a duty by the townspeople and in these annual plays arranged by the St. Mary's Dramatic Society so far a very happy double result has been scored—thousands have enjoyed the wholesome enter- tainment afforded and some hundreds of pounds have been diverted to local charities.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
A TICKETLESS TRAVELLER.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, Frederick Sher- wood, The Cross, Lymm, was charged with travelling on the Cheshire Lines Railway en Septemberls6, with- out having paid his fare.--A ticket collector said Sher- wood was a third-class passenger from Manchester to Warrington on Seßtember 15th. He was seen by a man to gat out of the train and cross over the line to the past end platform, and was in the act of leaving the station when witness asked him if he had come off the train. Sherwood replied -` No." He was also told by a passenger, who travelled in the same compartment as defendant. that he had come from Manchester, and wit- ness asked defendant for his fare. Defendant again replied that he had not come off the train.—Sherwood said he went to Manchester and was going on to Black- pool. He met a friend there and was seeing him off, ,vhen he persuaded him to go with him, and take a train from Warrington. He did so, and on arriving at War- rington his friend asked him to see if his cart was wait- ing for him. He crossed the line when the ticket collec- tor asked him if he had come off that train. He replied No." He did not attempt to leave the platform in any way.—Sherwood was fined 10s. and costs, and was ordered to pay the fare,—V. 10s. 9d. in all.

MARKET STALL RIFLED. At the Borough Police Court on Monday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, the following boys were charged with stealing MOO oranges, of the value of 5s 6d from the Warrington Market on November 22nd, the property of Michael Lyons, 8. Gardner's-row : Thomas Bibby, 12, Scott-street; William Henry Ellison, CS, Lythgoes-lane : John Rudd, 28, Stevenson-street ; Walter Mason, 2, Ayden's-yard ; Edwin Madigan, 28, St. Peter's-place ; George White. 20, Stevenson-street; Arthur Clare, 1, Webster's-yard; M. Keenan, 14, Black- hurst-street ; John and Alfred Taker, 8, Dial-street ; John Graham, 49, Haydock-street: Robert Burgess, 12, Dial-street; and Alfred Bate, 31, Haydock-street. All Pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable remarked that a larga number of market robberies had taken place of late, during the time the market was closed and open. It appeared that the prosecutor left his stall quite safe or Tuesday evening. and the following morning he dis- covered that the oranges had been abstracted. He im- mediately gave in formation to the police, and inquiries were made. Subsequently the boys were arrested by Superintendent Monaghan and Detective Clough, and when charged they admitted the thefts. Most of them had wretched homes, and several of them were news- paper sellers. In fact, the mother of one of the boys was charged that morning with having been drunk and disorderly. One of the boys said he took 15 oranges and ate 14 and gave one away. Another boy said he went to the stall three times and took 24 oranges, and gave 16 away. The Chief Constable said the whole of the boys went to sch ool,and were practically young thie 70S and did not seem to realize that they had done wrong. The boy Bibby had been there before, and had been birched for theft. Most of the lads were regular market thieves, and five of them were present when the stal was broken into. The magistrates retired, and on their return the Mayor said it was a very serious offence. AR the boys over twelve years of age would receive six strokes of the birch rod, and those under twelve four strokes, and would be kept at the Police Station until six o'clock.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court,
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court,
Minor Cases.

MoNDAv,—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Francomb and Smethurst, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. E. Woods, C. S. Burgess, S. Wright, J. W. Hayward, H. Thornton, G. Pilling, and W. Roberts. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—John Hill, Marsh House-lane was summoned for cruelty to a horse on November 19th by working it while it was in an unlit state.—He pleaded not guilty.—William Gibcon, R.S.P.C.A., said about 11 a.m. on the date named; he was in Church-street when he saw defendant's daughter driving a grey mare attached to a milk float. It was very lame on the off hind leg. The horse was in good condition, but was unfit for work.—On promising not to work the horse again, Hill was only ordered to pay the costs 4s. 6d. Fowt. ROBBERIES.—Thomns Ashton, 18, New-road and Thomas Carr, 27, York-street, both young men, were charged with having on Saturday night, at 11.20, stolen a couple of fowls of the value of 55., from a hencote at 29, Yo -k-street, belonging to Percy Clough.—Ashton admitted the' offence and Carr, for whom Mr. Steel appeared, denied it.—Prosecutor stated that the hencote was locked up on Saturday night, and after eleven o'clock he went into the yard where he saw two people When asked what they were doing they ran away, bu information was given to P.C. Woollacott who visited the homes of the prisoners and found a fowl in Ashton's house, and another in the yard of the other prisoner. Sergeant Bell stated that Ashton admitted to him that he and Carr took a fowl each, but that it was Ashton who broke open the door of the hencote.—The Chief Constable said Carr admitted the offence to him at the Polic4 Station.—Mr. Steel said the defendant Carr had hitherto borne an irreproachable character. He was in a publichouse until 11 o'clock when he went home, and his parents were prepared to state that he was in the house at 11-20. The black hen wa found in Carr's yard but what was easier than for Ashton to have thrown it there when he was surprised, so that he could have one hand at liberty to enable him to raise the latch to get out of the yard ?—The Chief Constable said many fowl robberies had been recently committed in Warrington although he did not suggest that Carr had had anything to do with them, but he would not say as much for the other defendant.—Ashton was fined 20s. and costs and Carr 10s. and costs.

- - FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Amethurst, Councillors Roberts, Wilkinson and Tinnion, and Messrs. G. Pilling and Hepperp. Ass &ULT.—Patrick Mooney. Stoney yard, was charged with assaulting Thomas Farrington.—Complainant stated that the defendant went to his work at Messrs. Poachin's in a drunken condition. Witness ordered him off the premises when defendant without any further provocation struck him in the face.—A fine of 13e. in the costs was imposed.

div.head: TEE TURNING OF STEPHEN RENNICK.
div.p: TEE TURNING OF STEPHEN RENNICK.
BY ADELINE 'SERGEANT, Author of "The Christl;! s Itc.se," "The Story of a Penitent. •••1." dx.

"He turned me out, miss, e did indeed, an' iO me till I'm black an' blue, an' told me I needn't never go 'ome no more. An' I won't, neither, if on'y you'll take me in, miss, and let me stay?" It was a dripping night. The rain had been falling all day in one steady, continuous downpour. September had set in with storm and tempest, and there seemed no present prospect of any change for the better.

Neily Rennick stood on the mat in the hall of a house in Soho Square. The rays of a lamp above her head fell full upon her short thin figure, and het pretty pointed face, with its eager expression, and large beautiful dark blue eyes. Her dark hair was very curly, and its pretty waves and rings almost hid the low broad brow, and gave something of a heavy look to her countenance; and the cheeks were pinched and wan,so that the dimples which ought to have been there had lost their pristine beauty, and the curved lips quivered and trembled as she spoke. It was plain that she had been a very pretty girl, but that ill-health and poverty and sorrow had played havoc with her good looks. Her dress was torn and shabby, her hat crushed and broken, the thin shawl wnich she had wrapped round her shoulders hardly concealed the deficiencies of her half-open cotton bodice.

Her words were addressed to a lady in white cap and moslin bib and apron, with a great bunch of keys hanging by a steel chain .at the side of her black dress. The lady was not quite young, and she was in charge of an institution which received destitute girls, and cared for them whenever it was possible to do so. She had known Nelly before she married Stephen Rennick, and would have been glad to help her but for one insurmountable obstacle —that all her beds were full, and the committee would not let her take in one single person more. "I'm very sorry, Nelly," ske said kindly, "and if you had come a week ago'we might have kept you, but it is quite impossible to-night. Every corner of the house is full."

"If you'd on'y let me sleep in the kitchen, Miss! I've tiowhere to go to; now father's dead, my step- mother won't have me near her, thota I'm sure I hain't done nothing to vex her, and now that 'e— Stephen Rennick's turned me out, I've not a place to lay down in, nor anything to wear but what I stands up in." . _

"It's no use, Nelly. I can't take you in, and vnu'd much better go to the workhouse infirmary. It's close by, and here's a shilling for you; but that's all I can do at present. You'll be quite com- fortable in the infirmary; the nursiirg is very good, and they are kind to the patients. You don't look fit to be out of doors to-night." Nelly accepted the shilling gratefully, and moved towards the door, but shook her head at the sugges- tion of a workhouse. "I'd better go to the river, I think," she murmured desolately, as she turned away. The lady's heart yearned over her, but she was obliged to shut her out: the house was already too crowded, and she could not take her in. She wondered often during the next few weeks what had become of Nelly; and she inquired of various dwellers in that part of the world, whether the girl had teen seen or heard of, but nothing was known of her. December came before the lady obtained any information as to the fate of Nelly Rennick; and then the information was brought by Nelly herself, aho arrived one evening, in new and mart array, with hands and face wonderfully clean, and in her arms the most decidedly lovely and attractive baby that the lady superintendent had ever seen.

Babies are not usually good to look at when they are only three months old. Nelly Rennick's baby had a white skin,large dark blue eyes, and—wonder of wonders !—a quantity of soft, silky hair, which curled over its forehead much in the same way that Nelly's did. It was fairly clean, but of course,it was commonly dressed, and not until Nelly had taken off its poor little red hood, with the trimming of grubby swansdown, did Miss Eden recognise the fact t hat it was a baby who would have done honour, in point of beauty, to a royal nursery. And it was not the beauty of mere chubbiness: it was a refined sort of beauty, inherited possibly from some un- known ancestor or ancestors, who had left more than a touch of it in Nelly's pretty, pinched face. "Why, Nelly, what a beautiful baby! Is it yours? " "Yes, Miss, it's mine," said Nally. 'laughing aloud with very joy. "Ain't she a duck ? Every- body admires her. Why, I can't hardly get along in the street for people turnin' round to say what a beauty she is. I went to the infirmary, Miss. They was very kind to me, an' give me lots o' things for baby." "Are you at work now, Nelly?" "No, Miss, I'm living with Stephen, my 'usband, Miss."

"But I thought you left him?" "It's baby done it,Miis," said Nelly triumphantly. "It's fair turned him, it has. He's not the same man since he've seen baby. He came au' looked at it, and everybody says to 'im, Wot a fine baby you 'ave,' and when 'e tak it in his arms. Miss, it just turned him, it did. He says, Nelly, if you'll come back to me, I'll give up the drink, an' never strike you again,' he says, so help me God. We the little 'un as done it,' he says, and I'm a turned man, Nelly, from this day forth.' says he. And so I've gone back t'un, an 'e comes 'oine reg'lar of a night, for he's got work, thank God, an' e fair worships the baby, Miss, he does." "I'm very glad to hear it," said Miss Eden; and she asked a few questions about Stephen Rennick's work, and Nelly's own requirements, before dis- missing her with gifts far her baby and sincere wishes for her happiness. "Heaven bless you, Miss" said Nelly—she was a fervent little soul, and half Irish by parentage. "May your bed be in heaveti! I'll tell Stephen how glad you was he had turned." "What is baby's name, Nelly?" Nelly stopped short and looked confused. "It's a queer name, miss," she said, with some reluctance, "but we calls her no hing but Baby and Beauty at present. She was christened Hortons Terriss." And it was some time after IN.lelly's departure that Miss Eden awoke to the consciousness that she must have meant "Hortense Therese," though why she should have called her first-born by a French name that she could neither spell nor pronounce, waS beyond Miss Eden's comprehension.

It came about in this way. When Nelly staggered away from Miss Eden's home, talking vaguely of the river, but meaning to go to the workhouse after all, she went first, as a sort of preliminary measure, to the court where she and her husband had lived for the last few months together. She did not intend to go back to him, but she thought of asking her landlady to go with her to "the 'ouse," and of bribing her with her shilling to give her a cup of tea with "a drop of something" in it. The landlady, however, was out, and Nplly was turning away from the house with a sensation of keen disappointment, when she was accosted by one of the other lodgers. "Madame! You want something! You are wet— fatigned ; is there nothing I can 'ave the honour to do for you ?" Ile was a Frenchman, who lived on-tho floor lower than the Itermicks' and was, therefore, of higher sociA standing: and he was so old, with so many wrinliles and crowfeet, and so much snow-white It • ir that she regarded him with some awe, as well as the usual contempt afforded by her class to all furei iers.

"Eli ?" said Nelly, turning her pretty pathetic face up towards him. "Am I wet, do you say ? I'm soakin', mister; an' my chap's tuned me out an' won't let me in again.''' :She burst into tears as she spoke. "Ah! le miserable ! le scilerat !" muttered the old man between his teeth "It is these accursed English who treat their wives in this brutal manner. Mon Dieu! if I thou;.ht that my Therese-- Come into my room and dry your clothes, my child," he said, addressing Nelly with great gentleness. "I had a daurshter like you—once:- for her sake, I shall be glad to see you. There is fire, there is coffee, you shall be w.elcome to all." have a shilling," said Nelly with hungry eager- ness. "I can pay you for the coffee, mister, and if you had a slice of 'bread as well—" Be put aside 11,0 proffered coin with some anger. "I ask you to visiz me as a friend, I do not sell my coffee," he said grullly. And Nelly, half frightened, half ress3ured, followed Lim to his room, which I was so neat and clean, that to her it seemed like a palace. Yet the furniture was poor and plain in the extreme, but it shone from the care that had been bestowed upon it. The old „Man, goneralle known in the neighbour- hood as Messeer, which .N-elly translated Mister, in order, as she thought, to save his feelings, was a native of Auvergne who. had come to London in search of a missing daughter, who had disappeared with an English tourist. Many years had elapsed since then, poor Ti,e,Ose Duverhay lay buried in a parish grave; but old Antoine Duvernay would not believe that his search could he fruitless, and continued to look for his daughter in the London streets, and to ask tiding of her from every passing stranger. This peculiarity of his was well known, and procured him much rough chaff from his neighbours, which, however, he very im- perfectly understood. Nelly was well aware of all this, and felt a little alarm, as well as some exultation, at being admitted into his abode. He gave her a very substantial meal, helped her to dry her shawl and .hat at the tire, and told her to come to him again if she wanted further help. "I'ui
