div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 3, 1904. FORESTER'S DINNER.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 3, 1904. FORESTER'S DINNER.
going into the workhus," said Nslli sorrowfuliy; in reply.

"Ifut-you'll be here again—outside—before long?" "P'raps so," said .Nelly, miserably. But when she came out a month later, with her baby in her arms, her first thouklit was of the old man and his invitation. She stumbled wearily up the stairs to his door, and, finding him out, sat down on the landing to wait. When at last he came she had fallen into a doze from very weakness, and the old man was roused to pity. He took her in and eared for her, telling her at last that she might have the use of his back room, while li slept in the front one—for he was the proud and happy possessor of two rooms, and although they were small they made a great impression upon Nefly. "Whatever shall I do," she said, a day or two afterwards, "to shew you how I feel for all yGur kindness, Mosseer ?"

"Have you named your baby yet?" said the old man abruptly. - "No, sir; I haven't." "If you would like to please me, call it by a name I used to know—a name I love. Call it after my daughter and my wife; it shall not be the worse for you !;f you do that," said lluvernay, in his halt- ing, foreign way. "Oh," said Nelly, pausing. "Well, I don't mind. And what were these names I'd like to know?" "Hortenge Therese."

"My! Hortons Terris—l'd never be able to remember it. Well, it's a queer name. But if you'd like it, Mosser, I'd be happy to oblige you. Nobody else hain't ever been such a friend to me as you've been. She shall be called after your wife and your daughter, so she shall, the ducky: and nobody shant say her nay." So Nelly-'s baby was formally baptised and registered Hortense Therese: and, although the young mother could not pronounce the names, and generally called the child "Beauty," yet she was secretly proud of it in her heart, and thought that her baby had a distinction not posscssed by any other child in the court.

IIL Meanwhile, Stephen Rennick was growing very much ashamed of himself. He was a tall, muscular, rather good-looking young fellow of three-and-twenty, with a dark complexion and heavy brows, overhanging deep-set brown eyes, which had a somewhat sullen expres- sion. He was a good workman' and could earn good wages when he was sober; but he had of late been drunk so often that his earnings had been next to nothing, and Nelly had been obliged to toil at the wash-tub. Then, in an access of drunken rage, he had thrust her out-of-doors, and since that day he had been ashamed to beg her to go back to him. The worst was that he saw her almost every day. She worked at the Idundry, and left her baby with a neighbour; and he knew that she was lodging at old Mosseer's; and it was well-nigh impossible for him te avoid seeing her sometimes as she ran up and down stairs, or crossed the road to her work. In similar circumstances a young couple in that class of life generally manage to drop out of sight of each other; the wife is afraid that her husband will drag her home by the scruffof her neck, and chastise herinto the bargain, if she comes within his sight. It says something for Stephen Rennick that, after the first day or two, Nelly was not afraid of him. When he met her he generally looked the °Qat way. Of the two, Neils, was far the happier. She he a p‘rotector, she had her work, and she had the baby's all-satisfying companionship by night if not by day. But Stephen had nobody; and his home wds very uncomfortable. Besides, he felt that he had treated Nelly badly, and that all the neighbours knew it. He remembered that he had struck her more than once—and lie was not so callous as to be without a sense of shame. Then there was the baby. The most beautiful baby that ever was seen the neighbours told him. He did not dare to look at it himself; and once, when he ventured to the house where Hortense Therese was out at nurse, the mistress of it shrieked reproaches at him, and dared him to cross her threshold. Nelly had been a favourite in the court, and the beauty °fiber baby was a credit to it; so that Stephen Rennick got no sympathy. It was more than lie knew how to bear. One wintry evening be planted himself in a corner of the landing when he knew that Neny was likely to come that way; and waited for her foot upon the stairs. It came at length—slower and heavier than usual; for she was carrying the baby, and, with her eyes fixed upon it, she never noticed the dark form that waited for her corning in the corner. "Nelly!" he said, stepping forward as she gained the topmost step. Nelly uttered a stifled little cry. But she did not try to run away. Perhaps she remembered that she was not strong enough to run far, with the baby in her arms. The light of a small lamp on the landing fell upon her face, and shewed that it was frightened and pale. "I won't hurt -yer," said Stephen, hurriedly. "You needn't be afraid of me. It's on:y—l wanted—a might I see the baby?" "You won't hurt her, Stephen." "Of course I won't hurt her. It's a girl. then ?" "Ay, it's a girl, poor thing," said Nelly, defiantly, "and I trust she won't have to go through all I've had to go through, for she's the prettiest baby as ever was seen, and everyone says so. Did you ever see a baby like her?" sne asked, forgetting that in all probability Staien had never looked at a baby ; before. "Such a white skin, and such lovely long I eye lashes and dark blue eyes, and soft 'air like silk; she's a reel beauty she is, if ever there was one." "Yes, she's a rare 'un," said Stephen, respectfully. Since everybody said it it must be true. "Nelly," he went on, "if you'll bring her back I'll promise you faithful never to take a drop o' drihk again. nor lift my 'and to you, but work for yoti an' keep you like a lady. I'm real downright lonely, and it do make me mad to 'ear everyone in the court a- talkin' of that baby of ourn and praisin' it up, and me that's its father never allowed a sight of it!" "Well, that wasn't my fault, was it?" demanded Nelly. it was mine, an' I humbly ax your pardon, Nellv. You'll come back to me, won't ye, my dear ?" And Stephen's eyes were full of unaccustomed tears, as he took Nelly and the baby bodily into his great strong arms. 'l'm a turned man," said S:ephen, with solemnity, "and it's the baby as 'as done it, for I'd be a brute if ever I knocked hsr about, nor her mother neither." The next step was to go to the old Frenchman, and explain to him, that matters being so happily arranged between husband and wife, Nelly Would not return to his rooms, but would go back to her "own little 'onie." She expected Mosseer to be gruff with her, but he was unexpectedly pleasant and gentle; he even asked them to supper, and gave them strange things to eat and drink, including wine out of an oddly shaped bottle and queer preserves in green and yellow pots. Nelly had not been so merry for many a long day, and baby was queen of the occasion. "That's a queer old customer," Stephen said to his wife, when they were in their own room. "He's been good to you, you say?" Nelly launched forth in his praises. "He must have money to live as he does, without working." said her husband, thoughtfully. "Yes, I think he has. I've seen him take gold out of that box against the wall; did you notice it ?" Stpehen nodded. "Perhaps he'll leave baby a fortune ! " cried Nelly, kissing the child and her husband by turns. "Per- haps he's an old miser, with 'eaps an' eaps of money stored away in that box!" "I wish we had some of it now," said Stephen. He meant no harm, and she meant no harm, but the remark recurred to their minds in later days with a sinister significance. .Nelly's statement that her husband was a "turned man" seemed to be justified by the facts. He no lotiger spent his evenings at the public-house, but came home soberly and regularly to his wife and child, bringing with him every week the earn- ings which he had formerly thrown away in drink. ,No wonder that Nelly looked smart and cheerful, and that baby's clothes improved every month in I quality, so that she soon became known as the labest-dressed child in the court. "Beauty," as she was familiarly called, did not lose her prettiness as she erew older. When she was big enough to toddle about she excited the admiration of every passer-by, and it was Nelly's delight to take her into the Park on a Saturday or a Sunday afternoon, for she was sure to be stopped by ladies who I wanted to admire the child, and aelt its name. Once even an artist proposed to paint her, but I there were difficulties in the way, for Nelly could not spare time to take her to his studio, and I Beauty was too shy and too spoilt to go alone. Old Antoine Duvernay was one of Beauty's most fervent worshippers. She was as much at home in his rooms as in her mother's, and NellY would, leave her there sometimes to the old man's measure- less content, when she was obliged to go out to her work. As the child grew a little older, and could say a few words, she told marvellous tales of the "pretty sings" she saw in Mosseer's room. Nelly laughed at these stories, but was a little puzzled too. "I never, see any pretty things there," she remarked one day. "Sings like xis," said Beauty, pointing to a little heap of shining coins upon the table, for her father had just brought home his weeks wage, and there was gold among it, as well as silver. Stephen looked at his wife and laughed. "It's what we said some time ago, Nell; the old chap'S a miser, with piles of gold in his boxes, and he lets Beauty play with it instead of toys. Why don't he let you bring some of it away with you, eh, my' Beauty ?" Beauty shook her curls solemnly, but said nc. more. And whether she talked to other children, or whether Nelly's tongue wagged a little too fast, or whether Stephen dropped a word or two to his mates, could not be discovered, but certainly. after

this little conversation, a report grew in the court: that "old Frenchy" was a miser and had hundreds of pounds—all in gold—stowed away in bags andl boxes in his room. The inhabitants of Newton Court were, on the I whole a decent and respectable set, and had no I thought of trying to rob the old man of his wealth; but the rumour brought him into unenviable notoriety, for he was considered very mean and stingy for not parting with any of his money, when , there were people on every side of him in the extremity of want "I s'pose he means to leave it all to Reality," more than one neighbour remarked to Nelly. "She'll] be quite an heiress by-and-bye. Why, what else could he mean, when lie asked you to call the child after his wife and daughter? it's very plain." And Nelly grew to believe it, in course of time: and Stephen, too. There was no bitterness in their thought& of the. old man's wealth until a time came when a great strike threw Stephen out of work. At first the men were cheerful and re,olute enough; -after a time i the cheerfulness died away, although the resolute- , ness remained. Stephen Rennick was One of the most dogged upholders of the workmen's cause. He held to it through all the vicissitudes of a terrible winter, when starvation stared him in the face, when Nelly's face grew pinched and grey once more, when—worst of all—Beauty's rounded limbs wasted, and her eyes were hollowed by hunger into a look of pathetic misery. The little money that Nelly could earn was not nearly enough to keep them; but Stephen was too proud to apply to the parish for relief, and refused to allow his wife to speak of the workhouse for herself and her child. Nelly had hoped that Antoine Duvernay would help them through this bitter time; but the old man had fallen into a state of senile decay, and seemed incapable of receiving ,a new idea. He crept about his rooms, scarcely ever venturing into the street. Nelly did all his shopping and cooking for him and kept hire clean and tidy, out of pure gratitude, for he never offered her anything in return. She had the key of his rooms, and went in and out as she would; there was no one to interfere. "The miserly old wretch!" Ster-hen burst out one day, when she came upstairs 'with an armful of clothes to wash. "The least he could do is to pay you for your time!" "Oh, don't speak, so, Steph&l. Remember, hi took me in when yo turned me o it. Don't we ow. 'aim noting for that ?" Stephen was alway s suoduect by an allusion to that time. He said no more; but there was an ugly frown upon his face. "And if I hadn't been here in the 'ouse," said Nelly, "you'd never ha' seen me an' baby, and you'd never have turned as you did, Stephen. "Turned! What was the good o' turning?" said Stephen, with ill-suppressed fierceness. "If I'd done just the same as I did before, I shouldn't ha' been a bit worse off than I am now." Then he seized his hat and went downstairs. The sense of wrong was very strong upon him. He had "turned," as Nelly always expressed it, and became a sober and industrious man for the sake of his wife and child; but he was at that moment no better off than the drunken brute who lived on the same stair, and had just done a month's "hard" f6i• kicking his wife until she had to be taken to the hospital. 'I don't see as how goodness pays any better than badness," said Stephen to himselT. He turned into a public-house and called for spirits—the first time he had done such a thing for many a long day. It was a strange public-house, And none of his -mates were there; so he sat for some time in silence, soaking himself with spirits, and revolving in his muddled brain a temptation which had lately become a continual torment to him. . _

Why should he not creep into old Duvernay's room and help himself to some of the gold which was kept in the old man's boxes Duvemay was too imbecile to know or care. It would do him no harm. It would mean life and health and prosperity to Nelly and the child. Besides, if, as seemed most likely, the old French- man had bequeathed his money to his god-daughter, for he had stood sponsor to Hortense Therese at the font, surely it would be quite excusable for Beauty's father to help himself, for her sake, to a little of the money that was waiting for her. It was the only reasonable thing to do. But for the brandy he would never have had the courage to put lts resolution into action. But, after a time, when his brain was sufficiently excited he slunk out of the public-house and made his way back to the loiging-house where Duvernay lived, and where his own home was situated. _

It was quite late, Nelly and Beauty had gone, to bed without waiting any longer for father. Stephen felt his way to the table, seized upon a key, whiah he knew was there, and left the room again. He did not know that Nelly Was awake, that her eyes had followed his movements through the dim- lighted room, and that when he left it she sprang up, and, hastily wrapping herself in a shawl and petticoat, followed hint- down the dark and narrow stair.

With a trembling hind Stephen fitted the key Into the lock, turndit, a,id opened the door. He pushed it back with his foot, but he did not fasten It, and Nelly was able, after a minute or two, to push it ajar and look into the room. And a strange sight it was that ske.savr. The old Frenchman, in tattered dressing-gown and skull cap, from which his venerable white locks floated to his shoulders, had left his bed, and was bending over the very .box on which Stephen's longing eyes had so frequently been cast. Stephen stood motionless in the shadow, but the old man seemed at once to grasp the fact- that he was present, for he turned round and nodded at him with a vacant smile.

"You 'ave come! it is well," he said. "I have bad a dream. My Therese she come to me, and she say, 'Father, I am in the grave, you must not keep the money for me, give it to those who have need. And you have need, have you not, mon pauvre ami? You have come for it, take it, it is yours—all yours." He snatched a candle from the mantelpiece and held it aloft. Its rays flickered on the very sight that Stephen had longed for—on a pile of golden coins, and a heap of canvas bags, evidently con- taining more gold, nearly filling the strong box which had excited his neighbours' curiosity. It was all true, thenel -Zuvernay was a rich man —a miser, and he was willing to give away his wealth. Stephen Rennick took two steps towards the box. "Take it," said the uld'man, with a strange, wild look. Was he really imbecile, or had he grasped by some wonderful intuition the force of the situa- tion? He plunged his hand into the box and held out a handful of gold. Stephen Renaick also held out his hand. Then Nelly sprang forward, and threw herself upon his arm. "No, Stephen, no, you shan't take it!" she cried. "How could you come note, Stephen, to take his cooney, when he's been so kind to me?" "How has he been kind? He's done nothing for said Stephen hoarsely. Then in a clearer "He's giving it to us; it isn't like—taking

div.head: SUCCESSFUL GATHERING AT THE LION HOTEL.
div.p: SUCCESSFUL GATHERING AT THE LION HOTEL.

The members of the Warrington District of the Ancient Order of Foresters held their first annual dinner at the Lion Hotel on Saturday, the gathering proving an unusually successful one. The primary object in view in making the venture was to stimulate an interest in the Order amongst those connected with it, and there is little doubt that object will be achieved. The attendance at the dinner exceeded all expectations, nearly 250 persons partaking of the repast served by Mr. Lee. The after proceedings were of the usual character—speech-making interspersed with song—and affordei considerable enjoyment. Bro. W. Hipkiss, D.C.R., presided and was supported amongst others by Bros. Simms (Newcastle- on-Tyne), High Chief Ranger; Stead (Newcastle-on- Tyne), Assistant Permanent Secretary; Hulse (Chester), High Court Trustee; and a number of past and present offices both of the Order of Foresters and other friendly societies in the town. Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., wrote originally accepting the invitation to dinner, but subsequently expressing his inability to attend. Captain Appleton also wrote expressing his regret that he could not be present.

div.head: LOYAL TOASTS.
div.p: THE LOYAL TOASTS.
Thwusual loyal toasts were heartily drunk on the motion of the CHAIRMAN.
THE ARMY AND NAVY.

This toast was entrusted to Bro. Chrimes, P.D.C.R. Having referred to what he described as the glorious past of the army and navy, he went on to speak of the volunteer forces and remarked that we in Warrington had every reason to feel proul that we were able to raise three companies of volunteers for servise in the war in South Africa. Foresters had every reason to feel proud that one of those companies was under the command of an honorary member of "Court Mercy," —Captain Appleton. (Applause.) . . .

, The toast hiving been drunk, Captain Smrru responded, and referred to the high state of efficiency of the local Battalion. He strongly advocated a fortnight's camp training for all volunteers, urging that if they were given the extra week's training as the Warrington volunteers had, they would be a credit to the country. (Applause.)

div.head: AVARRMGTON DISTRICT OF THE ODE.
div.p: THE AVARRMGTON DISTRICT OF THE ODE.

Brother LA.TROM, Newton-le-Willows, in proposing the above toast, said he was surprised to find that the Warrington district was perhaps the oldest district in the Order, and had taken a great part in the formation of the Order. The first dispensation granted to Scotland cime from Warrington, and the Foresters of the same town had the honour of granting alsoithe first dispensation to Ireland. He failed to see why the district should not be ambitious. and go in for the holding of a High Court in the Parr Hall. (Applause.) He coupled with the toast the names of Brothers L. Davies, D.S., and P. Peacock S.D.C.R. The toast was enthusiastically honoured. Bro. DAVIES in responding, entered into details as to the position of the district. As far as could be ascer- tained the total receipts this year had been £1693 13s. 6d.. together with £177 interest. In sick and funeral expenses they ha i paid out £1479, medical aid, £163 10s. 9d. and grants to members out of employment, £37 Bs. sd. After meeting all their liabili- ties they had increased their funds by £2OO. The membership of the district 'lumbered 1,125. The depres- sion in trade had effected tileir membership to a great extent. Connected with the district they had a Burial Society with funds amounting to £3,003, and a Widows and Orphans' Fnnd. He hoped that dinner would result in a revival in connection with their Order and that people would be induced to participate in the manifold benefits of their Order rather than pay to tontine clubs in the town. (Applause). Bro. PEACOCK remarked that it was his ambition to have a High Court held at Warrington. (Applause). Referring to the position of the order he pointed out that whena member was out of work there was no need for him to withdraw as they all subscribed to a sub- sidiary fund, ;to meet those cases, and from which the subscriptions of out of work members were paid. He wished every success in the future to the Warrington District. (Applause).

div.head: KINDRED SOCIETIES.
div.p: KINDRED SOCIETIES.

THE POWER OF COMBINATION. Brother MAYBURY, P.D.C.R., proposed the toast of " Kindred Societies." He remarked that friendly societies did not exist for the simple object of paying subscriptions and receiving benefits but existed for a far nobler ideal—the furthering of the bond of human brotherhood. He wished all the friendly societies throughout the country were more closely drawn together in a bond of union. If they were, so great would be the combined membership that they would have the power to make or mar any Government. During the pas* few years there had been several hitches in Parliament with regard to the conduct of Bills which would benefit friendly societies. If the members 1 of friendly societies would only sink ill lell political feel- ing and go n for greater union they could carry any- thing and everything they needed for the benefit of friendly societies and for the furtherance of their great objects, through the How of Commons. In Warrington friendly societies did show a greater spirit of unity than in many other towns and as they were the majority or the voters they could if they so desired ask anything they liked from the Town Council, and insist upon the granting of their demands. (Applause). Coupled with the toasts, which was cordially drunk was the name of Bro. Steel, P.P.G.M. (Oddfellow.) P.P.G.M. STEEL said he must congratulate the Foresters in the flrstplace on the gathering that night. Bro. Peacock said that it was inaugurated to court the favour of High Court, officials but it seemed to him it might have another object, to court the favour of those who were not Foresters. In Warrington the friendly societies worked together very harmoniously. It appeared to him that Tontine clubs constituted the greatest difficultyjthey had to contend with, but he thought any man who compared soberly the two organ- izations, must decide in favour of the friendly society. It was the principle of their orders to help a fallen brother, and he thought that that principle ought to apply with respect to lodges—the strong and healthy to assist any that might be having hard times. (Hear, hear). Then they might extend the principle between societies. If the Oddfellows could help the Foresters or the Foresters could help the Oddfellows they ought to do it. (Hear, hear.) There was a kindly feeling amongst them as friendly societies, and they slid not like to hear of any society going down. He hoped they would have many other such gatherings as the one that night. (Applause.) "TITE ORDER." SPEECH BY MR. A. H. CROSFIELD.

Mr. A. H. CROSECELD, who on rising received a very flattering ovation, proposed the toast pf "The Order.' Mr. Crosfleld wore the regalia of a F6rester and at the outset remarked that he was fully entitled to wear the decoration as it was many years since he had the privi- lege of joining that great society. He was extremely sorry he could not get to their gatherinc, earlier as he would have been deeply interested to hear the instructive speeches to whichle was sure they had listened. When he entered the room he heard Bro. Steel sound a very fine note when he referred to the' generous feelings which they should entertain for other societies,though he thought that at the same time they should take care i their great society continued to flourish. (Flear, hear.) He hoped it would not be considered out of place if he ventured to quotoi a few figures which he thought were very impressive, and which summed up briefly the history of the Order and showed the high position it had attained. The commencement of Forestry could not be traced. The earliest glimpse they had was in 1790 when there existed a Court of the Royal Foresters at Leeds. In 1821 the number of courts had increased to 93, and in 1834 they num- bered 358. In the last year there occurred a disruption over the general laws and the present Ancient Order of Foresters sprang into existence. To-day there were connected with the Order 9058 courts, with a member- ships of 929,720, and which possessed funds amounting to £7,765,000. (Applause.) In the last year alone the funds had increased by £329,112. The Order had now spread all over the globe where Englishmen had made , their homes. Last year 193,608 members received sick pay, and connected with tbe Order there was not only a sick and funeral fund but also an old age pension scheme, Ito which, however, up to the present; only 2,039 mem- bers contributed. The Ancient Order of Foresters—to their honour—had provided three lifeboats, and last year by granting £l9O to the funds of the Lifeboat Institution had brought the total of their grants to that fund to £7,386 Us. lid. (Applause.) He trusted they would forgive him for venturing to treat them to figures with which most present were familiar, but to his mind

, they were a magnificent record of the develop- ment of a free institution in the free country of England. (Applause.) At the end of his quota- tion there was a brief reference to the thorny question of old age pensions. He had not got a scheme in his pocket and knew., of the complications of the question, but he had given some time to reading the different schemes to provide old age pensions which had been put before the country—he was afraid the schemes had collie before us when there happened to be an election, and he was afraid the anticipating ideas which were put into the minds of the people before elections had not as yet been realized. (Laughter.) He thought it was too bad that so great and grave a question should be dangled before the eyes of our great democracy before we were in a position to deal with it. He was strongly in favour of old age pensions whenever the Government was in a position to deal—or attempt to deal—with the question successfully, and, he maintained,that could only be done by means of consultation with, and by takingithe advice of the great friendly societiesof the country. In the meantime, although no friendly society had as yet succeeded in grappling with so big and serious an undertaking, and although they must undoubtedly have considerable Parliamentary assistance given whenever a scheme was carried into effect, they had done a great deal in providing for sick benefits, by seeing every man and woman was

decently buried when the time came, and by making an effort to provide for the widows and orphans. Friendly Societies were a grand illustration of the English belief that self help , was the best help. A great historian writing 50 years ago the history of civilization, when advanced people thought Government interference was very bad, summed up the duties of the Government as being—to maintain order, to prevent the weak from being oppressed by the strong, and to carryout certain regulations with regard to public health. We had changed our views since those days. We knew the Government could do and should do a great deal for the masses of our population, but while we recognized that we still thought it was good,where we could do things for our- selves possibly better than the Government could do them for us, it was better for us to depend upon our our organization and our own hands. Legislative machinery moved slowly, and therefore it wts well to supplement Parliamentary work with individual efforts wherever possible. (Applause.) Besides the charitable work which was so nobly done by our great friendly societies, we knew that the great tendency and influence of those magnifi- cent institutions was to raise the self-respect and self reliance of the members and therefore increase the happiness of themselves and their families. (Hear, hear.) They acted upon the great principle which he firmly believed, that it was not the man who earned most who wig the richest,but the man who saved most; that it was not the man who ate most who was the strongest but the man who was able to digest his food; that it was not the man who read most who was the wisest, but the men who remem- bered most. He believed that was the great principle which underlay the wonderful fabric which had been reared in this country. (Anplause.) He thanked them for the honour they had. done him in allowing him to propose that toast, and he respectfully and earnestly wished their numbers might increase and that more and more of the toilers of the world might benefit by association with that great society, and that for all time prosperity might attend and waitupon their efforts. (Applause.) He ecoupled with the toast the names of their worthy chief of the High Court and their Assistant Permanent Secretary, who had come specially from Newcastle-on- rime, and also the High Court Trustee, who was well known and respected by all Warrington Foresters, owing to his previous welco.ne visits. (Applause.) The toast was enthusiastically honoured. In reply the HIGH Cam' R A.NGEFL said when one heard the Ion; record of the Warrington district and then heard that this was its first dinner, one wondered "why all this delay." He believed it was absolutely necessary for fri-ndly societies to pay attention to the social side of the question. All the political parties had their dinners and picnics, and generally the churches and chapels as well and if they were a necessity in those cases surely such things could do the friendly societies no harm.. The work they w re engaged in was of the best; they need not hesitate to let people know what they were doing. The order was making extraordinary progress financially, but he could not say the same numerically. Of late years trades uraions had developed considerably. He did not want to find fault at all with trades unions, but he had no hesitation in )saying that any of those unions which provided for sick benefits ought to be put undeor the same Act of Parliament as the friendly , societieg, ani he hoped Mr. Pierpoint, or Mr. Crosfield if he was eleoted, would give such a motion their surto- port. The friendly societies had to undergo the ordeal of being valued every five years, whereas the trades unions, he understood, had not, and if they went in for sick pay in the same way as friendly soeieties,it created a sort of unhealthy cemnetitioe. With reference to tontine clubs be would like to endorse what had already been said, and he must say he did not see why any in- telligent man should prefer to join a tontine to joining some per nanent society. In conclusioa Bro. Simms ex- pressed the hone that he would seue diy visit a [Ugh Court at Warrington. (Applause). A.P.S. STR4,I3 also hoped the remarks regarding the , holding of the High Court at Warrington would bear ' fruit, because he believed that a district like Warring- ton, which had taken such a prominent part in Forestry in the past, should have a prominent part to-day. IL C. T. HULSE also spoke, and strongly urged indi- vidual effort in pushily,' forward the work of the Order. PRESENTATION TO P.D.C.R. THORNLEY.

The High Chief Ranger then handed to P.D.C.R. Thornley a framed emblem and a necklet in recognition of his services, he having just vacated the district chief rangership, and remarked that he hoped Bro. Thornley would long retain the good wishes of his brethren. Bro. THORNLEY suitably returned thanks. "TOWN AND TRADE OF WARRINGTON."

P.D.C.R. Buizocx, in proposing the above toast re- marked that, thanks to its varied industries, Warringten had a fair share of employment in the present trade depresii on. Couniillor TENVIOV res )on led. FLa was not he said. one of Warrington's born sons—but he was proud of the town in many ways. It possessed many and im- portant industries, and among ether things he did not think there was a town in England that had done more to further the best interests of friendly societies and of another society—the Masonic Order—with which he was more at home. Warrington was justly noted for its variety of trade and the excellence of its productions, and it was possible and more than probable that it was because of the many institutions which existed, and which hart existed, for the helping and raising of the toilers generally, that Warrington would always be in the forefront of manufacturing communities. War- rington had been rather backward in many public matters in the past—say 30 or 40 years ago— and had had a lotiof leeway to make up. To do that meant spending a considerable amount of money. He did not believe in spending for the sake of spending, but that they should spend always with due , caution. That he would always try to do. He was sorry that at present trade in Warrington was not so robust as they would like, but he was pleased to say that whatever depression existed in Warrington, it was not so keen as in many other towns. Many of the rate- payers had not always taken the interest in the welfare of the town that they might have done. At times they I had taken a sort of enthusiastic momentary interest,but it soon died away. They ought always to strive to see that only men who had the best interests of the town at heart should go into the Town Council. So far as the present Council was concerned, he did not think the. town had ever had a more earnest and faithful body of men, and he believed they bad behind them a public opinion which would see that every man did his duty, and tried to make the homes and lives of the workers better and happier. (Applause:) During the evening musical items, which added much to the enjoyment of the proceedings, were given by Messrs. J. Rabbitt and Santall (Liverpool), and Master Pearce, and humorous selections by Mr. E. A. Sanders.

It." • "But you came here to take it—to steal it!" cried Nelly, who was never afraid to speak the truth. "And as to him giving it,don't you see he's gone silly, poor old man, and can't ell what he's doing or saying? Stephen, if you take one piece of his money I'll leave you for good and all. I thought you'd tarried from your evil ways, but if you do this no turning will make up for it. You'd always be a thief in my eyes, even though nobody else found you out." He was vanquished— He drew back and hid his face against the wall with a low cry. And Nelly drew nearer to the old man, who was leaning or had fallen against his. box. "Help me with him, Stephen; he's fainted, I think. Here, move him a little arid shut up the box, we don't want anyone to come in and see it open.. They might say— Help him to the bed, carry him, will you, Stephen? Open your eyes, Mosseer, we're all friends; don't you be afraid. Oh, Stephen, I'm afraid—l'm sorely afraid he's dead." She was right. Be had died as he bent over-that box of gold which he had cherished so fondly for his long lost daughter. But he had found her again— though Nelly, who wept for him, did not know that father and daughter had met in that land beyond the grave, where there are no partings, no sorrows no mistakes. To Stephen's infinite shame and confusion, more- oirer, it was found that the old man had left a will leaving all his property to the Rennicks. They benefited to a larger extent than they had thought possible; but, as Nelly could not refrain from point- ing out to her husband, the money was for the most part foreign coin and would have been difficult to get rid of and easy to trace, if it had fallen into UllaUthorised

"You were right, Nelly," said Stephen, humbly, sand I'm thankful you followed indo to the room. the temptation was sore, my girl, But I've had riy 'fuming,. and I've not been punished as I leserve. You'll see a difference from this time lerth ; for if ever a man wanted turning from the error of his ways, it's I that am that man. Please sod, I've turned now in right good earnest." And so he had. And that was the true history ot ;he turning of S.ephen Rennick. [THE END.]

div.head: CHRISTMAS CARDS, NEW BOOKS, Ett:
div.p: CHRISTMAS CARDS, NEW BOOKS, Ett:

What would Christmas be like without Moors. Tuck's cards? They are as essential to our happiness as all the other good things peculiar to the time of Peace and Goodwill, and form the means of conveying our best wishes far and wide. The chief difficulty is to make a selection. Where all are good as can be, how are we to say which are best? One's particular taste must help us, and to gratify that we have only to glance through the "thousand and one" novelties to discover that

every individual taste is catered for. To mention only a few series there are the "Ruby and emerald pastel" the "Floweepastei," the "Parchment," the "Celluloid," the "Jewelled gauze," the hand-coloured velvette, (clusters of flowers, true to nature on grey panel) 4 the, "Impressionist." the" Porcelain," and a host .of others _ _
equally attractive. Then there are Boxed Autograph Cards, Booklets, Calendars,_ and, last hut not least
Christmas Post oards. Neiiher ar':e the "little ones"

forgotten. For them Father Dick provides his "Animal "Toy Books galore, Painting Books, and a long-felt want in the form of a washable linen book I which is printed with bright pictures in fast colours, untearable, and new every time it's washed. What more can the mother of a family desire than a perfectly wholesome, everlasting Toy Book for one shilling? Mr. Kipling's new volume of stories, "Traffics and Discoveries," (Macmillan and Co.), derives inspiration from many sources. "The Captive" reflects the views of an American inventor, unwillingly drawn into the fighting line, on the British methods of conductin* the Boer War: "A Sahib's War" presents the point of view of a Sikh soldier on the same operations; while a third story with a South African setting shows Tommy Atkins's attitude towards the accusation of "barbarous methods." Motor cars, wireless telegraphy, life on a torpedo-boat during manoeuvres, and War Ofßce re- organization, serve to form the ground-work of the other stories, each of which is, throughout the book, preceded by an illustrative poem. Stt.nding out from all the rest of the volume in great contrast, both in the matter of subject and of treatment, is a beautiful story of dream-children entitled "They," which is told with rare delicacy of touch. The author's genius is, how- ever, apparent on every page, and the huge army of Kipling devotees will obtain prolonged satisfaction by the perusal of the book. Subscribers to Messrs. Macmillan's" Edition de Luxe" of the writings in Prose and Verse of Rudyard Kipling will shortly be able to add the twenty-second • volume to their book shelves. It contains "The Five Nations."
citing him_ while still in _a weak_ state_ of

a life'of dissipation. Chiefly through the ato lead Regina this plot is also frustrated, Marcell° awakens to. the villainy of his step-father, and in the end retribu- tion falls on the murderer. "Whosoever shall offend." . . . . is a finely conceived story of great freshness and vigour, full of exciting incident, and crowded with dramatic situations, developed with all the practised skill of this popular writer. Messrs. Macmillan & Co. have recently issued the work, and it will make an ac- ceptable present to all lovers of high- class fiction. Mr. Cutcliffe Hyne's new volume of stories, to which he gives the title of Atoms of Empire, (Macmillan and Company)covers a wide field,and many of the narratives carry the reader to scenes of danger and difficulty on the outskirts of civilization,where it is above all things necessary that the encroaching European should display qualities of strength and resourcefulness. There are stories of the West Coast of Africa, which throw into strong relief the pluck and endurance of British officials notwithstanding the effects of an unwholesome climate; a gruesome account is given of an outbreak of cholera onian African tramp steamer crowded with native passengers; and the running down and shipwreck of an Atlantic liner with a thousand souls on board is power- fully described. We are given a realistic story of the methods successfully adopted by two desperadoes who hold up and rob a full train in the Wild West of America; there are two grim narratives of lynching in the Southern States ; the story of a renegade British officer who becomes a slave dealer; and among the other contents of this volume of vividly told tales is an account of the destruction by fire of London,north of the Thames during mid-winter when the water supply was frozen. Every one of these tales glows with that inimitable descriptive power which at once brought fame to the author of Captain Kettle on his introduction to the literary world.
wm called Short Street, and it was a typical example of the mean streets which nearlyalcvays, and in all countries, lie near to a great minster, like sea wrack at tho foot of a rock.

"Short Street was a cul-de-sac, whereof one end was a gin-palace and the other an archway to the railway depot of a suburban Necropolis. Late at night the inhabitants were kept from sleep by the quarrelling of tipsy men who had been turned out of the public-house, and early in the morning they were awakened by the rumbling of the hearse that rattles the corpses over the cobbles of the street,_

`.oscar's home in Short-street was at number one, a grimy house with a soiled card in the fanlight above the door 2 saying 'Lodgings for single men. Besides himself there were four lodgers, three of them being porters at the funeral depot and the fourth head bar- man at the public-house. The barman had the parlour floor, and he generally brought home a number of noisy comnanions at closing-time to play cards and drink beer. "Oscar's bedroom in this house was not so much a room as a stifling closet of miserable aspect in which the refuse furniture seemed to make an effort to arrange itself in order—a threadbare carpet, an iron bedstead without foot or head, a painted washstand, a broken lipped water ewer, two or three rickety chairs, a table that was safest when it rested against the wall, a few pictures of race-horses on the remains of a dirty wall- paper and a looking-glass blotched by damp, like a sheet of ice spotted and scabbed by thaw. - "His landlady lived in the basement and was never seen except on Monday mornings, when she went round for her lodgers' rent some two or three hours before the collector called for her own. The only person whom Oscar saw constantly was the landlady's servant, Jenny, a typical cockney girl of the humblest class, untidy and unclean, but as bright as a London street sparrow, and with a big soft heart in her little vulgar breast."—From Hall Caine's new novel, "The Prodigal Son." The Christmas Double Number of the "Windsor Magazine" will be universally admitted to establish an altogether new record in magazine enterprise for total bulk and sheer variety and value of features, for it contains within its beautifully printed coloured cover, complete stories by Rudyard Kipling, Israel Zangwill, Agnes and Egerton Castle, Eden Philpotts, Hamilton Drummond; Frank Richardson, E. Nesbit, Ethel Turner, H. B. Marriott Watson, Fred M. White, H. C. Bailey, Harry Pain; and other favourite novelists. In addition to this wealth of complete stories, there is a large open- ing instalment of the long-expected sequel to She," by A. Rider Haggard. This story, under the title of " Ayesha, or the Return of' She,'" will fascinste the former subjects of " She-who-must-be-obeyed "and new. devotees alike. More than seventeen years have elapsed since the world was first spell-bound by the wonderful romance which led them through Kar, with its haunted tombs of a thousand ages, to the feet of Ayesha,, the strange and beautiful, whose supernatural .beauty and wisdom involved the whole great riddle of immortality, yet seemed to perish in the flames. How far that passing was from real extinction the author now sets forth to show in a narrative which will enthral public attention even more completely than the original She." The other leading serial feature will be a succession of romantic stories (each complete in a number, yet forming a connected story) by those famous writers, Agnes and Egerton. Castle. This series, under the title of "If Youth but Knew," will be found to surpass in vigour and charm even the former romantic successes of these clever collaborators. Many other important articles and enteri taming stories help to swell a bumper number, which throughout- is superbly illustrated, and to the whole is added a beautiful photgravure plate of Mr. Briton Riviere?s flue picture St. George." Altogether an amazingly fine number, and one that it is difficult to e onceive being bettered.

Run-through in-offs into baulk pocket,. Position L—red ball touching the cushion and 18 nches from the pocket, Cue ball 3 inches from he side cushion and 1 inch out of baulk. Position I—red ball touching the cushion and 23 inches rom tho baulk line, cue ball 10 inches rom the side cushion and 43 inches from the top ushion.

Diagram 32 shows two further positions for mn-through in-offs against the nap. In position 1- the run-through should be played with check - iide—left hand side in the diagram—just as :hough the stroke were being played with the lap, for the simple reason that as the cue ball 'as so short a distance to travel before it reaches :he pocket, the check side has practically no time to pull the ball much away from the lide cushion, and even though the ball may-be railed away a little, the check side has the ad- mntage of being pocket side off the opposing angle, and the pocket is thereby greatly enlarged. rhe stroke should not, however, be played too ;lowly as the more slowly the cue ball travels ;o3 the pocket, the more will the check side pull :he ball away from the side cush:on. .any case the stroke requires careful hand- ling, as the cue ball can only be got at by eaning well over the table. Were the balls on. he other side of the table, the stroke would )e still more difficult, as the long rest would have n be used. The run-through in-off shown at position B 3/1 Diagram 32 is an awkward one as owing eo the considerable distance the cue ball has to Tavel before reaching the pocket, check side nay easily pull it. too much away from the side :ushion to allow the pocket being found, not- arith-:ti,nding that the check side is pocket side off the baulk cushion angle. On the other hand, if running side be used, unless the ball, cora- mences to hug the cushion at once, the distance ± has to travel may not be quite sufficient to I.llow it to develop that clinging-to-the-cushion chid of motion, which is always necessary to !arry a ball into a pocket when playing these running-side run-throughs against the nap of the cloth. In any case when playing the stroke shown in position B on Diagram 32, if check side be used the stroke should be played at a pretty fast pace in order to reduce t-he effect of side against the nap of the eloth. Also for the same reason it is as well aot to strike the cue-ball with very much side. If on the other hand the stroke be played with run- ning side, as much side as possible should be imparted to the cue-ball and only medium pace should be used in order to give full play to the running side against the nap, the effect of which Is to cause the cue-ball to hug the cushion. The stroke could also be played without any side- at all, simply playing. at high speed full on to :-.le object ball and striking the cue-ball well above the centre.

Generally speaking, in all cases of run-throughs into a baalk pocket—the object ball being dead on a side cushion—check side should be used whenever the object ball is • not very far from the pocket, and running side should be used when the object ball is a long way from the pocket. When the object ball is above a centie pocket, running side must be used.
DIAGRAM 33.

to strike the cue-ball pretty high up and with plenty of left-hand side (were the balls on the other side of the table, right-hand side would, of course, have to be used), and aim must be taken full or almost full on to the object ball. Played in this way, the cue-ball will appear as though it is going to miss the red by inches, but the side which. it carries working against the nap of the cloth will gradually pull it towards the cushion, and the pull will be more and more apparent the nearer the cue-ball approaches the red, the reason of this being that as the pace of the ball slackens the effect of the nap increases. In fact, in play- ing such a stroke the clie-ball will often, reach the cushion some little distance away from the object ball and then hug the cushion all the way down to the ball. Naturally the position is a better one when the second object ball is the red (as shown on the ,liPgram) and not the white, for when the strokr.?. is well played the cannon will generally be made so full on to the second ball that often nothing but a pot into the baulk pocket will be left for the next stroke. div.head: NOTES ON THE GAME BETWEEN ROBERTS
div.p: NOTES ON THE GAME BETWEEN ROBERTS
AND INMAN.

The wonderful popularity of John Roberts was again proved by crowded houses afternoon and evening throughout the whole week at Messrs. Orme and Sons' large billiard hall, notwithstanding the fact that it was Roberts's third consecutive week in Manchester. Though Roberts hardly played as well as in his match against Harverson the previous week, he made many good breaks, and his play was as fascinating as ever to watch. Inman gave a most consistent display, and he was almost always the first to reach his points, and in the end wen by 746, the final scores being: Inman (rec. 2,750 9,000 Roberts Perhaps the most interesting feature of the match was Inman's break of 183, as the last 152 points of this break were scored off the rei ball. The break was note- worthy for the number of times that Inman had to play the long in-off into a top-pocket. Time after time the red ball, after striking the top and siie cushions, did not travel far enough down the table to leave a centre pocket in-off on, so that a top pocket had again to be resorted to. I was seated at the baulk end of the table in a favourable position to judge the angle, and several times, had the red ball been an inch 'or two nearer to baulk. the centre pocket in-off would have been on. In fact, more than once Inman placed his ball at the extreme edge of the D for a centre pocket in-off, but found that the stroke was just not on. Had he been playing with crystalate balls the break might easily have been much bigger, for often he would have been able to make use of the centre pocket instead of the top, owing to a crystalate rball coming off so much wider than an ivory ball when playing with extreme side, and no player needs telling bow much better it is to be able to play for centre pockets instead of top pockets, not only for the far greater certainty of the stroke itself, but also for the much greater ease with which the red ball may be brought into good position again. (My readers may remember that I went very fully into this question in an article on SIDE, which appeared in these columns some few weeks ago.) The very stroke that Inman I broke down at was a long in-off into a top pocket, a stroke that no professional really likes, and with cryfita- la te balls Inman could have played for the centre pocket. I had a chat with Inman after the break was over, and he fully agreed with all that I have now written con- cerning his great break off the red. `q Next week some notes will be given on the game at present in progress between Roberts and Bateman particularly on Roberts's great break, which at the time of writing these notes stands at 592 unfinished.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Workhouse Extension.

A meeting of this Board was held at the Workhousp on Wednesday, Mr. A. Brooks presiding. There werb also present :—Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson, the Rev. Father Mercer, Messts. A. J. Jolley, G. Mather, R. Forshaw, S. Davies, J. Payton, J. Flannagan, Mr. W. Seton, W. Houghton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. F. Avvbery, (master), and A. Wright (superintendent of Padgate schools). THE UNEMPLOYED QUESTION.---LARGE INCREASE OF VAGRANTS.

At a meeting of the House Committee, the Master reported a large increase in the number of vagrants. The total number of people in the House on Friday last was 495 as compared with 513 of the same date last year, a decrease of 18. The vagrants relieved during the previous week numbered 426 as against 308 for the corresponding week last year, an increase of 118 Some discussion took place with respect to the futility of ordering out of the Workhouse men to seek employ- ment and who mostly returned the same or following day ; also the growing force of unemployed who .are unable through various circumstances to obtain em- ployment, chiefly owing to the changed industrial con- ditions now prevailing. Ultimately the committee re- q tested the master to read a brief paper at their next meeting dealing with the problem and what appeared to be the solution thereof, so far as it affected the admis- sion into the workhouse of men still capable of working for their living. On the motion of Mr. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. Fort- SHAW, the minutes were approved. •

THE WORKHOUSE EXTENSION. The CLERK read a letter from Mr. Edward Lees, Rssistant secretary of tne Warrington branch of the Independent Labour Party, containing the following teselution :—" That this branch of the Independent Labour Party protests against the proposed extension of the Workhouse, believing that the circumstances can be better overcome by a reasonable extension, of out- door relief, instead of by the spending of a large amount of money upon a new building, with the additional expenditure in furnishing and providing an addition to the permanent staff, and we trust that the Board will re-consider the whole question." Mr. FORSHAW M )ved that the letter be suitably acknowledged. He thought it was little short of impertinence for people outside who could not be acquainted with the state of the House to tell the Board they did not know what they were doing. Mr. JOLI.EY seconded, and the motion was agreed to without further comment.

div.head: Puzzled Politician.
div.p: A Puzzled Politician.

Sir,—l should be pleased to have the opinion of your readers on the following subject : If a manthinks that some change is desirable , in our fiscal policy and that dumping ought td be prevented, that we oughtnot to allow bounty-fed goods to be deli4ered without a tax and free into the "(hilted Kingdom, if that man con- siders that the Education Act of 1902 is one of the 'worst and most unjust measures passed into law by any Government in the memory of living man, what ought he to do at the next Parliamentary election? Ought he to suitport a Liberal or a Conservative or ought he to leave them both severely alone? Is the country properly and truly represeute,d, or is there a lot of humbug ?—Yours truly, SAMBO.

The Extension of the Workhouse. Sir,—ln order to stop any further communications from outsiders, would it not be best for tke Guardians at their next meeting to test the matter by a decisive vote as to whether they are determined to go on with the extension at once, or accede to the request of a large number of ratepayers to delay the matter for a year or two. The latter should not be treated with con- tempt; besides, the Guardians themselves are very divided on the question. To shelve it altogether is almost out of the question. It is a pity that the rate- payers who are now cryinc, out against the scheme did not assist those members of the Board who, in the first instance, wished the matter to be delayed for a year or two, when it might have had some weight ; and not have waited until all arrangements had been made.— Yours &c.,
GUARDIAN.

Rev. H. Dunnico and Councillor Ellison. Sir —ln your issue of last week you published a letter from Councillor Ellison under the heading 'Councillor Ellison corrects the Rev. H.Dunnico." Might I suggest that such a discription is misleading. Councillor Ellison did not correct me. As stated last week regret having used the word compelled." It is perhaps impossikle to" compel "any man ID° apologise. If, however, the word" induced" is substituted for the word " compelled" my statement of the facts of the case is an accurate one. Councillor Ellison states that he gave" a plain straightforward statement of the facts of the case." I accept that version but in order that there may be no cause for mistmderstanding I venture to explain the meaning of that phrase. Briefly the " statement " may be summarised as follows: (1.) Councillor Ellison stated that he did net vote for Mr. Roberts. (2.) That he withdrew his support from Mr. Roberts prior to the election. 1'3.) That he regretted having done what he had and admitted that he had made a mistake. (4.) That he would not do such a, thing again if placed in the same circumstances. Whether this ought to be described as "a plain straight- forward statement" or "an apology," is a matter hardly worth discussing. It was on the strength of that state- ment and in view of the splendid service rendered to the cause of temperance by Councillor Etlison that the resolution referred to was carried. In conclusion I would again repeat that I have no desire to do Councillor Ellison an injustice. I regret that I used the word "compelled." Moreover I am extremely annoyed that such a regrettable incident has been re-introduced:into the colamns *of the press at this late date. This is the last letter I shall write in a controversy (unsought by me) unless compelled to do so in self- defence. Moreover I have written this purely in the interests of the "Temperance party" and in order to show that those of us who feel called upon to uphold the temperance flag will not allow any man (Trader or Non-trader) to play fast and loose with the principles .of the sacred cause we have at heart—Yours truly, HERBERT DUNNICO.

div.p: Our Markets -Parr Hall Set vices

- --- Sir,—lt has been of no little interest to me to read the correspondence in your paper these last few weeks e.t.a am glad that at least one of your readers has been roused to resent and protest against the filth, dirt and unhealthy odour permeating the fish market as the restilt of decomposition of fish and insufficient cleans- ing. Fos a considerable time it was my veryunenviable lot to be employed in the market area, and not once or twice but times without number I have gone hone after finishing my day's work unable to touch my food through nausea caused by the refuse and smell of bad fish &c. L.W.E. is right—the results even:from an heredi- tary point of view—trifling as that nay seem to passers by—are more far reaching and disastrous than appears on the -surface. I hope some decided steps will be taken as a matter of duty, by those who the ratepayers pay to do the duty.—Yours sincerely,
SANITUS.

Sir,—l think it is high time for some one to raise a solemn protest, in view of the startling events that have happened of late, and when we look at the sad use of the pulpit, in Scotland and Wales, where rivals stand face to face denouncing each other in God's House. Is it not meat humiliating to find men calling them- selves Christian preachers making such an exhibition of themselves aid encouraging strife and hatred? Are we not drifting, here in Warrington, to a low standard of Christian wership,when we find any minister encouraging his congregation to applaud hint, whilst attacking his opponents,. who dare to oppose him whether privately or politically. As a Nonconfevraist, I protest against the use of the pulpit, for personal or political purposes. Multitudes are still outside our churches, but their conversion will not be accomplished by examples of strife and passion. I trust your many readers will give expression in their own way upon this subject. —Yours Scc., DISGUSTED.

Sir,—l am a regular reader of your newspaper, and have come to the coluilasion that your correspondent, L. W. E. is an arrant coward. Mr. Dunnico has nothing whatever to fear from such. The magnificent receptios given to him in the Parr Hall on Friday last and then :again on Monday, along with the thousands who sit under his ministry week by week recompense him for the vulgar attacks made upon him by L. W. E.and his particular clique. If Mr. Dunnico will take my advice he will ignore all •Such epistles and persons. Everybody whose good opinion is worth having Imo ars full well that he is Sincere in all that he does. He is simply undermining his constitution and wasting valuable time by troubling himself with newspaper correspondence. The people of Warrington know that he is able to take care of him- self when necessary, and on that account I advise him to go on with his work. His numerous friends will be therewhen wanted. lam looking forward to L.W.E.'s introduction to the Markets Committee.—Yours truly, FAIR-PLAY.

your issue of the 26th inst. under the above I heading I notice another letter signed " I admit that your correspondent has in his previous letters advocated some very necessary reforms in regard to cleansing our markets more thoroughly, but if our friend is so much in earnest about this matter let him make a personal appeal to the members of the Markets Committee as he threatens to do and perhaps some good will come of it. It is doubtful, however, if he will have the courage to do this, for the simple reason that he has been afraid to disclose his identity in any of his letters up to date.lt isneedless for him to get impatient because other people do not move in this matter. This is not the only evil men have to deal with at the present time, and as this subject was first introduced by " L.W.E." it is not fair that be should expect other people to fire the bullets after he has made them. It is rather strange (and yet not altogether so, because it seems to be quite the fashion) that the name of the Rev. Herbert Dunnico should be dragged into this correspondence. Why ,should he be the only minister to be individually criticised when there are many others in the town who apparently have not half the grit and manliness to speak out fearlessly for the truth as Mr. Dunnico does. Taking the so-called "Parr Hall parson" all round, I question whether there is another who preaches a purer gospel, or who teaches higher ideals, or who carries out the laws of godliness, truth and love and the example of Christ better than he does. I do not know what "L.W.E." is,he may be a Socialist' or something else, but I take it from his letter he is not a Christian, nor does he appear to understand Christianity, because quite two-thirds of his letter is devoted to airing what I call his misconception of the religion of Jesus Christ. He seems to have a very poor opinion Christianity and Christians generally, but I believe tlfe former is true; whilst with regard to the latter, the e are many who call themselves Christmas but are only nominally so. The religion taught by Christ is "Love the Lord,thy God with all thy mind, il,nd soul, and strength, and thy neighbour as thyself,' and if this golden rule was accepted and adopted by all men, we should not have so much misery, poverty, degradation and sorrow, so many "sick and despairing hearts" in the world as we have at the present day. It is only as we apply this rule that we can be of real service because it not only includes a spiritual, but also a practical method of helping our fellow creatures. Our friend cannot give the people anything better than real Christianity to enable them to rise to something higher and better than their present condition both spiritually and materially. The great drawback of to-day, that which stands in the way of all true pro-

div.p: gross, that which prevents the uplifting of the masses to a truer and nobler plane of life, is not Christianity, but selfishness. If Christ's injunction "Do unto others as you would they should do unto you," was only accepted by our politicians, our great men, employers offlabour, and also by the working classes themselves, I believe we should have a better state oV things. Now if Mr. Dunnico can attract to Parr Hall men who have not been in the habit of attending places of worship, but who have hitherto wasted their time in other ways not to their credit or benefit, and if by his plain and straightforward preaching he can induce them, as I believe he has induced many, to become sober, thought- ful and steady men, good citizens, husbands and fathers then I say he is doing a great and glorious work, and all honour and Godspeed to him. With reference to the children who search for rotten fruit, &c., in our markets, I may say thatlwhilst I believe the eating of this refuse thust have a bad effect upon their health, yet Ido not believe they are all "poor, underfed children," nor do many of them come from the slums. I have seen lots of well-dresse4 and apparently well-fed boys rooting amongst the refuse heaps, and I am certain they were not so unclean in body and soul as "L. W. B." makes out. Many of them belong to respectable parents and good homes, and although some of them maybe poor,l do not doubt they are children whb get a plentiful supply of the ordinary luxuries of life. Then in regard to the poor urchins , whom your correspondent heard singing Christmas hymns as Christmas carols, I agree with him that the Majority of them do not sing in praise, but for a modest copper, and I should say also, in many cases, for the fun of the thing. By the way let me remind our friend they are not all Christians who turn these children away from their doors with "hard words and empty bags," and again what reasonable minded person would countenance such indiscreet giving as " L.W.E." seems to advocate? There are so many claims upon the purses of people now-a-days,so`much extra to be spent on thenecessaries of life,so many organised charities to support. So great are the claims made upon the money of an people, and especially Christian people, that they are obliged to brinecommonsense to bear upon their almsgiving. In conclusion I trust our friend will not think me unkind if I ask him in a straightforward way. What is he doing in a practical manner to make this town and , onr:country better for his livinglin it? Let him write and talk as mach as he likes, but above arl let him ,do something practical. Ido not ask him to answer me this question but leave him to settle the matter with his own conscience.—Yours ere., E. W. EVANS,

div.head: MR. PHILIP SNOWDEN AT ' WARRINGTON.
div.p: MR. PHILIP SNOWDEN AT ' WARRINGTON.
The Progress of the Labour Movement.

Mr. Philip Snowden, chairman of the Independent Labour Party, visited Warrington on Wednesday even- ing, and addressed a meeting held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, under the auspices of the local branch of the party. There was a large and enthusiastic audience, Mr. James Ball, elective auditor, presiding. The CHAIRMAN expressed the hope that when the next election came, their friend Mr. Snowden would be returned to represent Blackburn in the interests of labour. (Applause.) He proceeded, to refer to the Increase in wealth production during the nineteenth century. There was, he said, more than sufficient for all the people who dwelt in the land and yet there were numberless men, women, and children who were ill-clad, badly-fed, and badly housed. Instead of being used for the development of human life, wealth production was simply kept for profit: The mere maintenance of Free Trade would not cure the evils they deplored. The policy of Protection in other countries had not cured this disease of the social organism. If they were going to attain proper conditions they must have those who valued human life put forward upon governing and administrativelbodies. The Independent Labour Party existed to further that object. '(Applause). Mr. PHILIP SNOWDEN, who was enthusiastically re- ceived, said it was three years and a half since he last visited Warrington. During that period great things had happened in the fortunes of the labour movement of Great Britain. He was glad to know that the labour movement in Warrington had shared in the prosperity and success of the general labour movement during the last few years. The Independent Labour party was • started a dozen years ago with a very clear and definite object. It arose primarily out of the discontent of a number of earnest reformers who were very much dis- satisfied With the past achievementsof political parties and with the uses to which democratic political power had been pat. They believed in the possibility of creating a political party which would use political power in order to redress the glaring anomalies of enormous wealth on the one hand and abject poverty on the other. Speaking as one knowing something el the state of the labour movement and from his close connection with all sections of it, he could say that they were more than satisfied With the progress they had made. (Applause). They had already done what they started to apcomplish. They had for the first time in British history laid deep, solid, and permanent the foundations of a democratic Labour party. (Applause.) They had to-day associated with the Independent Labour movement in Great Britain a larger number of adherents than were connected with either of the two other political parties. (Applause.) In everything that went to constitute a political party they were the greatest political party in Great Britain to-day. That to some might appear to be a somewhat audacious claim to make. They had, however, a larger membership than that of either of the other political parties, probably than both combined. They who were connected with the Labour party believed that those who professed membership of political parties should contribute to the funds. They had a Million and a half of men and women identified With the political 'labour movement, an./ all of them were bringing forth fruits meet for their political salvation, by paying for their own polities. (Applause.) The labour movement of to-day had become recognized as a permanent abiding factor in British polities. They were surrounded by those who would seduce them on every hand. Every temptation was placed in their way to try and win them from the path of rectitude and independence. He did not say they had passed all difficulties, but he was quite certain that they had got too far and their progress was too real for the present labour movement ever to become the political disaster which was the fortune of former attempts to form an independent workers' party. (Applause.) The idea of those who had been associated with the movement had been not merely to form a political party composed of manual workers but a party composed of all who were in general agreement in regard to what was justice for labour and in regard to certain labour principles. (Hear, hear). They appealed mainly to the working classes because it was the condition of the working classes which had been so shamefully neglected by politicians in the past. (Applause.) The united labour movement was a combination of the Independent Labour Party, the socialists, the trade unionists, and to somelextent, and they hoped by and' by to a larger extent, the Co-operative movemant (Applause.) These bodies had combined because it had been recognized that there was a "great deal in common between the movements, that they really had the same object in view. It was an evidence of the expansion of the original trade union idea that now the phrase of "A fair day's wage for a fair day's work" had been superseded by the demand that labour should have everything to which, in justice it was entitled. (Ap- plause.) If they clung to the old methods or trade unionism, relying only upon voluntary association and leaving politics entirely in the possession of the other side, it would be quite impossible for labour to emerge successfully from any great conflict. There was no need for him to spend five minutes in reminding them of the iniquities of the Government with which the country had been cursed for the last ten years. All he had to say was that they (the workers) had invited all they had received, and therefore they ought to be blessed, for did not one of the modern beatitudes say "Blessed is he that gets what he wanted, for he has not been rdeceivedj" ? (Laughter.) Continuing, Mr. Snowden said there were forces at work which would compel the co-operator before long to place himself side by side with the trade unionist and other members of the workingclasses who were united to work out their industrial emancipation. So long as the co-operative movement confined itself almost exclusively to the distribution of goods made by private capitalists, so long would private capitalists tolerate the movement. But let the competition of the co-opera- tive system interfere with the profits of private capitalism and the, final struggle would be indeed imminent. It was quite true that one of the political parties was never tired of telling the Labour party that it agreed with nine-tenths of what they (the Labour party), said, and yet it never missed an opportunity of trying to ridicule their socialism. and to prove the impracticability of every item in their programme. Mr. Chamberlain had promised them a general election after a reasonable time had expired. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Snowdon) did not care how soon that time came, for so far as the Labour party were concerned, they were ready for Mr. Chamberlain and for all other opponents who had the courage to enter the arena. (Applause.) He was quite certain that, let the general election come sooner or later, the one party which was going to emerge from the [conflict having proved beyond the possibility of a doubt that it had a future before it in which it would unite the whole of the democratic forces of the country would be the Indepen- dent Labour Party. (Applause.) He believed the main sins of omission on the part of politicians in the past were due not to heartlessness or selfishness, but to an utter ignorance of the condition of the people. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Snowden alluded to Sir Henry Campbell- Bannerman's reception of a deputation of Manchester unemployed. He would not be so dishonest as to impute to Sir Henry any crime greater or more illeimons than that of absolute ignorance of the conditions. How could men in his position, how could Mr. Balfour from the comfort of a fur-lined overcoat and £40,000 a year understand the position of a starving man unable to

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 3, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 3, 1904.

find work? With all the heart in the world, it was an 1 intellectual impossibility for such men to appreciate the gravity of the industrial situation and to do what the necessities of the case demanded. The other political questions on which the coming election would be fought sank into absolute insignificance when compared with the terrible gravity of want of work. (Applause.) Iflthe next Liberal Government made an honest attempt to carry nine-tenths of the Labour party's programme into effect he wouldpledge the Labour party that the Liberal Government would receive no more earnest and whole- hearted support in their endeavour than from the Labour group in Parliament. (Applause). They, were deter- mined to build up a party which should be the biggest and most powerful political party ever known in the history of the country. They would never be content until they had placed in Parliament a sufficient number of men not only to exercise a dominating influence on legislation but tO take the reins of Government them- selves. (Applause).
