• A. H. Rathbone,the Secretary of the Latchford Club, writes :-:—Allow me to correct your report of the result of the Bankfield and, Latchford match in your last Saturday's issue. You therein represented the match as being won by Bankfield,by one goal to nil, whereas the result was a draw of one goal each, Latchford playing one sub. one reserve, and one man short, having no outside right during the whole otthe game, and I think I may safely say that the game even with this weakened team, was in Latchford's favour, and that the visitors had hard lines in not winning.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football. (By " Ovalist.",

Warrington were tot expected to win on Saturday at Hanslet, but out of sheer colAraryness they did so. This is their first victory on Yorks soil this season, and should do them a power of good. Need- less to say the result was the cauae of much satisfac- tion in Warrington, where ninety-nine people out of every hundred had no idea that football was possible anywhere, seeing that Warrington was shrouded in impenetrable fog, and the ground was hard as iron. However, the conditions were different in Yorks, and even in places much nearer home—l hear that there was bright sunshinA on the Appleton Golf links all 1 afternoon—and football was quite uninterrupted. There had been much more snow at Leeds, and this sufficed to keep the ground warm, for when cleared the turf was found to be soft and perfectly playable.

The fact that the side was practically at full strength must have encouraged the Warrington men. Boardman came back to the forwards' and his presence is always felt by somebody. Anyhow he gave this particular section of the team the required stiffening, and the eight fairly astonished. the Hunslet natives at times. The homesters were certainly handicapped by the absence of three good forwards in Glew, Wilson, and Barradough, but there was no scamity of substitutes. Three thousand spectators assembled to witness what is always an interesting game, and usually a victory for Hunslet. Warrington have been made to look very small fry once or twice at Parkside, and their triumph on Saturday was quite exhilarating—to the favoured few from Warrington.

Throughout, the game was of a lively order, and clever movements from each side followed each other rapidly. Warrington early showed that they meant to have possession of the ball, and consequently there was seine hand to hand passing on the visiting side which caused Goldthorpe, Brother and Co. consider- able trouble. Nevertheless, the home team was the first to trouble the scorers, W. Goldthorpe putting over a penalty-kick. Goals are the usual preliminary to victory at Hunslet, and joy was expressed at the event. This was short-lived, however, for Fish equalised very neatly before the interval, at which time the teams crossed over on level terms.

Resuming, Hunslet attacked hotly and once more got ahead by the same means as before. fter this, Warrington took the bit between their teeth, so to speak, and rushed the burly Parksiders to the verge of the line. Here the two Davies' s combined cleverly, and the younger one parting nicely to Ishervrood, the centre dashed over in fine style. Fish adding a goal from a none too easy angle. This apparently gave the homesters a stimulus and by desperate efforts they got within hailing distance of the Warrington goal. Albert immediately popped the ball over and brought the flunslet score to within one point of Warrington's. The atmosphere fairly quivered and the snow melted with excitement after this, but Warrington kept their heads—and the ball when they could—and Henslet were compelled to admit defeat by one point.

farring- Warm praise is unquestionably due to the Vi ton forwards for the way they buckled to ups'et the calculations of the Homesters. As a rule the Hunslet forwards are able to do just what they like with War- rington at Parkside, and the consequence has been that the Warrington backs have had small chance of distinguishing themselves. On Saturday, Warrington controlled the paeks remarkably well, and the rear division was kept In full occupation. The two , Davies's passed out smartly, and were always a bit ahead of the home pair. It was superior finish which pulled Warrington, through and got them the only try of the match. Ishm. v » and Fish were con- tintally to the fore, and it was gratifying to see the centre displaying something like his old form. Hallam also came out of a trying ordeal well. More than once he saved the situation when a score seemed certain, but this is characteristic of him especially away from home. The two Goldthorpes again proved themselves the most reliable men on the home side. But for them Hunslet would sink rather rapidly in the League table.

. -- Oldham were again concerned in the best nerf mn- ance of the day, but this time they were on the losing side. Leeds certainly accomplished a remarkable performance in taking down the leaders at Water- sheddings, though two clubs named Warrington and Leigh had previously morally accomplished the feat. Leeds made no mistake about it as the score of S-2 shows plainly. Wigan and Bradford drew after a great strirggle, so Oldham still hold pride of place. No scorifig at all happened in the matches betwecn Swinton and Hull, and Batley and Wakefield. Poor Leighlsuccumbed by 2 goals to 1 against Hull Kings- ton Rovers after having'aad all the game and, as usual a try disallowed. The Mather-Laners will have to take their own referee with them yet !

To-day Warrington appear at home again and will doubtless get a rousing reception. Widnes furnish the opposition, and though I cannot expect a good game, thore will be a keen struggle, Widnes as a rule do not play football when they come to Warrington, but go in for spoiling the well meant efforts of the home side. There should be no question about the result. Both fore and aft Warrington ought to prove much the stronger side. And it must not be forgotten that four points are at stake in this match!
Hockenhall takes his place again in the first team to-day vice Jack Davies. Otherwise the side is the same as against Hunslet and should be capable of giving a good display.

The " A " team will have a severe task at Widnes to keep their record from being broken, but a good side will make the journey, viz., Knight, full back ; Brooks, Berry, Roberts, Short, threequarters ; Duck- worth and Jordan, half backs • Morrison, Coleman, Hewitt, Lunt, and Harmer, forwards. J. Davies has been rather severely knocked about in his last two matches, and is in consequence having a week's rest.

Hockey. BY R.G.P.] Last week's frost caused a blank day in the hockey world, none of the class clubs being able to fulfil the fixtures, owing to the hardness of the ground. Stock- ton Heath first eleven should have played at home, and seeing that they have up to the present played six matches away and only one at home, this was somewhat unfortunate.

This week Stockton Heath first eleven travel to Western (Manchester), and a good level game should result. The following teams have been chosen to repre- sent Stockton Heath :—First (away), R. G. Pierpoint goal ;E. E. Woods ad L. Fairclough, backs ; J.

div.head: IRON TRADE.
div.p: THE IRON TRADE.
Midland Iron and ,Steel Wages Board.
TO BE OR NOT TO BE.

The meeting of the standing committee of the Mid- land Iron and Steel Wages Board on Thursday, Sir Benjaman Hingley, Bart, presiding—was of mere than usual importance inasmuch as the question of the fu- ture of the board and the sliding scale came up for consideration. It will be remembered (says the Birmingham Post) that the operatives' section gave notice to terminate the sliding scale, and that out of this action arose the whole question of the future of the board. A canvass of the trade was made in order to obtain additional support,and it was understood that the result was to be reported to the meeting. Much unneces- sary reticence was displayed concerning the:report and the deliberations of the committee. At first there was an attempt to limit the official communication to the statement of the fact that it had been decided to lay the whole matter before a full meeting of the board to be held on December 12. It scarcely needs to be pointed out that reticence on such a matter is likely to produce the opinion that the result of the recentinquiry has been adverse, and that the members of the committee are at variance—an opinion which is not calculated to improve the future prospects of the boaid. As a matter of fact, however, we are able to state that the result of i the canvass s regarded favourably, and that the committee will be justified in recommending the continuance of the board. As to the sliding scale the position is less simple. Wages will continue to be regulated by it until February 4, but so far nothing further seems to have been done to put the scale on the new basis for which the operatives are asking, and as at present intended the accountants will not be revired to take out the returns for November and December of this year. This latter result alone is regrettable, for the omission will cause a gap in the periodical returns.of the Board, which at present form the only measure—and a very scanty one at that—of the condition of the trade. It is therefore to be hoped that the instruction to the accountants will be con- tinued, even if the figures are not used for the settle- ment of wages in February next. In the interval it will remain for the standing committee to devise such an amendment of the scale as will prove acceptable to I both sides. Concerning wages, the accountants certified that they had examined the returns of iron made by the eleven selected firms for the months of September and October, 1904, and had verified the same with their books. They certified'the net average selling price to have been £63s. 9.11 d. The return of the different kinds of iron and the average selling price of each was as follows:

Tons. 2 s. d. Bars Angles and tees Plates and sheets 1,751 6 16 10.03 Hoop and strip and miscellaneous 5,030 518 10.02 The total quantity in round figures was 27,429 tons. In accordance with the resolution dated July 315t,1902 the rate of wages for puddling remains Bs. Gd. per ton and millmen's wages are in proportion. The rate remains in operation until Saturday, February4tb 1905. In one respect the return is slightly more favourable than .hat of the preceding two months—viz., the out- put shows an increase of 2,207 tons, which is spread over each of the items. The average selling prices, however, are shown to have continued their downward Icourse, the general average being 2s. 2•42 d. less. The detailed comparison with the preceding two months shows the following increases and decreases :—Bars increase 1,671 tons, decrease is. 1.75 d. ; angles and tees, increase 117 tons, decrease 155 d.; plates and sheets, increase 120 tons, decrease is. 1.44 d. ; hoops, Scc., increase 299 tons, decrease is. 8.26 d. When compared with the return for September and October last year, the follow- ing results are shown :—General average, us. 610 d decrease ; total output, 3,857 decrease; bars, decrease. 1,469 tons, decrease 10s. 748 d.: angles and tees decrease 214 tons, decrease 12s. 5•88 d. ; plates an sheets, decrease .904 tons, decrease 15s. 5.25 d.: hoops, &c., decrease 1,268 tons, decrease us. 11•52 d.

div.head: COLLISION IN THE MERSEY. -- Five Runcorn Men Lost.
div.p: COLLISION IN THE MERSEY. -- Five Runcorn Men Lost.

A disastrous collision occured in the Mersey Channel off Formby on Wednesday, seven seamen, including five Runcorn men being drowned. "The Blanche," a steamer of 86 tons register, belonging to Mr. William Dwland, of Liverpool, was making for that port with gravel from Fleetwood, and her cre,v of nine were experiencing the lively satis- faction of nearing home and friends, when a hopper, No, 66 from London, came into collision with the Blanche with disastrous results to the latter, which soon afterwards sank on what is known as Taylor's Bank. The hopper tried to get to Liverpool, but she was in evident difficulties, and was towed with the Vigilant to the New Bt ighton Lighthouse, near which she was beached. On Thursday morning she was found adrift, and was again beached between Seacombe and Brighton.

FIVE RUNCORN MEN LOST. Only two members of the crew of the Blanche sur- vived. Captain Ravenscroft, of Runcorn, aged 56, was her captain,and he had command of eight men. Their names were : Ralph Ravenscroft, of Runcorn, brother of the captain, aged 42. Andrew Rennie, 43, chief enginner, of Liverpool. John Jones, 25, second engineer, of Liverpool. Walter Cagill, 28, able seaman, of Runcorn. Ralph Rathbone, 50, fireman, of Runcorn. Robert Harrison, 26, able seaman, of Runcorn. John Gibson. 70, able seaman, of Runcorn. Harry Constantine, 28, fireman, address unknown. The only survivors were engineer, Jones, who lives at 84, Cleopas-street, Toxtetb, and Robert Harrison, of 36, Bold-street, Runcorn. The engineer Jones has narrated a story of terrible privation endured by the survivors. A number of men managed with great difficulty to clamber on to the up- turned keel of a boat, and in spite of the swell righted her and rowed away in the hope of reaching Formby lightship. Three of the party were soon carried away by the waves and three died from sheer exhaustion. Harrison and Jones then had the boat to themselves. Finally it drifted ashore on Taylor's Bank, and these two men, leaving their deal companions, dragged themselves, in spite of their cold, exhausted condition, to the sewage pumping house, where such comforts as were available were placed at their disposal.

div.head: BIG RECREATION SCHEME. Messrs. Crosfield's Employees
div.p: BIG RECREATION SCHEME. Messrs. Crosfield's Employees
Intended Venture.

We understand that the Labour Council representing the employees of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, proposes to carry out an extensive recreation ground scheme for the benefit of the workpeople. Every employee of the firm contributes weekly one penny towards a recreation fund, and there is a considerable sum in hand. The idea is to secure a plot of land out- side the town—Sankey is suggested—with a view to building a club house, and providing a bowling green, cricket and football field. Such a general recreation ground would undoubtedly be a great boon to the large number of employees at Bank Quay. We hope to be able to give further particulars s'wtiv.

div.head: SUCCESS OF GROSFIELD'S BAND.
div.p: THE SUCCESS OF GROSFIELD'S BAND.
DINNER AND CONCERT AT THE WORKS.
Mr. A. H. Crosfield and Recreation.

It was a notable day in the history of Messrs. Crosfield's band when the members had the honour of winning the handsome fifty-guinea. challenge cup in the national junior competition at the Crystal Palace. Besides speaking volumes for the good training and perseverance of the instrumentalists, the victory was considered to reflect credit upon the town and hearty congratulations have been lavished upon the band. Mr. Arthur H. Crosfield,who has taken a great interest in the development of music at the works, decided to fittingly celebrate tha event by inviting a representa- tive gathering of employes to dine with him in the well-appointed'Assembly Room on Saturday evening. Occasion was also taken to present the workmen who had rendered twenty-five years' service and upwards to the firm, with beautifully framed photographs of themselves. The arrangements were in the hands of Mr. John Willett and Mr. T. Rigby, and the function passed off with gratifying success. The guestsnumbered 150, and included in addition to the members of the band, the managers, sub-managers, foremen, Works Council, Fire Brigade, a section of the Volunteer Com- pany and Ambulance Corps, the sick club committee, and long-service employes. The room which serves many admirable recreative purposes 'presented a bright and cheerful appearance, the tables being ornamented with choice flowers. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who had a very cordial reception on enter- ing the room, presided and was supported at the head of the table by Mr. F. J. Lord and Mr. F. Newall. Later in the evening Mr. Henry Roberts attended. An excellent dinner was well served by the Warrington I Cafe Company. After the tables had been cleared I the assembly settled down for an enjoyable smoking I concert and a little speech making. MR. CROSFIELD AND THE KING. HIS MAJESTY AS PEACEMAKER. In proposing the toast of " The King" Mr. Crosfield said: I know it is usual to submit this toast with very little preface but as I am speaking amongst friends, and as I have not mentioned the incident to you before, perhaps ladies and gentlemen you will be interested in knowing that before His Majesty ascended the throne I ha,d'the honour to meet him on several occasions. I believe I was one of the first who ventured to recommend the then Prince of Wales to try that royal and ancient game of golf,—l trust without detriment to state affairs. (Laughter). You all know the keen interest the King takes in those out door sports and games which are so associated with English life, and how admirablyhe combines them with all the work and responsibility upon his shoulders (Applause). Few men, lam sure, very few men, of his years lead a life so full of activity and energy as the King. (Hear, hear). In connection with to-night's proceedings I think algo we shall naturally recall the pleasure and delight theging himself takes in music,and his desire to see it spreading more and more widely among his people. (Hear,hear). The King has pointed out how it brings all classes closer together in more friendly contact and relation each with the other. But our King has done more than bring classes closer to- gether ; he has brought nation.s'together—(applause)— and his unfailing tact and dignity, kind heart and bon- homie and strong common sense have endeared him not only to our own people, but to all the other nations he has visited, and by his wise and courageous mission he has well earned the title of" Edward the Peacemaker." (Applause). lam not one of those who believe we can yet put an end to war. Science will hasten the day, as the hideous carnage and awful waste and misery it en- tails become more and more ghastly and more of a crime against civilisation. But even if the Western nations could settle their differences in other ways, it would still be necessary for a considerable time to maintain sufficient forces in Europe as a protection against the East. But meantime the grand principle of settling differences by arbitration) is making progress and that thanks chiefly to the efforts of strenuous men like the widely admired and respected President of the great republic of the west—(hear, hear,)—and the President of the French republic, and I must say most of all by the enormous influence and the good influence of our own King. (Loud applause.) The,toast was enthusiastically honoured, the National Anthem being sung. THE CONCERT.

The musical programme to which the company was then entertained, wasan unusually interesting one. The whole of the items were contributed by local artistes who acquitted themselves with great credit and were rewarded with hearty applause. The Warrington Male Voice Choir gave the choruses "Crossing the plains ", "Comrades' song of Hope" and" Martyrs of the arena" with fine spirit and expression, Mr. S. Hassall ably con- ducting. The amusing quartette "There was a tack" by a glee party selected from the choir proved a popular item, and Mr. J. Willett, jun., scored a success with an affective interpretation of " I seek for Thee in every flower." Master Tom Barton rendered a violin solo with taste and skill, and Mr. J. Corrin was heard to advantage in "Take a pair of sparkling eyes." The voices of Messrs. Hassall and Millington blended well in the duets " Two beggars" and" Flow gently, Davis" and Mr. G. Gough sang "The Young Royalist!' in highly creditable style. The flying Dutchman "was well sung by Mr. J. Broadhurst. The humour of the evening was supplied by Mr. P. Hignett who created great mirth and was enthusiastic- ally encored. Mr. F. Atkinson wasanable accompanist THE TOAST OF THE PRESIDENT.

Mr. JOSEPH TAYLOR, jun., proposed the toast of "The I President." Mr. Crosfield, he said, practically gave them the works band and he had helped them materially with his kind words and encouragement to attain the success they were noT/ celebrating. They trusted he might live long to assist them and to enjoy the greater successes which they hoped to win in the future. (Loud applause.) Mr. J. WILLETT added a few words. He said he had known the Crosfield family for about thirty-eight years and they had always been willing to do everything in their power for the benefit of the workingmen. (Ap- plause.) They ought to be proud to have Mr. Arthur Crosfield with them. They hoped he might have health and strength to fight the battle which lay before him and that he would be successful and become the representative of Warrington in the House of Commons. (Loud applause.) The toast was drunk with great enthusiasm, the assembly singing " For he's a jolly good fellow" and raising loud cheers. MR. CROSFIELD AND THE VALUE OF RECREATION. WHAT IS BEING DONE FOR THE FIRM'S EIVIPLOYEES.

In responding Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD said : Ladies and gentlemen, I thank you all for the cordiality and kind- ness of your reception, and Mr. Taylor for the nice things he has said about me. I also thank Mr. Willett for part of what he has said. (Laughter.) Some of you may know that I take an interest in politics; and in political work I one a great deal to Mr. Willett's zeal and energy. (Hear, hear.) But ladies and gentle- men, to-night is a night off. I am not going to be lured on to politics—(laughter)—even by my inde- fatigable friend Willett. (Hear, hear.) The only word I have to say on politics is this, that never since the firm was started in 1815 has favour on the one hand been shown in the matter of employment, or disfavour on the other because of a man's political opinions. (Hear, hear.) Neither my grandfather, the founder of the firm, nor my uncles would have allowed it; nor yet the late Chairman of the Company— (applause)—who was always in matters of religion and politics a strong advocate for toleration. Well to-night we meet to celebrate the victory of our band. (Loud applause). I have not been able to do much to further the musical development which has taken place amongst the employees of this firm of late years, but lam extremely glad to have been able to do a little,more particularly at the commencement. (Hear, hear.) We all appreciate the value of the good train- ing your conductor has given you, and on behalf of our Board I also want to thank those managers who have spent a good deal of time and trouble in helping this movement forward, and in the third place I wish most heartily to congratulate every member of the band who won the victory. (Loud applause.) We have every reason to be proud as a firm, and I hope it is not too much to say that. we may also as Warringtonian.s regard it as a very creditable performance. I hope we may .yet see the day when the band will achieve yet higher dis- tinction. (Applause.) This victory strikes as perhaps the most signal event that has occurred during the progres- sive movement to which I have alluded, and which has already helped to improve the conditions of employ- ment at Bank Quay. Id 9 not want to exaggerate what has been done, but I think any o'ne who reads the pamphlet describing our progress of late years will agree that we have all reason to feel great satisfaction in it. (Hear, hear.) Situated as we are in a town we are of course in some rErpects handicapped as against those firms whose factories are in the country. Never- theless a great deal has been done, and let me say at once on behalf of my co-directors as well as on my own account how glad we are that the Works Council has taken a prominent part in this advancement. Directors, and managers may assist with advice, and sometimes with pecuniary aid. That .is all right mid necessary but in the main we believe in THE -PRINCIPLE OF SELF HELP all through--(hear, hear,)—and we rejoice to see the Works Council take a keen interest in the work and largely supplying the initiative. If I may so express it we desire to see the Works Council the motor muscle in this progessive development—(applause)—and above all

things we want every man about the place to feel that he is a member of a concern which is foremost amongst the pioneers in England of a new and more enlightened system of Works government. (Loud applause.) Because then whether it be our lot to negotiate with competitors, or buyers, or sellers, or to manage a staff, or control machine, or work with our own hands and muscles, we shall in each and all of these different capacities take more pride in our work and feel more of that satisfaction on which Ruskin dwells in seeing the work well done. (Applause.) Speaking next about I music Mr. Crosfield said: I have before quoted in Warrington what Professor Huxley has said about literature, that it is the most enduring form of refined pleasure, and I think you will all agree that Professor Huxley is perfectly right in that. (Hear, hear.) But at the same time 'think that the

MOST REFRESHING FORM OF PLEASURE at all events after a good day's work, is music. (Hear, hear.) Some of you probably remember the xsthetic craze that swept over this country I think some fifteen years ago, when people dined off lilies and generally made themselves ridiculous. There is not much:of that left now-a-days and when a man tells me he cannot dis- tinguish " God Save the King" Asfrom the "Old Hundredth ", I fully respect him. (Laughter.) The dther day I attended n very interesting concert. and sitting next to me was a gentleman whom: I often meet in business. I won't mention his name or giveyou any clue to it, but do you know in the middle of a most interesting bit of music he began to whisper to me something about the advance or reduction in certain markets of the price of a commodity in which we are all interested. (Laughter.) When the concert was over I treated him to a little banter. But my friend was perfectly frank; he said, "When lam listen- ing to chamber music of that kind I feel exactly like a woman with a balance sheet in her hand; she can never tell why certain figures should be put on one side and certain figures on the other. (Laughter.) I simply cannot make head nor tail of this class of music you seem to so thoroughly enjoy." (Laughter rand cheers.) Fortunately there are very few people—and my friend is certainly not one of them—who have not a certain amount of latent capacity for music, if it is only developed. I have known many instances where people of the most wooden teraperament—(renewed laughter)— who, given time and opportunity, have developed a considerable amount of musical skill and taste. I remember my old music master at Uppingham—where my father sent me to school—talking about theldevelop- ment of musical taste that was taking place in England. It has gone on more rapidly since then. (Hear, hear.) Don't you think, ladies and gentlemen, this very development of !music in our own works is a significant fact and an illustmtioa of the way in which this 'refining in- fluence of music is permeating all ranks of the people. (Applause.) I know there are a great many other demands on your time and leisure, and of course it would be a great mistake if we devoted our attention exclusively to music. (Hear, hear.) If as the years run on I have an opportunity of furthering a taste for literature in any way, it would give me very great pleasure to make that endeavour. (Hear, hear,) Then we all like to encourage our HEALTHY OUT DOOR GAMES and athletics, which are of great value in developing the physique and morale of the people, strengthening the stamina of the race, yes, and I will say, building up English character. (Applause.) The works are well represented amongst the volunteers and I do hope that there will always be a substantial number of employees and a contingent of managers from these works who will devote themselves to that loyal and patriotic duty. (Applause.) There are several admirable institutions that have been organised to which I might allude, our fire brigade, of which we are very proud, our ambulance corps, our choir and so forth, but I will only repeat in conclu- sion that I am delighted the Works Council has taken such a keen interest in developing these admirable in- stitutions and societies which are of such benefit to our entire concern. I trust they will continue to flourish and prosper and so enable us to realise still better ideals and raise the old firm to a still higher and more honourable position in the country. (Loud applause.) -11 PRESENTATION TO OLD EMPLOYEES.".. VI r. CRISFIELD then performed the pleasing duty of presenting most of the following old employs with framed groups :—G. Glea,ve, 53 years' service': A. Middleton, 51 years; D. Smith, sen., 50 years; J. Law- ton, 44 years ; P. L. 11111, 41 years; M. Lomas, 41 years; J. Willett, 38 years; N. Hough, 37 years; G. Vernon 37 years ; W. Johnson, 35 years ; J. Hall, 34 years; J. Wynn, 32 years • J. Roughley, 32 years; P. Johnson, 30 years ; J. Kirkham, 30 years ; 'J. Unsworth, 29 years; T. Corkin, 29 years; T. Bridson, 28 years; J. Jackson, 26 years; H. Bloomfield, 26 years ; C. Harrison, 25 years; J. Caldwell, 25 years; A, Long, 25 years. Several of the veteran servants were prevented by indisposition from attending, and with these few exceptions all received their gifts at the hands of Mr. Crosfield. Mr. LOMAS referred to the remarkable growth of the firm during his connection with it. When he first joined the Istaff a field where rabbits disported themselves might be seen where part of the works now stood. He hoped the business would continue to prosper. (Ap- plause.) Mr. NATHAN HOUGH, who is associated with the shipping department, said that when he first became connected with the firm they had only two sailing flats. As showing how the business had prospered they had now six steamers and four flats. (Applause.) In handing a photograph to Mr. Long, Mr. Crosfield said the name of "Long," went back to the early days of the firm. The recipient's father, "Jacky" Long, was connected with the concern in the time of Mr. Joseph Crosfield. (Applause.) After the presentations Mr. Crosfield had to leave the gathering Co attend the Foresters' dinner at the Lion Hotel and the chair having been taken by Mr. Henry Roberts, the musical programme was resumed. SPEECH BY MR. H. ROBERTS. At the close, Mr. WILLETT proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Roberts whom, he said, some of them had known for a good number of years. He was a very active and energetic man and they were nleased to have him with them that evening. Mr. Willett also moved that the caterers and artistes be thanked. The vote was heartily accorded. In responding Mr. ROBERTS said he hoped he might as time went on, he more and more incorporated in what he might call the family /life of that great concern. (Hear, hear.) The particular and special duties which he had to perform did not come quite as closely in association with his hearers' daily life and occupation as those of the other directors, notably their very good friend Dr. Markel. (Applause.) At the same time there were many means by which perhaps he mirilit occasionally Toe of service to them in their individual capacities, and he hoped every man connected with the firm, as long as he (Mr. I Roberts) remained associated with it, would, if he had any desire to do so, look upon him (Mr. Roberts) as his personal friend. (Applause.) He had had a somewhat lengthy and varied experiencel and during the course of that experience he had picked up a little knowledge which occasionally turned out to be useful in more ways than at present he felt in- clined to refer to. There were occasionally times when a man wanted advice and assistance and so far as lay in his (Mr. Roberts's) power and so far as his ability and experience allowed him he would be only too happy at any time that the members of the concern, no matter what their positions were, individually or collectively, might come to him, and if he could be of use to them it would be/a pleasure to him to renderassistance. In conclusion Mr. Roberts paid a tribute to the admirable services rendered by the vocalists and expressed the hope that the company would have many other opportunities of listening to them. (Applause). The choir having rendered the part song "The long day closes " ahighly successful function concluded with the singing of the National Anthem. THE UNEMPLOYED.

div.head: Warrington Guardians and the Question.
div.p: Warrington Guardians and the Question.

The question of the unemployed in Warrington was discussed at considerable length at a meeting of the House Committee of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians, which was helA yesterday, and at which there was a full attendance of members. The Workhouse Master, Mr. J. F. Awbery, read a paper dealing with the question. He advocated the appointment of an additional relieving officer so that cases of out-relief could be more thoroughly inquired into and all improper cases refused. Without going into detail he suggested that the distress which existed might be met by the establishment of relief works upon I which men could earn sufficient to maintain themselves. Another method was by the proper organization of existing charities upon lines which had proved so suc- cessful whenever it had been adopted. By this means de- serving cases could be treated and the charities generally administered without the waste attendant upon the present organization. A long discussion ensued upDri the paper but the question of taking any action on the lines suggested by the master was adjourned to the meeting of the com- mittee to be held next Frilly week.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. The weekly meeting of the above society was held on Wednesday night in the Wesleyan schoolroom. Mr. T. Gandy occupied the chair. The appointed lecturer, Mr. Silcock, being unable to attend, Mr. Jenkins very kindly filled the gap, and gave an interesting account of " The lives of two working men." The paper was very well received, and at the conclusion Mr. Jenkins was accorded a hearty vote of thinks, on the motion of Mr. A. Birch (presi- dent),seconded bk Mr. J. Midwood. PRESENTAMON.—The Rev. John Gunnell having given up the leadership of the adult's week-night class meeting at the Wesleyan Chapel, the members met on Tuesday night to show their gratitude to the rev, gentleman for his labours on their behalf, by presenting him with a handsome lamp. Mr. George Faulkner, the present class leader, presided. Mr. T. Gandy made the presentation in a suitable speech, and his good opinion of Mr. Gunnell, was cordially endorsed by the members. Mrs. R. Garnett also made a few remarks. Mr. Gunnell acknowledged the gift and thanked them very much for their kindly thoughts of him.

div.head: FREE TRADE V. PROTECTION.
div.p: FREE TRADE V. PROTECTION.
SOCIAL SERVICE LEAGUE'S SPIRI TED
DEBATE.
Verdict for Free Trade.

It was generally understood that the subject dowiz for discussion at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Social Service League held on Thursday, was that of the respective merits of Free Trade and Protection as the fiscal policy for this country. Such, however, was not the case, as Alderman Bennett who led the debate took as his topic" Preferential trade in the Colonies as compared with our present fiscal system." The debate as usual, was held in the Golborne-street Schools and attracted a large attendance. The president of the League being absent when the proceedings were opened, the chair was occupied by Mr. Edmund Osborne, the deputy Chairman of the Debating Society, the greater portion of whose introductory remarks were confined to a eulogistic appreciation of Alderman Bennett's honesty and sincerity of purpose. Dealing with the subject down for discussion he expressed re- gret that it should have been more a party question, an expression which was endorsed unanimously by those present. Alderman BENNETT at once showed himself an enthu- siastic imperialist, who, to use his own words, believed ' that, if properly united, the British Empire would practically have in its own hands the future of the world. This is one of Aldermanßennett's great ideals and no one who listened to his speech could doubt his earnestness. At the outset he said" I sometimes wonder whether the empire, as it is at present, is any use to us, and I am sometimes inclined to think that it is not. Last year it cost England £lOOOOO,OOO for the Army and Navy which we have to keen for the maintenance of the Em- pire, and quite recently the same object involved us in an expenditure of £250,000,000. For the Empire to be of any material value to us, he urged, we must have an - imperial federation—a federation which would practi- cally mean that the colonies would be in the truest sense of the word, extensions of England. This im- perial federation, he contended, could only be brought about by a union for war, a customs union, and a union for consultation. Our inperial Parliament, he said, as it was at present, and our imperial army and navy, were only imperial in name and were elected and ma in- tomcod by the population contained in England. Greater and closer union, he contended, was necessary, and that could only be brourcht about by the adoption of what he described as the line of least resistance—the inauguration ~.of a commercial union by preferential treatment of the colonies. He maintained that the colon as had offered to give the mother country per- ferential treatment, and that it was our duty to accept that offer and to impose preferential tariffs. The adoption of such tariffs, he stated, would not increase the price of living in this country, using as an illustra-. tion the case of France, where. he said, in spite of an increase of 100 per cent in the tariff impomed re,,n meat,the price of that article to the consumer w aut advanced.. He stated that since Canada's preferential treatment of 'this country, our trade with the Dominion had greatly increased, and contended that the effect would be the same in the case of the other colonies, and that our trade would increase to such an extent, and even though welost the whole of our foreign trade—th,Nugh he would not admit the possibility of such a thing happening—we would not be affected. "To my mind," he said, in con- elusion," preferential trade is the only way to bring; about Imperial commercial federation. Imperial con- ference must follow, and we should have a grand united Empire in whose hands the future of the world will practically lie." The debate was soon taken up with spirit, although there was a preponderance of opinion in favour of Free Trade principles. Mr. E. Wynne Jones took Alderman ' Bennett to task for his contention that agriculture- would benefit by protective tariffs. Was the agricultural I labourer in Germany, the best protected country in the world, any better off than the same class of worker here? Not at all. What We wanted to do to increase the prosperity of England was to remove the present unequal laws. The land laws needed amendment and the mining royalties which were such a drawback to- manufacturers should be materially reduced. The first supporter of Alderman Bennett's arguments was Mr. John Gandy who declared that although he was steeped in Liberalism he believed the present system of free i \worts to be unfair. The foreigner had the run of our markets which were the finest in the world and did not contribute a farthing in taxation. He believed in taxi ng manufactured goods from abroad which we in England were able to produce. "If the Government can rise when two fishermen are shot by the Russians" said Mr. Gandy "Why can't they rise when thousands of their countrymen are starving far want of employment through foreign competition ?" There is no more sturdy supporter of Free Trade in Warrington than Councillor James Evans and he at once expressed the strong conviction that articles could not be taxed without enhancing the price to the consumer. The last tax of is. per sack of flour he said caused the price of bread to advance id. per loaf. Councillor Evans emphasised the fact that under the Protective regime in England food was much dearer. "You can neither retaliate nor protect" he said "and do justice all round." A warm support to retaliatory measures was forth- coming from Mr. HAWTHORNE, who described the pre- sent condition of things as being simply ridiculous. We would. he believed, export far more if we had" fair trade." He differed from Councillor Evans as to the effect of the is. duty on corn. The bakers' union, her said, raised the price for a week, but afterwards it went down to the usual figure. Mr. W. WRIGHT took occasion to drive home the lessons of the Sugar Convention. We were now paying .C 8,000,000 more for our sugar than before the Conven- tion, and he considered that was proving that Protective- , measures adversely affected the consumer. If the excess of England's drink bill over those of America and Ger- many could be diverted into channels of industry there would be no talk of retaliation. As one who has visited America Mr. Hamm declared himself much better satisfied with the conditions of life in this country. Mr. R. OSBORNE made a pertinent query. How, he he asked, was the English farmer to benefit by Protection if he did not get a better price for his wheat, and must not that increased price raise the cost of bread to the consumer? Armed with a Government Blue Book, Mr. J. Elwell quoted figures to support his Free Trade contentions. Depression in agricultural districts he attributes to absolete and unjust land laws and to excessive railway rates. The effect of the Sugar Convention had been to. stop the supplies from Russia and other countries, and had it not been for the Convention sugar would have been as cheap to-day as it was before. The latest re- turns in regard to our exports to Canada where we had a preferential tariff, showed that our trade with the dominion had decreased 5 per cent. while America, dispite the tariff, had been able to increase her trade by 12 per cent. In reply, Alderman BENNETT described some of the arguments on the other side as " red herrings and turnip lanterns." He was in favour of the nationalisation of land but such questions had nothing to do with the point under discussion. Preferential trade seemed to be the only possible policy for drawing the empire together and he quoted the resolution of the Colonial premiers in favour of such measures., From 1898 to 1902 our exports to Canada increased from £6,000.000 to £10,000,000. Taxation would not neces- sarily „increase the cost of the commodity to the con- sumer. It should be borne in mind that all taxes imposed, went into the Exchequer and were available for the reduction of other taxation. There were some expressions of dissent when Alder- man Bennett declared that Mr. Chamberlain had always had the interests of the workingclasses at heart, but the Alderman retorted" He has done more for them than any living man." To test the feeling of the meeting a resolution was moved by Alderman BENNETT and seconded by Mr. HA.WTHORNE : "That in the opinion of this meeting the policy of preferential trade will be beneficial to agriculture, will not materially enhance the price of food, will foster trade between the various parts of till empire and will gradually lead to true Imperial union.' The verdict was overwhelming against the motion, 8 voting in favour and 43 against. In moving a vote of thanks to Alderman Bennett the Rev. H. DIINNICO expressed himself against retaliation not so much on financial as on ethical and religious grounds. He believed it was opposed to the brotherhood of men and the beneficence of God. The vote was heartily accorded.

WONDSRFUL DISCOVERY.—This is the age of research and experiment, when all nature, so to speak. is ransacked by the scientific for the comfort and happiness of man. Science has indeed made giant strides during the past century, and among the—by no means least important—discoveries in medicine comes that of THERAPION. This preparation is unquestionably on of the most gen- uine and reliat.le Patent Medicines ever introduced, and has we understand, been used in the Continental Hospitals by Ricord, Rostan, Jobert, Velpeau, Maisonneuve, the well- known Chassalgnac, and indeed by all who are regarded as authorities in such matters, incl iding the celebrated Dille- mand, and Roux,by whom it was some time since uniformly adopted, and that it is worthy the attention of those who require such a remedy we think there is no doubt. From the time of Aristotle downwards a potent agent in the re- moval of these diseases has, like the famei philosopher's stone been the object of search of some hopeful generous minds ; and tar beyond the mere power—if such could ever have been disc wered—of transmuting the baser metal into gold is surely the discovery of a remedy so potent as to re- plenish the failing energies in the one case, and in the other so effectually, speedily and safely to expel from the system the poisons of acquired or inherited disease in all their protean forms as to leave no taint or trace behind. Such is the new French Remedy THHRA.PION, which may certainly rank with, if not take precedence of, many of the discoveries of our day, about which no little ostentation and noise have been made,and the extensive and ever-increasing demand that ha, been created for this medicine wherever introduced appears to proce that it is destined to cast into oblivion all those questionable remedies that were formerly the sole reliance of medical men. OLDHAM v. LEEDS. THREE PLAYERS ORDERED OFF. It was fortunately found possible to play this impor- tant game on the Oldham ground, which after the snow had been cleared away was found to be in good order and quite safe for this game. About 8,000 spectators witnessed the struggle, which proved fast and exciting, and though marred at times by over-keen play, was nevertheless a splendid struggle, ending in a well- deserved victory for the Headingley fifteen. At half- time nothing had been Scored. Both teams suffered badly from excitement when the issue was rejoined after the interval. The first result of the unnecessary temper displayed was the ordering off of Cash, one of the Oldham three-quarters, for striking a tackler. Just after this Wormald, 'who had left the field through a badly kicked head, rejoined his colleagues, so that instead of Leeds it was now Oldham who were a man short. Leeds had kept up their super- iority even when shorthanded, but now that Oldham were in similar plight a singular thing happened. Leeds were penalised for a scrummage infringement a few yardsinside the centre, and on the touch line, and from this difficult place Ferguson kicked a very fine goal. To be two points behind after all their attacks naturally stung the Leeds men, who thereafter assaulted the Oldham goal in desperate and sustained fashion. Old- ham's defence was sound, cool, and skilful, and it was not until seven minutes from the finish that a dashing movement begun by Mosley,' and taken part in by Phil Thomas and Llewellyn, ended in a splendid try. Just afterwards Ward, the Leeds half back, and Owens (Oldham) recei‘ ed marching orders. In the last five minutes, in which the light was very poor, Webster could be seen emerging from the ruck with the ball,and after a strong fifteen yards' run he made the Leeds victory secure by scoring close to the posts for Little- wood to add the goal points. Result :-Leeds, 1 goal and 2 tries (8 points), Oldham 1 goal (2 points). SWINTON v. HULL: A POINTLESS DRAW. This fixture took place at Swinton; before 2,000 people. Half-time arrived with no score. The Lions towards the close made big efforts to break through,and when Molyneux kicked over the line, and Wallwork reachlxl the ball first, a claim for a try was made. The referee, however, gave a dead ball, as the leather stuck in the snow close to the rails, and under Ordinary cir- cumstances would have struck them. A well-contested game ended in a pointless draw. BRADFORD v. WIGAN. ThiS engagement took place at Central Park, Wigan, where the ground, although hard at certain parts, was playable, and where some 8,000 persons assembled. During the earlier stages of the game Bradford had all the best of the play, and at length Eagers transferred smartly to Mosby, and that player passing to Dechan, the wing man raced over at the corner, Mosby just miss- ing the goal. After this Dechan was prominent again, and Wigan being penalised Mosby landed a goal. In a subsequent breakaway by the home forwards Brown was only brought down a few feet from the line, whilst a little later Smales (Bradford) in endeavouring to relieve the pressure kicked across the field to Merchant, and that player registered a try beneath the cross-bar, for Mason to add the extra points, the score at half time being I,goal, 1 try (5 -points) each.-In the second half Wigan had rather the best of the hostilities, but there was no scoring and the game ended in a draw. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. LEIGH. Played at Hull, and the Rovers scored their first league victory ageinst Leigh on the Craven-street enclosure. When half-time was reached each team had taken a penalty goal, Medley putting on the points for the Rovers, and Burgess for Leigh. Uninteresting play marked the second half. There was a sting and" go " now and then; but it provoked no excitement. To- wards the close Leigh appeared to gain the upper hand. Taking a pass from Burgess, Johnson crossed at the corner, and a try was claimed. It was, however, dis- allowed. A fine goal dropped by Sinclair put the Rovers ahead just in tinie. Result :-Kingston Rovers 2 goals (4 points), Leigh 1 goal (2 points). BATLEY v. WAKEFIELD TRINITY. This match at Mount Pleasant was well attended, bu it was primarily a forwardione and very little good back play was witnessed. A pointless draw was the result.

The Examiner Saturday, December 3 1904 RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT 1 COUNCIL. Damages to a Motor Car. COMPENSATION CLAIMED. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural. Di- strict Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday. There were present :—Messrs. S. Woodward (in the chair), C. Roylance, H. Eyes, P. Mounfield, G. Egerton, Warbur- ton, A. Broome, J. H. Davies, T. Wright, S. Woodward, G. Pilling, E. Bretherton, C. Horton' J. Spruce, J. Rutter, J. Hallows, J. Whitley. R. Billington, J. Mounfield, J. B. Chadwick, G. F. Ashton (clerk). NV. E. Hough (assistant clerk), J. Swinton (surveyor), J. Farrington (inspector), and Dr. Adams (medical officer of health). COUNTY COUNCIL EXPENDITURE. Thb Clerk submitted the following details of the new County rate :—General County purposes, £2,098 19s. 9d.; general police purposes, £233 3s. 7d. ; police district purposes, £766 is. 7d. ; general elementary education, £2,798 14s. 3d,; general higher education, £932 18s. id.; elementary purposes. £3O is. 6d. ; total, £6,859 18s, 9d. The last amount is a new item, and with its inclusion the net decrease as compared with the last balf-year is £1.79 16s. 4sl. The Clerk reported that a Hundred Bridges Rate fo r the Hundred of Buckiow of one sixteenth of a penny in the £, producing £46 us. 6d., had been levied. HELSBY SEWAGE SCHEME. A DELAY. A letter was read from the Engineer of the Sewerage system suggesting that the carrying out of the scheme be deferred until next spring as the cost would then be less than if the work were done during the- winter months. It was resolved that the suggestion be adopted. MOTOR CAR DAMAGED. COMPENSATION CLAIMED. Messrs. A. Browne and Co., solicitors, Warrington, wrote claiming £lO on behalf of Mr. Heyl-Dia, of Stretton for damages alleged to have been caused to the tyres of his motor car by newly cut macadam stones in the road at Stretton being left unrolled, unsanded and ungravelled on November 14th. Mr. Swinton said that none of the District Council roads at Stretton had had macadam placed upon them, and none required rolling on the 14th November. He had done no road repairing at all in that district. Mr. Billington : It is evidently the County Council. Mr. Heyl-Dia has got hold of the wrong people this time. Mr. Woodward: I think we can reply stating that none of our roads in the neighbourhood of Stretton have been recently macadamed and that we cannot therefore be held responsible for the damage to the motor tyres. It was decided to reply in the manner suggested by the chairman. RESIGNATION OF MR. COLLIER. Mr. Collier, of Helsby wrote resigning his seat on the Council. He did so,he said, with deep regret, on account of ill health. He thanked the members of the Council and the officials for the kindness which had been ex- tended to him while he had been connected with the Board. It was decided to accept the resignation. TILE ACETYLENE GA S PLANT. The clerk reported that an inquiry had been held at the Workhouse into the applicati on of the Board for power to borrow £3OO for an acetylene gas plant at the new hospital. The Local Government Board Inspector had instructed him to make application for £4OO as the plant would cost over £3OO. It was decided to amend the application to one of £4OO. Mr. Woodward reported that work at the hospital was progressing favourably. SMALLPDX AT MOORE. Dr. Adams reported that during the past fortnight a case of smallpox had occurred at Moore. The patient had been removed to the Isolation Hospital. Several cases of diptheria had occurred at Frodsham and on account of the prevalence of that disease and of scarlet fever, he recommended the closing of all the schools in that district until the Christmas holidays. The Chairman asked what steps were taken with regard to the disinfecting and cleaning of the schools which -.,ere closed. Dr. Adams said the schools would be disinfected as a matter of course. When that had been done the school managers could cleanse and limevvash the schools at their option. Mr. Woodward said he had not been satisfied for some years with the course taken with regard to the disinfec- tion and cleansing of the schools. The periodical out- break of epidemics pointed to some hotbed,of latent disease. He moved that in all cases where schools were closed they be thoroughly disinfected and limewasbed. Mr. Pilling seconded and the proposition was carried. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Fortnighly Meeting. The fortnighly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday, when there were present Messrs. A. R. Norman (in the chair), C. Roylance, B. Byes, J.Mounfield, G.Egerton Warburton, A. Broome, J. H. Davies, T. Wright, S. Woodward, G: Pilling, E. Bretherton, C. Horton, J. Spruce, V. M. Morris, J. Rutter, J. Hallows, R. Billington, J. Moun- field, J. Whitley, J. B. Chadwick, G.F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), and Cunnah (master of the Workhouse.) DEATH OF THE WORKHOUSE CHAPLAIN. Before the commencement of the ordinary business the Chairman remarked that it was their meloncholy duty to record the death—and he was sure they did so with the deepest regret—of the Chaplain to the Work- house. The painful suddenness of the circumstances tinder which Mr. Bennett was called away intensified the grief caused to those friends and relatives who were left behind. He was sure they would all wish to express their deepest sympathy with the relatives. Personally he had not had the pleasure of the acquaintance of Mw. Bennett but those ' who had spoke in the highestterms of his geniality and kindness. He would ask them to join with him in passing a resolution of sympathy with the relatives in the great trouble they had been called upon to bear. The resolution was carried in silence. Mr. Norman announced that it was intended to erect a memorial to Mr. Bennett in the Church at Little Legh. RESIGNATION OF MR. JOHN COLLIER. Mr. J. Collier, Helsby, wrote resigning his seat on the Council on account of continued ill-health. The resignation was accepted. CHRISTMAS FARE AT THE WORKHOUSE. It was decided to again supply special food to the inmates of theiworkhouse on Christmas Day. The menu on that day for dinner will be roast beef, plum pudding, coffee or tea, and in the evehing tea, snuff and tobacco will be provided. The children will be given sweets and oranges. LOCAL GOVERNMENT IiOARD IN4iPESTOR'S VISIT. Mr. B. T. Dewey, Local Government Board Inspec- tor, who was present at the meeting, said he must con- gratulate the Board upon the lowness of pauperism in their district, He had been through the !louse and had found everything in good order, though he was dis- appointed to find very little progress had been made in the carrying out of what to him were some necessary additions to the hospital., in the shape of the provision of new lying-in wards and a nurses home. Their present lying-in wards were obsolete. Be understood an archi- tect had been requested to prepare plans for a surses home, and he hoped the work would be got well in hand shortly after Christmas.
